lessonKeywords.description: the way elements like lines, shapes, or colours are arranged to create a visual beat
a style of art-making that captures the movement of the artist.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Rhythm is created by repeating elements to create a visual tempo or beat
Rhythm can be created through line, colour, shape, pattern and composition
Rhythm helps guide the viewer's eye around a piece rather than settling on a particular focal point.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Rhythm is a visual beat that utilises pattern and repetition across an artwork to direct your eye across the work.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Rhythm is just another way of saying pattern

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can manipulate wire and paper to produce rhythm in a sculpture.

teacherTips.teacherTip: You could experiment widely here with the materials used in the sculpture. Nylon tights can help create forms as would mod rock. Clay / plasticine could be used as an alternative base.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Proportion in Western art is the size and relation of different parts in a piece of art to each other
Western ideas of proportion can aid in drawing mathematically and accurately, but they can embed ideas of the 'norm'
Rules of proportion change depending on the culture
We can play with proportion to create new ways of looking at a subject

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Proportions are relative to the unique form you are observing. They relate to the different sizes of the different parts but may be different for each person, place or object
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Proportions are set rules and always apply

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can create a drawing using proportions and distort them for effect.

teacherTips.teacherTip: It is important to draw out the differences between Western and non-Western methods of proportion. Avoid descriptions of 'ideal' proportions and reference differences when discussing Western approaches to proportion.

lessonKeywords.description: using different elements to create visual interest and complexity in a work
uses the elements of art, to create ideas or feelings rather than realistic pictures of things.
when you place very different things next to each other to make each one stand out more.
to put two different things side by side to highlight how they are different

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Variety is the use of different elements to create visual interest and complexity in a work
Variety can be achieved by using different colours, shapes, sizes, textures, lines and materials
Variety can be created by contrasting elements such as light/dark, rough/smooth, or large/small

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Artwork that employs variety can do so in a unified way to still create work that is cohesive.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: For artwork to employ variety, it needs to be overwhelming or not unified.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can understand and apply variety in my artwork

teacherTips.teacherTip: It will help if you have a range of found objects or materials with relief surfaces that you can print with. Examples include - bubblewrap, relief wallpaper, pen lids, rulers, shoes, packaging, string etc.

lessonKeywords.description: how heavy or solid an object feels or looks.
how heavy or light an element looks in an image
the empty space around objects in an artwork
the style and arrangement of text in design

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Mass relates to solid matter, but in an artistic sense it refers to visual weight
Objects with more mass are more likely to grab the viewer's attention
Graphic design uses mass to determine what will carry the most significant visual weight

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Whilst an object in real life may have a certain physical mass, if it is depicted in an image its visual weight might not represent this physical mass accurately. Especially compared to other items. This is due to the use of visual elements.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: An object has the same mass whether in real life or in a 2D representation.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use visual weight to create a typographic design

teacherTips.teacherTip: This lesson demonstrates how to work with a gelli plate or just with stencils. You can make DIY gelli plates with many tutorials available online. A damp cloth is best used to clean the plate and roller and to tidy up edges. Some glossy magazines work better for gelli prints than others.

lessonKeywords.description: elements are arranged so the artwork feels stable and even
elements are different and not the same on both sides
the same on both sides when split down the middle, creating a mirror image that looks balanced.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Balance is the visual weight of each element and how it is distributed to make the composition feel stable.
Balance in an art work helps to lead the viewer's eye around the artwork and create a sense of unity.
Creating work that is imbalanced can be used to depict unsettled emotions in an artwork.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Asymmetrical designs can use visual weight to create a type of balance even if the work is different on both sides.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Asymmetrical designs don't balance.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can produce examples of balance in 2D and 3D forms.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Explore your suuroundings for interesting materials that could be used for students to experiment with balance in their sculptures. Artists are referenced within the deck. It would enhance the lesson to review these artists and share their work visually with students.

lessonKeywords.description: the distance between the background and the front of an image
the area at the front of the picture space
replicates how your eye sees a scene with more colour and detail towards the front

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Depth is the illusion of distance between the foreground and background of a composition on a flat surface
There are several ways of creating depth in an image, such as overlapping objects
Shading and contrast can also be used to create an illusion of depth

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Depth can be entirely imaginary or realistic. Artists can manipulate elements to create the illusion of shapes, colours and lines standing out or recessing in an image.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Depth can only be created in a realistic scene or in a realistic way.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use a range of methods to create depth in my artwork

teacherTips.teacherTip: For Task A, consider using artworks you have seen in galleries or musuems first hand or you could use works made by older students from your school. Additional information on referenced artists can be found in the additional materials.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Scale is the relative size of an object or artwork in relation to its surroundings and to itself.
Artists can use scale to create drama or tension, or to emphasise a point.
Scale can be used to manipulate how the viewer interacts with the work.
Artists can use small components to create enormous art works.

lessons.lessonTitle: Art can change the world: text based art

lessonKeywords.description: a belief, goal, or movement that someone cares about deeply and is willing to support and defend
a short and catchy phrase that can promote an idea, message or product
a style of text where each letter is written separately and clearly using the capital letters of the alphabet

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Artists can influence change through creating artworks related to causes.
Artists make artworks about causes for many reasons, including to bring joy and raise awareness.
Slogans are effective ways for artists to communicate their message about a cause.
Block lettering is a style of text that can have great impact on the viewer as it is clear and easy to read.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: There are many reasons why artists make artworks about causes including to bring joy, to celebrate and to inspire hope.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: All artworks about causes are created to warn audiences.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can create a slogan-based artwork to influence change.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Adapt the different causes to your school and community context.

Bright, swirling patterns in the letters have impact and seem fun, but it isn't as effective at communicating the message." Thanks for having a go at this task.
In our lesson "Art Can Change the World: Text-Based Art," we've covered the following: Artists can influence change through creating artworks about causes they feel passionate about.
They can use slogans as a powerful way to communicate their messages.
Block lettering is a style of text that can have great impact on the viewer as it is clear and easy to read.
Well done, everyone, for joining in with this lesson.
I feel it is so important that we use art to change the world, and why not use text-based art? Really get our message out there with some catchy, powerful slogans.
I really enjoyed teaching you, and I hope you've enjoyed this lesson too.
Look out for slogans, stay powerful, and I'll see you at another art lesson soon.
Until then, stay creative!.

00:11:28.417 --> 00:11:30.870
"Nothing Can Separate Us," 2020,

257
00:11:30.870 --> 00:11:33.030
is one of her most well-known works.

258
00:11:33.030 --> 00:11:35.070
It uses bright colors, bold patterns,

259
00:11:35.070 --> 00:11:37.920
and this powerful slogan to spread joy and positivity

260
00:11:37.920 --> 00:11:39.330
and bring people together.

261
00:11:39.330 --> 00:11:40.323
I'm here for it.

262
00:11:41.880 --> 00:11:44.190
Bob and Roberta Smith is a British artist

263
00:11:44.190 --> 00:11:47.370
known for his bright, bold, and powerful text-based artworks

264
00:11:47.370 --> 00:11:50.100
about art-related causes.

265
00:11:50.100 --> 00:11:53.223
His paintings feature slogans in brightly colored lettering.

266
00:11:54.480 --> 00:11:57.480
In his playful work "Draw Hope," 2022,

267
00:11:57.480 --> 00:12:00.000
he uses wordplay with two meanings of draw,

268
00:12:00.000 --> 00:12:03.780
a discipline in art and the verb to pull something in.

269
00:12:03.780 --> 00:12:06.420
This communicates his message that art is important

270
00:12:06.420 --> 00:12:07.713
and gives people hope.

271
00:12:09.870 --> 00:12:11.070
Let's have a check for understanding.

272
00:12:11.070 --> 00:12:12.270
True or false?

273
00:12:12.270 --> 00:12:14.820
Lakwena Maciver and Bob and Roberta Smith

274
00:12:14.820 --> 00:12:17.970
both use colorful slogans to communicate their messages.

275
00:12:17.970 --> 00:12:20.370
Pause here and decide, is this is true or false?

276
00:12:26.880 --> 00:12:29.040
Well done if you selected True.

277
00:12:29.040 --> 00:12:31.830
Maciver's "Nothing Can Separate Us," 2020,

278
00:12:31.830 --> 00:12:34.110
uses bright colors and bold patterns,

279
00:12:34.110 --> 00:12:36.750
and Smith's "Draw Hope," 2022,

280
00:12:36.750 --> 00:12:38.350
uses brightly colored lettering.

281
00:12:39.960 --> 00:12:43.350
To write a slogan, an artist can think of important words

282
00:12:43.350 --> 00:12:44.913
associated with the cause.

283
00:12:45.780 --> 00:12:46.613
Here's Aisha:

284
00:12:46.613 --> 00:12:47.970
"The important words that I thought of

285
00:12:47.970 --> 00:12:50.700
related to my cause of every child having the right to play

286
00:12:50.700 --> 00:12:55.407
were right, play, happiness, joy, and bright."

287
00:12:56.430 --> 00:12:57.263
Here's Andeep:

288
00:12:57.263 --> 00:12:58.860
"My cause is climate change,

289
00:12:58.860 --> 00:13:01.200

290
00:13:01.200 --> 00:13:06.200
My keywords are light, off, switch, turn, save, and energy."

291
00:13:09.030 --> 00:13:11.550
To write a slogan, an artist can use rhyme,

292
00:13:11.550 --> 00:13:13.923
repeated letters, or a play on words.

293
00:13:16.170 --> 00:13:17.003
Here's Aisha:

294
00:13:17.003 --> 00:13:18.930
"I chose right and bright as they rhyme.

295
00:13:18.930 --> 00:13:20.550
I wanted to include the word play

296
00:13:20.550 --> 00:13:22.170
as that is the main point of my message.

297
00:13:22.170 --> 00:13:25.293
I added shine as it sounds positive and rhymes.

298
00:13:26.310 --> 00:13:28.887
Play is a right, so we should shine bright."

299
00:13:32.010 --> 00:13:32.843
To write a slogan,

300
00:13:32.843 --> 00:13:35.700
an artist can use between four and seven words,

301
00:13:35.700 --> 00:13:38.707
use punctuation rather than conjunctions.

302
00:13:38.707 --> 00:13:40.590
"I removed some words and the conjunction

303
00:13:40.590 --> 00:13:42.600
to make it shorter and catchier,

304
00:13:42.600 --> 00:13:44.550
Play is a right, shine bright."

305
00:13:44.550 --> 00:13:46.410
Yeah, I think that's working.

306
00:13:46.410 --> 00:13:47.467
And here's Andeep:

307
00:13:47.467 --> 00:13:49.530
"I removed some of the keywords from my list

308
00:13:49.530 --> 00:13:52.050
and decided on a simple, memorable command.

309
00:13:52.050 --> 00:13:54.150
It's almost like a protest chant.

310
00:13:54.150 --> 00:13:55.980
Turn the lights off!"

311
00:13:55.980 --> 00:13:58.203
Absolutely! Let's save energy.

312
00:13:59.820 --> 00:14:01.140
Let's have a check for understanding.

313
00:14:01.140 --> 00:14:04.560

00:14:04.560 --> 00:14:06.810
a, "Respect is something people should do

b, "Respect starts with you, pass it through,"

00:14:14.340 --> 00:14:16.020

319
00:14:16.020 --> 00:14:18.330
Pause here while you decide which is an effective slogan

00:14:18.330 --> 00:14:19.713
for respecting others.

321
00:14:25.680 --> 00:14:27.120
Well done if you went for answer b.

322
00:14:27.120 --> 00:14:30.030
Indeed, "Respect starts with you, pass it through"

323
00:14:30.030 --> 00:14:32.013
is pretty effective as a slogan.

324
00:14:33.360 --> 00:14:35.610
And now it's time for your next task.

325
00:14:35.610 --> 00:14:38.790
Write a slogan that communicates your cause effectively.

326

You could think of important words associated to your cause,

327
00:14:43.260 --> 00:14:46.830
use rhyme, repeated letters, or a play on words,

328
00:14:46.830 --> 00:14:48.603
use between four and seven words,

329
00:14:49.530 --> 00:14:51.870
use punctuation rather than conjunctions.

330
00:14:51.870 --> 00:14:54.210
So pause here while you have a go at this task.

331
00:14:54.210 --> 00:14:55.910
I'll see you when you're finished.

332
00:15:01.680 --> 00:15:03.150
It's good to be back with you.

333
00:15:03.150 --> 00:15:05.220
How did you get on with that task?

334
00:15:05.220 --> 00:15:07.740
You may have tried a few ideas before deciding on one,

335

and there are many possible outcomes,

336
00:15:09.120 --> 00:15:10.770
but you might have something like this.

We've got "Respect starts with you, pass it through,"

00:15:18.180 --> 00:15:19.263
Great slogans.

341
00:15:20.700 --> 00:15:22.500
And now we're on to our final learning cycle,

342
00:15:22.500 --> 00:15:24.063
styles that impact the viewer.

00:15:37.657 --> 00:15:39.450
"Yes, if the text was really small,

they wouldn't be able to read it."

00:15:41.587 --> 00:15:44.070
"If I see colorful text, I think of positive things,

351
00:15:44.070 --> 00:15:45.750
so I think it can."

352
00:15:45.750 --> 00:15:46.800
What do you think?

353
00:15:46.800 --> 00:15:48.450
Do you agree with these ideas?

354
00:15:48.450 --> 00:15:50.150
Pause here and share with someone.

355
00:15:55.620 --> 00:15:57.270
Thanks for sharing.

356
00:15:57.270 --> 00:15:58.740
The style of text is important

357
00:15:58.740 --> 00:16:01.020
in effective communication of a slogan.

358
00:16:01.020 --> 00:16:03.003
Which of these has more impact and why?

359
00:16:03.870 --> 00:16:05.570
Pause here and share with someone.

360
00:16:12.450 --> 00:16:15.570
I wonder if you selected the text on the right.

361
00:16:15.570 --> 00:16:18.510
This style of text is called block lettering.

362
00:16:18.510 --> 00:16:20.190
Block lettering is a style of text

363
00:16:20.190 --> 00:16:22.800
where each letter is written separately and clearly

364
00:16:22.800 --> 00:16:24.903
using the capital letters of the alphabet.

365
00:16:25.740 --> 00:16:28.680
It's often used for headings, signs, slogans, and posters

and can have great impact on the viewer

as it's clear and easy to read.

Let's have a check for understanding.

00:16:34.440 --> 00:16:35.760
Complete the sentence:

00:16:35.760 --> 00:16:37.350
The style of text where each letter

00:16:37.350 --> 00:16:38.910
is written separately and clearly

00:16:38.910 --> 00:16:41.760
using the capital letters of the alphabet is called...

373
00:16:41.760 --> 00:16:43.713
Pause here and complete the sentence.

00:16:49.320 --> 00:16:50.730
It's called block lettering.

375
00:16:50.730 --> 00:16:54.060
Well done if you completed the sentence in this way

376
00:16:54.060 --> 00:16:55.860
with these words.

377
00:16:55.860 --> 00:16:57.180
To draw block lettering,

378
00:16:57.180 --> 00:16:59.550
artists can use a ruler and pencil

379
00:16:59.550 --> 00:17:01.140
to draw parallel guidelines,

380
00:17:01.140 --> 00:17:04.440
approximately the height that they want the letters,

00:17:04.440 --> 00:17:07.833
and then draw the word using separated, capitalized letters.

382
00:17:10.710 --> 00:17:12.270
Draw another line for each letter,

383
00:17:12.270 --> 00:17:14.370
parallel from the original line,

384
00:17:14.370 --> 00:17:17.070
and join the ends of each letter with a straight line.

385
00:17:18.930 --> 00:17:21.570
Artists rub out any internal lines within the letters

386
00:17:21.570 --> 00:17:24.603
for the final stage of creating block lettering.

387
00:17:25.980 --> 00:17:27.300
Aisha has used a ruler

388
00:17:27.300 --> 00:17:29.880
to ensure that the spacing and size of her block lettering

389
00:17:29.880 --> 00:17:31.080
is consistent.

390
00:17:31.080 --> 00:17:32.823
She then transfers the text.

391
00:17:34.500 --> 00:17:35.340
Artists think carefully

392
00:17:35.340 --> 00:17:37.770
about the surfaces used in their artworks.

393
00:17:37.770 --> 00:17:39.720
Our choices of color, tone, and texture

00:17:39.720 --> 00:17:40.983
all impact the viewer.

Here's Aisha:

00:17:42.893 --> 00:17:44.580
"I prepared a ground for my artwork

by using washes of warm colors.

I wanted the background to feel positive like the sun.

I kept the washes light

401
00:17:56.190 --> 00:17:58.320
Consideration of the principles of art,

balance, and contrast

00:17:59.760 --> 00:18:02.013
can help to bring emphasis to your slogan.

to contrast with the soft background.

00:18:07.890 --> 00:18:09.210
I hope that it reminds the viewer

of grass and outdoor play."

00:18:11.490 --> 00:18:13.053
It's a really nice association.

00:18:14.400 --> 00:18:16.980
How successfully has Andeep used balance and contrast

00:18:16.980 --> 00:18:18.810
to bring emphasis to his slogan?

411
00:18:18.810 --> 00:18:21.263
Pause here and share with someone what do you think.

Thanks for sharing.

"The warm, limited color palette suggests energy and heat

and reminds me of global warming.

I think the darker red at the bottom needs to contrast more

00:18:42.060 --> 00:18:43.920
Let's have a check for understanding.

00:18:52.050 --> 00:18:53.450
Pause here while you decide.

00:18:59.370 --> 00:19:01.470
Well done if you selected answer c.

00:19:01.470 --> 00:19:04.083
Indeed, this is an example of block lettering.

425
00:19:05.460 --> 00:19:07.800
And now it's time for your next task.

00:19:13.380 --> 00:19:15.207
First of all, have a go at drawing a slogan

00:19:15.207 --> 00:19:16.753
using block lettering.

00:19:16.753 --> 00:19:20.920
Pause here, and I'll see you when you're finished.

00:19:24.671 --> 00:19:25.795
It's good to be back with you.

00:19:25.795 --> 00:19:27.390
How did you get on with drawing your slogan

00:19:27.390 --> 00:19:29.640
using block lettering?

00:19:29.640 --> 00:19:31.290
You may have drawn something like this.

00:19:31.290 --> 00:19:32.197
Here's Aisha:

00:19:32.197 --> 00:19:34.410
"I drew my block lettering onto plain paper

using a pencil and ruler

00:19:36.000 --> 00:19:37.410
to ensure that it was straight

00:19:37.410 --> 00:19:39.240
and that the text was aligned.

I then rubbed out all of the pencil guidelines."

For the next part of your task,

I would like you to create a ground or select the surface

00:19:45.960 --> 00:19:48.450

00:19:48.450 --> 00:19:51.210
You should consider the choice of materials

00:19:51.210 --> 00:19:54.300
and whether your slogan will be able to stand out,

446
00:19:54.300 --> 00:19:56.250
consider how the color, texture, and tone

00:19:56.250 --> 00:19:57.753
can support your message.

Transfer your slogan to a dry prepared ground or surface.

449
00:20:01.950 --> 00:20:04.793
Pause here while you have a go at this part of your task.

450
00:20:11.190 --> 00:20:12.270
It's good to be back with you.

451
00:20:12.270 --> 00:20:14.790
How did you get on with that part of your task?

452
00:20:14.790 --> 00:20:15.623
Here's Aisha:

453
00:20:15.623 --> 00:20:17.580
"I created a warm toned background

00:20:17.580 --> 00:20:19.650
which would feel positive like the sun.

455
00:20:19.650 --> 00:20:21.570
I then transferred the outline of the text

456
00:20:21.570 --> 00:20:24.327
to the painted ground once it had dried."

457
00:20:26.580 --> 00:20:28.530
Next, I would like you to add color and pattern

458
00:20:28.530 --> 00:20:31.860
to communicate your message and inspire change.

459
00:20:31.860 --> 00:20:32.693
Pause here while you have a go

460
00:20:32.693 --> 00:20:34.383
at this final part of your task.

461
00:20:40.890 --> 00:20:42.480
It's good to be back with you.

462
00:20:42.480 --> 00:20:43.860
This is what Aisha has come up with.

463
00:20:43.860 --> 00:20:44.827
Let's hear from her.

464
00:20:44.827 --> 00:20:45.810
"I used a bright green

00:20:45.810 --> 00:20:47.970
to stand out from the softer background.

00:20:47.970 --> 00:20:50.250
It reminds me of grass and being active outside

00:20:50.250 --> 00:20:51.630
which supports the message."

468
00:20:51.630 --> 00:20:53.193
It's all coming together.

00:20:55.987 --> 00:20:57.840
"I also edited my work digitally

00:20:59.340 --> 00:21:01.440
Bright, swirling patterns in the letters

have impact and seem fun,

474
00:21:07.230 --> 00:21:09.810
Thanks for having a go at this task.

475
00:21:09.810 --> 00:21:12.630
In our lesson "Art Can Change the World: Text-Based Art,"

476
00:21:12.630 --> 00:21:14.130

477
00:21:14.130 --> 00:21:16.710
Artists can influence change through creating artworks

478
00:21:16.710 --> 00:21:19.110

479
00:21:19.110 --> 00:21:20.040
They can use slogans

480
00:21:20.040 --> 00:21:23.220
as a powerful way to communicate their messages.

00:21:23.220 --> 00:21:24.750
Block lettering is a style of text

00:21:24.750 --> 00:21:26.520
that can have great impact on the viewer

as it is clear and easy to read.

484
00:21:29.130 --> 00:21:31.050
Well done, everyone, for joining in with this lesson.

485

I feel it is so important that we use art

to change the world,

488
00:21:37.110 --> 00:21:38.520
Really get our message out there

489
00:21:38.520 --> 00:21:40.833
with some catchy, powerful slogans.

490
00:21:41.940 --> 00:21:43.110
I really enjoyed teaching you,

491
00:21:43.110 --> 00:21:45.270
and I hope you've enjoyed this lesson too.

492
00:21:45.270 --> 00:21:47.490
Look out for slogans, stay powerful,

00:21:50.850 --> 00:21:52.383

lessonKeywords.description: art that does not depict a recognisable picture, place, person or object in the real world
art that is purposefully temporary, work that will change over time
an art form based on designed activities on film or confined to a time and place

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Not all art is representational or permanent, some forms of art push 'traditional' boundaries.
Abstract art does not depict a recognisable picture, place, person or object in the real world.
Performance art happens live and is constantly changing.
Ephemeral art doesn’t last forever.  It is purposefully temporary and will change over time.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Art may not be a recognisable image and may exist only in a specific timeframe.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Art should be something we instantly recognise and physically last a long time.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can discuss different artforms and use mixed media to create an abstract artwork.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Create your own abstract artwork to model to the pupils.

lessons.lessonTitle: Art, empire and museums: who owns art?

lessonKeywords.description: the gathering of art by a private or public institution
the process of a country taking over another
when an artwork or artefact is returned to the country of origin
to select artwork and organise art for presentation

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Museums and galleries have a range of artefacts from around the world and often link to histories of Empire.
Museums are rethinking the ethics behind collections in terms of colonialism.
Some indigenous communities are asking for their artefacts to be given back and this is known as repatriation.
Understanding the original purpose of artefacts is vital as this may differ to how they are shown in museum collections.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Some artwork held in the collections of public institutions in the UK were created by civilisations that were colonised by the British Empire.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: All of the artwork held in public institutions within the United Kingdom originates from there.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explore, research and curate a display showing an understanding of context and history.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Do some background research on the artefacts. For Task A, prepare options for different online gallery and museum colletions for the pupils to explore.

contentGuidance.contentGuidanceLabel: Depiction or discussion of discriminatory behaviour
contentGuidance.contentGuidanceDescription: Discriminatory behaviour or images, whether on the grounds of race, gender, disability, religion or belief or sexual orientation, or otherwise.

contentGuidance.contentGuidanceLabel: Depiction or discussion of discriminatory behaviour
contentGuidance.contentGuidanceDescription: Historic or outdated representations of people that may portray inequality or injustice.

lessons.lessonTitle: This is art: the power of collaborative making

lessonKeywords.description: working together with one or more people to communicate common meanings or achieve common goals.
a group of people who share something in common, such as a location, interests, or activities

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Artists often explore their feelings, experiences and observations of the world and communicate meaning.
Artists can collaborate and work together to communicate common meanings or achieve common goals.
When artists collaborate, they develop common values and beliefs to enable them to form a community.
The use of hands in art symbolise many things such as emotion, support, affection, beliefs and can represent community.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Art can be a collaborative process. When artists collaborate, they work together to communicate common meanings or achieve common goals.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Art can only be made by one artist, working alone.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can create a collaborative piece of work that builds community spirit.

teacherTips.teacherTip: It would be useful to consider the possibilities for the outcome beforehand, to plan for materials and facilitate group work. Task B3 can be adapted for small groups of students or whole class involvement. The materials can also be adapted as needed.

lessons.lessonTitle: “I can’t draw!" Building confidence through drawing techniques

lessonKeywords.description: exploring unusual ideas, materials, or techniques without worrying about rules or the outcome
an exact or very close copy of something. It’s made to look just like the original object or artwork
a method an artist uses to explore drawing in different ways

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Drawing can be a range of things, from creating replicas to exploring a variety of techniques.
We can build confidence in drawing by experimenting with different techniques.
Drawing with machines or objects removes control from the artist and records marks which are unexpected.
One of the most important aspects of art making and learning is that it is fun!

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Drawing can be detailed and replicate an object, but it can also be many other things. Artists often play with techniques and process to try out different ways of exploring drawing and this can lead to experimental and exciting discoveries.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Drawing has to be a replica of what is being looked at.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use a variety of drawing techniques to create different art works.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Consider the materials to be used for the drawing machines and try beforehand to make this part of the lesson manageable.

lessons.lessonTitle: Viewpoints and techniques: disability and art

lessonKeywords.description: an artist's own personal opinion, experiences and point of view
the different ways in which artists use the materials and media they work with.
controlling a brush or tool with the foot or mouth to create a painting

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: In art, a viewpoint relates to an artist’s personal opinions, experiences and point of view.
Art by disabled artists gives the audience powerful ways to think about viewpoints as it shows their unique experiences.
Art by disabled artists may use different techniques to share their viewpoint.
Mouth and foot painting are techniques where the brush is controlled with the foot or mouth to create a painting.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Art is for everyone whatever their circumstances and is not always created through using hands. Artists can create art in innovative ways without using hands.  Art is a way for all of humanity to express their viewpoints and diverse experiences.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Art must be created with the hands.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explore how artists with disabilities share their viewpoints.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Encourage discussion amoungst pupils about their viewpoints and opinions of a view or subject local to your context.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Appliqué has been used throughout the centuries, using various techniques for both functional and artistic purposes.
You can create varied designs with appliqué using different methods of stitch and also by bonding fabric.
A template is often used to help replicate shapes at the correct size.
Felt is a popular material for appliqué because it’s thick and easy to work with.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Appliqué goes beyond just decorating fabric, it's a powerful form of art that can reflect cultural heritage.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Appliqué is just a form of decorating fabric and has no connection to colour or culture.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Embroidery has been used throughout the centuries to produce functional and artistic outcomes.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Embroidery goes beyond just being a decorative process, it is a powerful form of art that can reflect cultural heritage.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can make an embroidery sampler to practice different stitches.

teacherTips.teacherTip: If an embroidery hoop cannot be used to keep fabric taut, thicker pieces of fabric such as felt can be used instead. Thicker fabrics make it easier to have more control when sewing.

lessonKeywords.description: a traditional Japanese method of folding, twisting, or binding fabric before dyeing

a design that repeats

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Dyeing is the process of applying colour to textiles, fibres, or materials using natural or synthetic dyes

By using natural dyes you can achieve a range of colours

containing leaves, flowers and plants

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Printing with botanical forms allows artists to create environmentally friendly art.
Printing techniques create unique textures that are difficult to achieve with other techniques.
Artists use culturally traditional techniques to connect with the past whilst adding their own style.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Hammering too hard can damage the fabric or crush the plant too much, causing it to bleed or smudge. In Tataki-zome, it’s important to tap gently and evenly so the natural colours and delicate shapes of the plants transfer clearly and beautifully.

warp threads go up and down; weft threads go across

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Weaving has been used throughout the centuries, using various techniques, for both functional and artistic purposes.
You can create patterns and simple designs, like stripes and checks, when weaving.
You can apply understanding of colour theory in weaving.
Artists can take inspiration from cultural or natural motifs and apply these in their work.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Weaving goes beyond just making fabric; it’s a powerful form of art that can reflect cultural heritage.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Weaving is simply a way of creating fabric for clothing and has no connection to colour or culture.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can design a pattern to weave with paper.

teacherTips.teacherTip: When preparing a cardboard frame for the basic ‘over-under’ weaving pattern, demonstrate the importance of leaving a small section uncut at the bottom of the frame. This "anchor" helps keep the warp threads stable, making it easier for pupils to weave without the threads slipping out of place

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: The creative industry is a broad sector that includes fashion, art, music, film and design areas.
In fashion, designers often begin with a mood board to collect inspiration, colours and textures.
Fashion silhouettes explore the shape and style of a garment.
The fashion industry helps people express identity, culture and style.
Fashion can challenge or reinforce stereotypes, especially around gender, body shape and culture.

lessons.lessonTitle: Telling a story: pitching ideas to an audience
lessons.unitTitle: Being curious about spatial design and architecture

lessonKeywords.description: a short, clear presentation that explains an idea and persuades others to support or choose it.
a set of instructions or goals for a project that guides the design process.
an outline of your idea showing how it meets the brief and why it’s the best option.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Architects respond to 'requests for proposals', creating an outline of how they would meet the brief for a project.
Architects have to pitch their ideas in a clear and concise way and show how their idea is unique to win the job.
When presenting an idea, architects think of it as a story, with a beginning, middle and end.
Public speaking is a crucial skill and there are techniques we can use to help with our nerves.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: A strong pitch is more than just facts. It’s a story with a clear beginning, middle and end that shows your idea solves a problem and stands out from the rest.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Some students think pitching means just reading out facts about the design.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can create and confidently pitch a design idea.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Remind students it’s okay to pause, breathe and speak slowly — confidence comes with practice, not perfection.

lessons.unitTitle: Being curious about spatial design and architecture

lessonKeywords.description: using resources in a way that can be maintained over a long period of time without depletion or harm to the environment or future generations.
a small scale model that is used for planning and testing before a building is constructed.
the three-dimensional shape and structure of an object.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Architects make choices about the materials they use and this impacts how a building looks and feels.
Different materials allow architects to create unique designs that push visual and structural boundaries.
Architectural materials can have eco-friendly properties, enabling sustainable building designs.
Small components can be built up to make larger structures.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Buildings can be constructed from different materials. These may include traditional stone and brick or modern sustainable materials.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Buildings are all made from solid materials, brick, stone or concrete.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can create a maquette for a building design.

teacherTips.teacherTip: This lesson can be adapted to your local environment by using examples of buildings and building materials in your local environment.

lessons.unitTitle: Being curious about spatial design and architecture

lessonKeywords.description: a construction made by people, for example, a pylon or a bridge
the art and science of designing and constructing buildings and other structures

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Spatial design is the practice of creating and organising physical spaces for people to use.
Spaces and building design are influenced by the time and place you find them.
Architects draw from a range of cultural, social and historic inspirations, creating innovative and exciting designs.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Buildings are made in lots of different shapes and sizes, and are often decorated in ways that are personal to their communities.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Buildings are all rectangular in shape with pitched roofs and walls the same colour.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can understand the purpose of architecture and how it responds to its location to develop my own design.

teacherTips.teacherTip: The additional materials contain construction sheets that can be used as a basis for the built structures. However, students can also develop their own structural designs of buildings.

lessons.lessonTitle: Playing with colour in architecture and interiors
lessons.unitTitle: Being curious about spatial design and architecture

lessonKeywords.description: the art or process of designing the interior decoration of a room or building.
feeling healthy, happy and comfortable.
how we experience a space using our senses.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Architects use colour to influence mood, making spaces feel calm, vibrant, or welcoming.
Colour highlights design elements, drawing attention to specific areas or features and enhancing spatial perception.
Colour can be incorporated by using different materials, such as glass, paint or natural materials.
Colour can be used to support health and wellbeing.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Colour in a room can have a big impact on the way a space feels and how we feel in that space.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Colour is just used to make a space look good.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can create my own design using colour purposefully.

teacherTips.teacherTip: This is adaptable to your local situation. Use real-world spaces (cafes, hospitals, schools) to spark discussion on how colour affects mood and wellbeing.

lessons.lessonTitle: Technical drawing techniques to communicate ideas
lessons.unitTitle: Being curious about spatial design and architecture

lessonKeywords.description: a technique used to show depth and space by making objects appear smaller as they get further away
the spot on the horizon line where all diagonal lines appear to meet in a perspective drawing
a horizontal line that represents the viewer’s eye level in a drawing

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Perspective is important in technical drawings to show how a building will look from a specific viewpoint.
There are two key parts of a perspective drawing, the horizon line and vanishing point.
The key rule is to ensure all parallel lines converge at the correct vanishing point(s) on the horizon line.
The lines artists use in perspective drawings aren't always tight and precise.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Remember: the vanishing point sits on the horizon line, which is your eye level. All diagonal lines must meet at the vanishing point—even if it’s off the paper!
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Students often place the vanishing point too low or high, or forget to use it consistently, which causes the drawing to look distorted or unrealistic.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can produce a drawing that creates the illusion of depth and space in architectural design.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Encourage freehand sketching before using rulers to build spatial awareness. Think about buildings in your local area, in particular block shaped buildings.

lessons.unitTitle: Foundation workshops: revisiting elements of art and principles of art

lessonKeywords.description: the sense of weight or heaviness of an object or element, making it feel solid and substantial
a 2D area with a defined boundary, such as a circle
the amount of space an object occupies, giving it a three-dimensional, chunky, or filled appearance
the perception of space within an artwork, making things look far away or close up
the position of objects, relative to each other in a scene, to create depth and balance

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Mass, shape, volume and depth are used to draw the viewer’s attention to certain areas, enhancing the composition.
Depth can help to establish the relationship between different elements, making the composition more dynamic.
Variations in volume and depth can create visual intrigue, making a piece more engaging to look at.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Mass can be symbolic due to the materials used. Materials can carry more or less visual weight.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: In 3D or sculptural work, mass is just about how much it weighs and its physical presence.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use unconventional materials to explore mass, shape, volume and depth

teacherTips.teacherTip: Select a set of unconventional materials suitable for your group that challenge pupils to think about creating mass, depth, shape and volume in your specialism.

Exploring the mass and depth means paying close attention

311
00:14:15.390 --> 00:14:18.690
to the spatial relationships and visual weight in your work.

312
00:14:18.690 --> 00:14:19.620
Pause here and decide.

314

Well done if you selected true.

315

Mass means real or perceived weight,

316

and depth is about creating space within an artwork,

317
00:14:33.600 --> 00:14:35.793
so spatial relationships are key.

318

Which materials have been used here?

320

The materials you used here are glue, gesso,

322

spray paint, thread,

323

an old envelope and card, and scrim and fabric.

324
00:14:58.410 --> 00:15:00.060
Unconventional materials and techniques,

325
00:15:00.060 --> 00:15:02.940
can make your artwork feel more powerful.

326
00:15:02.940 --> 00:15:05.730
You could use thick layers of blue, spray paint,

327
00:15:05.730 --> 00:15:07.950
and things like sand, plaster or fabric

328
00:15:07.950 --> 00:15:10.110
to build up the surface.

329

This adds physical texture

330

and makes part of your piece feel more solid.

331
00:15:14.880 --> 00:15:18.690
You could combine different materials like paper, metal,

332

333
00:15:20.940 --> 00:15:22.830
This variety creates interesting layers

334
00:15:22.830 --> 00:15:25.230
and makes your work seem more three-dimensional.

335
00:15:26.910 --> 00:15:29.400
You could try impasto, thickly applied paint,

336
00:15:29.400 --> 00:15:32.463
plaster, or gesso, to create bumps and ridges.

337
00:15:33.300 --> 00:15:36.300
This textured effect makes parts of your artwork pop out,

338
00:15:36.300 --> 00:15:37.833
adding a sense of mass.

339
00:15:40.620 --> 00:15:42.060
You could, instead of brushes,

340

use objects like sponges, cloth, or even your fingers.

341
00:15:45.750 --> 00:15:48.420
This can give you unique textures and a sense of rawness

342
00:15:48.420 --> 00:15:50.733
that makes your artwork feel more intense.

Creating texture in my work will add to the sense

00:20:34.770 --> 00:20:36.900
In our lesson, mass, shape, volume, and depth,

00:20:38.730 --> 00:20:40.140
Mass, shape, volume, and depth,

00:20:45.930 --> 00:20:47.463

00:20:48.330 --> 00:20:50.700

00:20:53.670 --> 00:20:55.290

lessons.unitTitle: Foundation workshops: revisiting elements of art and principles of art

lessonKeywords.description: the arrangement of elements within a piece of art
place contrasting elements side by side to create tension, interest
what you want to achieve, i.e a goal or aim

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Artists use compositions to organise elements within their work.
Good composition can enhance balance, contrast and focus, helping to tell a story or evoke emotions.
Composition allows artists to highlight important features, create depth and establish a visual rhythm.
Compositional techniques help create a structured arrangement that guides the viewer's eye and conveys meaning.
A successful composition activates the visual language for effective communication of ideas and feelings.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: A successful composition creates structure and activates the visual language to convey meaning.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: The arrangement of the elements has no effect on the overall effectiveness of the composition.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can create considered and successful compositions using key techniques.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Think ahead to decide how best to elicit intentions from your students and how your specialism might offer ways to create quick compositional experiments.

lessons.unitTitle: Foundation workshops: revisiting elements of art and principles of art

lessonKeywords.description: a mark made by a moving point, which can vary in length, width, direction, and texture
something representing or standing for something else, for example, a heart symbol can represent love
to communicate or show something to someone i.e. sharing a message, idea, or feeling

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Line is used in different ways within each endorsement, including light drawings in photography and drawing with stitch.
The quality of a line can convey mood e.g. jagged lines might evoke tension, while smooth lines can feel calm.
Lines can also carry symbolic meanings, such as the use of horizontal lines for stability or vertical lines for growth.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Lines are vital for all work across every specialism. There are many ways line can impact your work.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Lines are only useful in drawing and painting

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can experiment to explore the effect of line in 3D space

teacherTips.teacherTip: If you are looking for a group challenge, this lesson presents a great opportunity for collaborative work.

lessons.unitTitle: Foundation workshops: revisiting elements of art and principles of art

lessonKeywords.description: ensuring the elements look like they belong together
using a range of elements to create visual interest
a visual beat made by elements in your work
how the visual weight is distributed in the artwork

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Unity brings together different elements to create a harmonious whole. It helps us understand work as a single entity.
Balance creates a sense of stability and order, making the artwork feel grounded. It can be symmetrical or asymmetrical.
Artists might use areas of light and dark or bold colour to bring unity, variety, rhythm, balance.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Pattern is an important element in art but unity can be felt without artwork looking like a repeat pattern.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Your work needs to be full of obvious pattern for it to feel unified.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can create unity, variety, rhythm and balance in experimental compositions.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Try to help students select motifs from their own creative journey to support you when marking holistically.

lessons.unitTitle: Foundation workshops: revisiting elements of art and principles of art

lessonKeywords.description: an area enclosed and defined
the three-dimensional shape and structure of an object or artwork, often showing depth, volume and mass
a connection or link between two or more things

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Shape and form are fundamental elements of design that help artists communicate ideas and emotions visually.
Different shapes can evoke specific associations or emotions.
Form gives depth and volume to a piece, making it more dynamic and realistic, especially in sculpture and painting.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Shapes are inadvertently created all the time in the gaps between objects in your composition. We call this the negative space.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Shapes are only found in the positive space made by an actual object.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can manipulate shapes and forms to develop my visual language.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Review the slide deck and tailor the outcome to your own specialism and themes. Supporting information on artists can be found in the additional materials.

lessons.unitTitle: Foundation workshops: revisiting elements of art and principles of art

lessonKeywords.description: how light or dark a colour is
what we see when light hits an object
the pure colour itself, like red or blue
how intense or vivid a colour is

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Variations in tone create the illusion of 3D space, makes objects more lifelike, and attracts attention
Colour is a powerful tool in the communication of a thought, idea or emotion
Colour encompasses both hue and tone, and its combination can influence how viewers perceive and react to the artwork.
Different colours can symbolise various ideas or emotions, allowing artists to communicate more than just the visual.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Colour is the overarching name for what we see but it is made up of hues and tones.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Hue and colour mean the same thing.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use colour and tone to express ideas and feelings in my work

teacherTips.teacherTip: This is a great lesson as a review as it encourages lots of reflection around how students are using colour to communicate.

lessons.unitTitle: Foundation workshops: revisiting elements of art and principles of art

lessonKeywords.description: a repeated design or arrangement of shapes, colours, or lines
how artists use elements like colour, shape, and pattern to communicate ideas and emotions

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Patterns create a sense of rhythm and movement, drawing the viewer's eye across the artwork.
Repeated motifs can enhance the quality of an artwork, giving it a richer, more complex appearance.
Patterns can have historical or cultural significance, allowing artists to connect with tradition or convey narratives.
Patterns can evoke feelings or memories, influencing how a viewer interacts with the piece.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Pattern can be irregular or regular.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Patterns need to be regular and ordered.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can experiment using pattern in new and exciting ways.

teacherTips.teacherTip: You could have some examples of pattern in sketchbooks or old work as live examples to explore.

lessons.unitTitle: Foundation workshops: revisiting elements of art and principles of art

lessonKeywords.description: is how something feels or looks like it would feel
the illusion of how a surface feels. For example, painting an area to look rough or shiny
something you can physically sense and touch

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Texture can make an artwork more engaging by providing a tactile quality that draws viewers in.
Different textures can evoke different feelings. For example, rough textures might convey rawness or chaos.
Texture can create contrast, emphasising certain areas or elements and adding a sense of three-dimensions.
Textures can carry meaning, reflecting concepts like decay, growth or transformation.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Texture is one of the tools artists use as a visual language to communicate.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Texture is only a visual quality, it doesn't add meaning to your work.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use texture to make my work more engaging.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Apply this lesson to your classes theme or project to encourage them to think broadly about how they apply visual language.

lessons.unitTitle: Foundation workshops: revisiting elements of art and principles of art

lessonKeywords.description: the size of an object in relation to another object or the world
a way of representing 3D space on a flat 2D surface

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Artists use proportion, scale and perspective to emphasise parts of the artwork.
Artists use proportion, scale and perspective to manipulate how the viewer interacts with the work.
Artists change the proportion, scale or perspective to develop new ideas.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: You can make very subtle changes and experiements and they can have a big impact on your work - that's the value of experimentation!
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Experiments should include radical or very exaggerated changes.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use scale, perspective and proportion to distort my work and impact how my audience feels.

lessonKeywords.description: objects made from clay that are shaped and then baked until hard.
The shape or 3D structure of an object that has height, width, and depth.
The practical use or purpose of an object.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Pottery has been around for thousands of years and is a job within the creative industries.
Pottery can take various forms and has multiple uses and functions from practical uses to artistic storytelling.
Contemporary artists use the pot in different ways to convey ideas and meaning.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: While pottery is often associated with functional items like bowls and vases, it has been used throughout history and in contemporary times as a medium for artistic expression and storytelling.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Pottery is only used for making practical items like bowls and pots, and it doesn’t have any artistic or cultural significance.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can investigate pottery and experiment with different shapes and texture to create a pinch pot.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Prepare the clay in advance by dividing it evenly into ball shaped pieces. You may need to spray lightly with water to maintain moisture or cover with a damp towel.

lessonKeywords.description: decorating the body to express who we are
an art technique where different materials are glued onto a surface to make a new artwork
an idea or belief about a group of people or an individual, that might not be true, which can lead to unfair judgments

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Body adornment is the practice of decorating or modifying the body through our hair, nails, skin, clothing or jewellery.
Body adornment is used widely across the globe in various forms and contexts.
Body adornment shows identity, including: gender, religion, family, social status and sexuality.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Body adornment often holds deep cultural, religious, or personal meaning. It can express identity, heritage, beliefs, or social status, connecting individuals to family traditions or cultural values— beyond just aesthetic appeal.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Body adornment is only about appearance or fashion trends.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use body adornment as a form of communication.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Prepare a variety of collage items and a diverse range of current beauty advertisements before the lesson.

lessonKeywords.description: a hand-made figure, human, animal, or abstract form, that is controlled by a person
regular, mathematical shapes like circles, squares, and triangles with clear, defined edges
free-flowing, irregular, and natural curves

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: A puppet is a hand-made figure, human, animal, or abstract form, that is controlled by a person.
Puppets come in different forms, they can be 2D or 3D, can be made from different materials and come in various sizes.
Puppets use human characteristics to convey a type of personality; these can play into stereotypes of people.
Puppets can tell stories, challenge ideas, and promote political change.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Different cultures use puppets to tell important stories, share cultural traditions, perform rituals, and even address social or political issues. Puppets can express powerful ideas and emotions, not just for fun but also to convey deeper messages.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Puppets are only used for children's entertainment.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can create an imaginative puppet that uses shape and pattern to tell a story.

teacherTips.teacherTip: To differentiate the task further, provide worksheets with various puppet body parts for pupils to trace or cut out to support their designs.

lessonKeywords.description: is a method of stitching layers of material together to create a blanket, often includes patterns or images
the practice of challenging traditional ideas or social norms
is a sign, object, or image that stands for something else
is the use of symbols to express deeper meanings or ideas

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Quilting is a method of stitching layers of material together to create a blanket, often includes patterns or images.
Quilting has been used by artists as a form of activism, to raise awareness about social issues.
Quilting is often collaborative with several people working on a project together.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: While quilts are often used for warmth or decoration, many artists use quilts to share powerful stories and messages. Quilts can be a way for artists to speak out about important issues and make sure voices are heard.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Quilts are just blankets or decorative items and don’t have any deeper meaning.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain what subversive quilting is and design a quilt square to tell a story.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Having computer access would help pupils research a range of symbols for their quilt story design.

contentGuidance.contentGuidanceLabel: Depiction or discussion of discriminatory behaviour
contentGuidance.contentGuidanceDescription: Historic or outdated representations of people that may portray inequality or injustice.

lessonKeywords.description: the process of making fabric by interlocking two sets of yarn or threads
vertical threads that run up and down in weaving
horizontal threads that run up and down in weaving
long, continuous strands of fibers used in textiles

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Weaving is a method of making fabric by interlacing two sets of yarns or materials at right angles.
Weaving is one of the oldest crafts and is practised by various communities worldwide.
Contemporary artists use different materials to weave, often giving their work deeper social or political meaning.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Weaving goes beyond just making fabric; it’s a powerful form of art that can tell stories and reflect cultural heritage.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Weaving is simply a way of creating fabric for clothing and has no connection to storytelling or culture.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can create weavings using different techniques and reflect on how materials can convey meaning.

teacherTips.teacherTip: When preparing a cardboard frame for the basic ‘over-under’ weaving pattern, demonstrate the importance of leaving a small section uncut at the bottom of the frame. This "anchor" helps keep the warp threads stable, making it easier for pupils to weave without the threads slipping out of place.

lessonKeywords.description: the designing and hand making of individual objects and artefacts
physical items used to achieve a goal
the resources that artists, craftspeople and designers use to create work
designed to be practical and useful rather than simply attractive

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Craft is designing and hand-making unique objects, building creative, intellectual, and practical skills with tools.
Craft was seen as lesser than Fine Art because it was functional and often practised by women.
Artists like William Morris challenged the divide between art and craft, blurring the boundaries in their work.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Craft is the creation of objects and artworks requiring both artistry and technical skill. It includes both functional and non-functional items and embraces contributions from all genders and communities.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Craft is only about making functional objects and is less important than Fine Art.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can define what craft is and challenge traditional boundaries.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Computer access may be helpful to support design ideas.

lessons.lessonTitle: Mixed media sculptures: combining diverse materials and techniques

lessonKeywords.description: combining materials so they work visually and physically
testing new techniques, found objects, or recycled elements

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: The choice of materials becomes part of the message; each one can evoke different emotions, histories, or associations.
Successful mixed media sculpture depends on understanding how to physically and visually integrate different materials.
Mixed media expands creative boundaries, encouraging experimentation, recycled elements, or unconventional techniques.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Each material should have a purpose — it must add meaning or structure, not just make it look busy.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Mixed media just means throwing lots of materials together.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can choose and combine materials to make a mixed media sculpture that is expressive, integrated and experimental.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Encourage students to think about why they use each material. Test small ideas first, then build bigger so their sculpture feels intentional and connected.

lessons.transcript_sentences:
Hi, I'm Miss Blue, and I'm really excited to be learning with you today.
I hope you find our lesson as interesting as I do.
Let's get started.
The outcome of this lesson is: "I can choose and combine materials to make a mixed-media sculpture that is expressive, integrated, and experimental.
Let's go over our keywords.
Integration: combining materials so that they work visually and physically.
Experimentation: testing new techniques, found objects, or recycled elements.
Let's go over our lesson outline.
We'll start with exploring materials and meaning.
So what do these objects make you think or feel? We have two bottles, a rusty chain, a pile of knitted cloth, and a close-up of a tree.
Pause the video while you come up with a response.
Let's go over some ideas.
Jacob says, "The plastic bottle makes me think of waste and recycling.
The rust makes it look old, like it has history." Sofia says, "The folded blanket feels safe and comforting.
The wood feels old.
It could symbolize aging or time passing." Mixed media sculptures.
Mixed media sculpture brings together different materials to create new meanings, emotions, and possibilities.
Artists use many different materials to tell stories and share ideas.
Each material carries feelings, memories, or cultural meaning.
Mixing materials can create new possibilities and surprising effects.
Sculptures can be powerful when everyday or recycled objects are transformed.
Many artists from around the world have used mixed media, combining everyday, recycled, or unexpected materials to express powerful ideas.
This includes: Tracey Emin, who often uses everyday and personal materials such as fabric, neon, found objects, and even her own belongings, to create deeply emotional works.
By combining these materials, she explores themes of memory, identity, and vulnerability.
Han Sai Por is known for working with stone and natural materials, sometimes combining them with industrial elements.
Her sculptures reflect on the environment, human impact on nature, and the relationship between organic and man-made forms. Lygia Clark created interactive sculptures using simple everyday materials like rubber, fabric, and cardboard.
By inviting people to handle and manipulate her works, she challenged the boundary between art and life, focusing on healing, play, and participation.
Tony Heaton often uses recycled or everyday objects, including old wheelchairs, walking sticks, and disability aids, in his sculptures.
These materials are reimagined to comment on disability, access, and social barriers, turning lived experiences into powerful visual statements.
Let's think about how materials carry meaning.
The materials chosen for a sculpture can change how we feel about it and the stories it tells.
Every material has associations.
Fabric can remind us of home, comfort, or memory.
Metal can suggest strength, industry, or even coldness.

lessons.lessonTitle: Carving techniques: from concept to finished sculpture

lessonKeywords.description: a small 3D model used to test and refine sculptural ideas
the natural pattern and direction in wood or stone guiding carving
removing large material areas before refining detail

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Artists typically begin with sketches, maquettes, or 3D references to guide the process and avoid costly mistakes.
Skilled carvers learn how to read the grain, texture, or fault lines in the material to avoid cracking or chipping.
Carving typically moves from blocking out large forms to gradually refining shapes, adding surface details and textures.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Skilled carving is deliberate - starting with planning, respecting grain, and refining in controlled stages.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Carving is just about 'chipping away' randomly until a shape appears.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can plan, test and carve a form, showing awareness of material properties and moving from block to detail.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Encourage students to turn their work as they carve; changing the viewpoint helps them see emerging forms and avoid overworking one side. Ensure safety guidelines are adhered to and safety equipment is worn appropriately.

lessons.lessonTitle: Deepening the understanding of the principles of 3D sculpture

lessonKeywords.description: the empty space around and within a sculpture, that shapes its impact
how individual parts of a sculpture relate in size to each other and the whole
the practical method used e.g. carving, modelling, assembling, casting

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: 3D sculpture is not just about outer shape but how it occupies space and how negative space contributes to its impact
Realistic or abstract, understanding proportions relating and scale of the piece is essential for coherence and impact.
Deepening knowledge of techniques allows for more effective expression and creativity.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Sculpture also uses negative space, scale and proportion to create meaning and viewer impact.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Sculpture is only about the outside shape.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can analyse how space, proportion and technique affect sculpture, and apply this to my own creative making.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Model exploration rather than finished outcomes. Give short demonstations and allow pupils to problem solve, take risks, and refine their ideas through independant making.

lessons.lessonTitle: Exploring assembling: creating sculptures from multiple parts

lessonKeywords.description: how elements relate in space, rhythm and balance within a sculpture
combining mixed or found objects into a new three-dimensional work
the strength, balance and durability of how sculpture arts connect

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Working with multiple parts needs a strong composition, the elements relate spatially, rhythmically and aesthetically.
Assembling invites experimentation with different materials, objects and reconfigurable forms.
Artists must plan how parts fit together and support one another, ensuring the sculpture is stable and durable.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Assemblage is not random; artists carefully plan how objects interact. Each choice affects rhythm, meaning, balance and stability.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Assemblage is just sticking things together randomly.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can create a sculpture from multiple parts that demonstrates strong composition, explores material play and is stable and durable.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Encourage risk-taking but also push students to refine. Remind them that 'play' is part of creativity, but they must stem back, reflect and adjust to improve balance, rhythem and durability.

lessons.lessonTitle: Thematic development: crafting expressive and cohesive sculptures

lessonKeywords.description: using objects, forms or materials to suggest deeper meaning
repetition or flow that guides the viewer's eye across the sculpture
the purpose or message the artist wants to communicate

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: A theme needs intentional choices in form, material, and symbol to communicate meaning and resonate.
Repetition, contrast, and rhythm reinforce the theme and connect all parts of a sculpture intentionally.
A sculpture reflects the artist’s intent but must also consider how viewers interpret and respond emotionally.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: A sculpture is powerful when choices are intentional. Materials, forms, and symbols must link clearly to a theme; without this, the work can feel random instead of meaningful.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Choosing intresting materials or shapes is enough to make a sculpture 'meaningful'.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use form, material, and symbolism with rhythm and contrast to make a sculpture that shares my intent and connects with viewers.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Encourage students to keep linking back to their sketchbooks - every choice should be justified by their theme. Ask probing questions to push intentionality and deeper thinking.

lessons.lessonTitle: Casting methods: reproducing and enhancing sculptures

lessonKeywords.description: hollow form used to shape liquid or pliable casting material
multiple copies of a sculpture from one mould
surface treatment (polish, paint, patina) that changes appearance and durability

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Different casting materials offer various textures, finishes, weights and durability.
Stages in model making: mouldmaking, casting, curing and finishing all require focus to ensure accuracy and quality.
Casting enables the creation of multiple copies or editions of a sculpture, making art more accessible and versatile.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Different materials give different textures, weights, weights and finishes - same mould different outcomes.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: All casts look the same no matter what material is used.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain and apply casting stages to create a small sculpture, experimenting with materials and finishes.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Encourage risk-taking – allow students to pour or mix independently after demonstrating. Stress safety and promote self and peer reflection. Compare and contrast textures, finishes and editions made by peers.

lessons.transcript_sentences:
Hi, I'm Miss Blue and I'm really excited to be learning with you today.
I hope you find our lesson as interesting as I do.
Let's get started.
The outcome of this lesson is I can explain and apply casting stages to create a small sculpture, experimenting with materials and finishes.
Our keywords are: mould: hollow form used to shape liquid or pliable casting material; edition: multiple copies of a sculpture from one mould, finish: surface treatment, such as polish, paint, patina, that changes appearance and durability.
Casting methods: reproducing and enhancing sculptures.
Let's start with mould and materials.
What do you think these sculptures would feel like? Pause the video while you come up with a response.
Lucas says, "I think the figure sculpture would feel cold to touch.
It looks like it's metal.
The surface of the face looks smooth and the hair I think would feel grainy." Jun says, "I think the concrete would feel rough, especially in the center where the light is catching the texture." Casting: one shape, many outcomes.
Casting is a way of making a copy of an object or sculpture.
The process has four stages: model, mould, cast and finish.
Different materials change the weight, texture, and strength of the cast.
Artists use casting to make one design into many versions.
Many artists use casting in their work, including: Hew Locke, using casting and metal finishes to explore colonial histories, creating sculptures that mix beauty with critique of Empire.
David Umemoto works with concrete casting, giving his sculptures architectural forms and rich surface textures.
Karen LaMonte experiments with casting in different materials such as glass, bronze, and ceramic to explore the human figure and clothing.
Different materials can be used to make moulds: Alginate: fast, fine detail, short life.
Silicone: flexible, durable, many casts.
Latex: brush-on, flexible, weaker.
Plaster: cheap, rigid and fragile.
Clay: simple press or support moulds.
Fiberglass: strong, lightweight, large-scale.
Polyurethane: strong, detailed and less flexible, Fabric and wood: cheap, easily available.
texture, transferred to the cast, better for large scale concrete sculptures.
Different materials used to make the moulds will give a different effect to the finish on the completed cast.
Here's an example of experimenting with texture when creating a mould.
On the right, you can see concrete cast into a fabric and wood mould.
A wide variety of materials of different textures can be used to create a mould.
Have a look at these interesting picture examples of aluminum cast into a sand mould.
So why does the mould material matter? Pause the video while you come up with some ideas.
The mould material controls how much detail is captured in the cast.
Flexible moulds like silicone can pick up fine details and allow easy release.
Rigid moulds like plaster are cheaper, but may break and lose detail on undercuts.
The mould's surface quality, rough, smooth, or porous, affects the finish of the cast.
Choosing the right mould material is key for both accuracy and durability.
Let's decide if this statement is true or false.
The material of the mould has no effect on the texture or finish of the final cast.
Pause the video while you decide if this true or false.
If you said false, you would be correct.
Why? Because the mould material actually controls how much detail and texture is transferred onto the cast surface.
Creating a mould.
To create a mould, we must first create a small model to be cast.
This can be made from a number of different materials, such as clay, wax, plasticine, card, foam board, wood, or found objects.
First, you would create a small model to cast a mould using a found object like this rubber duck.
Make sure there are no undercuts, so the model can be released easily from the mould.
This is important, especially if casting in plaster.
Coat the model or object to be cast with a release agent.
Place the object into a container, making sure it's sealed to the bottom.
Pour the mould material slowly over the top and tap to release any bubbles.
Allow the mould to finally cure.
Remove the model from the mould and it is now ready to use.
Let's test your knowledge.
Put these steps in the correct order for making a mould.
A: Pour material, place in box, make model, remove model.
B: Place in box, make model, pour model, remove model.
C: Remove model, pour material, make model, place in box.
Or D: Make model, place in box, pour material, remove model.
Pause the video here while you come up with the correct answer.
If you said D, you would be correct.
The correct order is to make the model, place it in a box, pour the material, and then remove.
Your task now is to create your own model.
Select which material you will use to create your model.
Options include clay, wax, plasticine, foam board, strong card, wood, or found objects.
Consider: Undercuts.
Avoid deep overhangs that trap the mould.
Detail.
Make sure textures and shapes are clear.
Surface.
Seal porous materials so the mould doesn't stick.
Strength.
The model must hold shape when silicone or plaster is poured.
Pause the video here while you work on this task.
Your responses may have looked something like this.

Create a mould using the model created in Task A1.
Make sure there are no undercuts.

Place model inside a container.
Mix casting material.
Slowly pour materials over the model.
Tap gently to release any air bubbles.
