Another element to consider in your design

114
00:05:44.280 --> 00:05:46.473
is the use of islands and bridges.

115
00:05:47.790 --> 00:05:50.400
So here we have the outer edge

116
00:05:50.400 --> 00:05:51.753
and here's the island.

117
00:05:52.950 --> 00:05:56.400
For instance, if you cut the outer edge of the letter O,

118
00:05:56.400 --> 00:05:59.013
the inner circle, the island, will be removed.

119
00:06:02.070 --> 00:06:03.360
To counter this,

120
00:06:03.360 --> 00:06:05.250
stencil artists use bridges,

121
00:06:05.250 --> 00:06:08.190
connecting elements that hold islands in place

122
00:06:08.190 --> 00:06:10.650
and help to keep the stencil in place.

123
00:06:10.650 --> 00:06:13.380
Who can see the outer edge and island

124
00:06:13.380 --> 00:06:14.463
and the bridges?

125
00:06:15.810 --> 00:06:19.050
Consider the use of islands and bridges in your design

126
00:06:19.050 --> 00:06:21.753
to avoid losing details unintentionally.

127
00:06:25.020 --> 00:06:28.113
A well-created stencil can be used for multiple prints.

128
00:06:29.130 --> 00:06:31.440
Pause here and share with someone which of these prints

129
00:06:31.440 --> 00:06:34.863
are you most drawn towards, and why?

130
00:06:43.290 --> 00:06:44.700
Thanks for sharing.

131
00:06:44.700 --> 00:06:45.533
I'm most drawn

132
00:06:45.533 --> 00:06:48.330
towards those green letters against the white.

133
00:06:48.330 --> 00:06:50.193
Very bold and stands out clearly.

134
00:06:52.860 --> 00:06:55.080
Let's have a check for understanding.

135
00:06:55.080 --> 00:06:57.663
What material is a screen usually made from?

136
00:06:58.650 --> 00:07:00.303
Is it A, cardboard?

137
00:07:01.200 --> 00:07:04.170
B, solid plastic sheet.

138
00:07:04.170 --> 00:07:06.450
C, clear glass.

139
00:07:06.450 --> 00:07:09.810
Or D, fine mesh stretched over a frame.

140
00:07:09.810 --> 00:07:11.040
Pause here while you decide

141
00:07:11.040 --> 00:07:13.563
what material is a screen usually made from?

142
00:07:22.470 --> 00:07:25.050
Well done if you selected answer D.

143
00:07:25.050 --> 00:07:27.480
Indeed, a screen is usually made

144
00:07:27.480 --> 00:07:29.823
from fine mesh stretched over a frame.

145
00:07:33.330 --> 00:07:36.030
And now it's time for your first task.

146
00:07:36.030 --> 00:07:38.190
I would like you to create a simple stencil

147
00:07:38.190 --> 00:07:39.600
inspired by a theme,

148
00:07:39.600 --> 00:07:43.530
for example, nature, architecture, logos.

149
00:07:43.530 --> 00:07:45.843
Focus on clear shapes that will print well.

150
00:07:47.520 --> 00:07:50.010
So pause here while you have a go at this task,

151
00:07:50.010 --> 00:07:53.340
creating a simple stencil inspired by a theme.

152
00:07:53.340 --> 00:07:56.090
Enjoy your task, and I'll see you when you're finished.

153
00:08:03.780 --> 00:08:05.250
It's good to be back with you.

154
00:08:05.250 --> 00:08:06.780
How did you get on with that task

155
00:08:06.780 --> 00:08:10.050
of creating a simple stencil inspired by a theme,

156
00:08:10.050 --> 00:08:12.720
for example, nature, architecture, logos,

157
00:08:12.720 --> 00:08:15.300
focusing on clear shapes that will print well?

158
00:08:15.300 --> 00:08:17.550
You might have created something like this

159
00:08:17.550 --> 00:08:18.840
and said something like this.

160
00:08:18.840 --> 00:08:19.673
Here's Jun.

161
00:08:20.887 --> 00:08:23.850
"I made this stencil design of an autumn leaf.

162
00:08:23.850 --> 00:08:26.400
I decided to keep the overall shape simple,

163
00:08:26.400 --> 00:08:29.730
as I think this will help to create a bold print."

164
00:08:29.730 --> 00:08:31.200
You're absolutely right.

165
00:08:31.200 --> 00:08:33.693
Boldness and simplicity works really well.

166
00:08:36.480 --> 00:08:39.690
And now we're onto our next learning cycle, Screen printing.

167
00:08:39.690 --> 00:08:43.083
We are getting right into it. So excited.

168
00:08:44.460 --> 00:08:46.200
To use a screen for printing,

169
00:08:46.200 --> 00:08:49.620
ink is pushed through the screen mesh using a squeegee,

170
00:08:49.620 --> 00:08:51.753
but only where the screen allows it.

171
00:08:52.920 --> 00:08:55.110
Designs can be transferred to a screen

172
00:08:55.110 --> 00:08:57.993
using stencils or screen filler fluid.

173
00:08:59.550 --> 00:09:02.490
This process requires securing your cut stencil

174
00:09:02.490 --> 00:09:05.463
over the top of the screen using tape or clamps.

175
00:09:08.310 --> 00:09:10.320
If using screen filler fluid,

176
00:09:10.320 --> 00:09:12.630
transfer your design onto the screen

177
00:09:12.630 --> 00:09:16.023
by tracing a reference photo through the screen mesh.

178
00:09:18.690 --> 00:09:20.560
So here we see the reference photo

179
00:09:21.540 --> 00:09:22.443
being traced.

180
00:09:25.950 --> 00:09:28.470
Next, paint on the screen, drawing fluid

181
00:09:28.470 --> 00:09:30.723
into the areas you want to print through.

182
00:09:35.040 --> 00:09:36.930
Once the drawing fluid is dry,

183
00:09:36.930 --> 00:09:40.590
use a squeegee to drag the screen filler fluid across.

184
00:09:40.590 --> 00:09:43.953
Once dry, wash off the screen gently in cold water.

185
00:09:48.870 --> 00:09:50.490
Once the screen is completely dry,

186
00:09:50.490 --> 00:09:52.923
it's ready to print with screen printing ink.

187
00:09:56.701 --> 00:09:58.200
And here we can see

188
00:09:58.200 --> 00:10:01.473
the screen on the left and a print on the right.

189
00:10:04.530 --> 00:10:07.380
With the stencil and screen securely together,

190
00:10:07.380 --> 00:10:09.810
apply a thin bead of ink horizontally

191
00:10:09.810 --> 00:10:11.193
at the top of the screen.

192
00:10:12.540 --> 00:10:15.120
To press the ink through the stencil and screen,

193
00:10:15.120 --> 00:10:17.760
onto the surface underneath, use the squeegee

194
00:10:17.760 --> 00:10:20.373
to collect the line of paint and pull down.

195
00:10:22.290 --> 00:10:24.060
A pull is one movement of dragging

196
00:10:24.060 --> 00:10:26.370
across the screen with the squeegee.

197
00:10:26.370 --> 00:10:30.690
The pressure and angle control how well ink passes through.

198
00:10:30.690 --> 00:10:33.040
It's a movement to really take great care with.

199
00:10:34.260 --> 00:10:36.900
Use a smooth, even pressure with the squeegee

200
00:10:36.900 --> 00:10:39.873
and lift carefully to reveal the print underneath.

201
00:10:43.260 --> 00:10:46.260
Too much pressure pushes ink underneath the stencil,

202
00:10:46.260 --> 00:10:48.810
making the edges blur and the print messy,

203
00:10:48.810 --> 00:10:50.703
while too little will leave gaps.

204
00:10:51.720 --> 00:10:53.823
It's always about finding that middle way.

205
00:10:55.320 --> 00:10:58.110
It's also important to use the right amount of paint

206
00:10:58.110 --> 00:11:00.210
to cover all areas of the stencil,

207
00:11:00.210 --> 00:11:02.710
without running out towards the base of the print.

208
00:11:04.410 --> 00:11:07.623
Aim for consistent, even pressure for a clean result.

209
00:11:10.500 --> 00:11:12.350
Let's have a check for understanding.

210
00:11:13.740 --> 00:11:16.683
What happens if you press too hard with the squeegee?

211
00:11:18.630 --> 00:11:20.883
A, the print becomes sharper.

212
00:11:22.590 --> 00:11:26.253
B, ink floods under the stencil and edges blur.

213
00:11:27.990 --> 00:11:30.813
C, the stencil cuts through the mesh.

214
00:11:32.340 --> 00:11:35.103
D, the screen won't release any ink.

215
00:11:36.487 --> 00:11:38.130
Pause here while you decide

216
00:11:38.130 --> 00:11:40.780
what happens if you press too hard with the squeegee?

217
00:11:49.350 --> 00:11:51.300
Well done if you selected answer B.

218
00:11:51.300 --> 00:11:55.170
Indeed, ink floods under the stencil and the edges blur

219
00:11:55.170 --> 00:11:57.170
if you press too hard with the squeegee.

220
00:12:01.260 --> 00:12:04.050
Many contemporary artists use screen printing

221
00:12:04.050 --> 00:12:05.430
for graphic communication

222
00:12:05.430 --> 00:12:07.683
and contemporary fine art audiences.

223
00:12:09.039 --> 00:12:12.510
Omeima Mudawi-Rowlings incorporates screen print

224
00:12:12.510 --> 00:12:15.450
and textile-based printmaking into her practice,

225
00:12:15.450 --> 00:12:18.060
creating works that celebrate cultural heritage,

226
00:12:18.060 --> 00:12:19.803
pattern and community.

227
00:12:21.300 --> 00:12:24.300
Fae Kilburn uses linocut and screen print

228
00:12:24.300 --> 00:12:26.310
to explore themes of identity,

229
00:12:26.310 --> 00:12:28.950
accessibility and lived experience,

230
00:12:28.950 --> 00:12:32.253
often with bold compositions and tactile surfaces.

231
00:12:33.540 --> 00:12:38.040
Hend Al-Mansour employs silkscreen and relief printmaking

232
00:12:38.040 --> 00:12:40.350
to create immersive installations,

233
00:12:40.350 --> 00:12:42.000
exploring Islamic pattern,

234
00:12:42.000 --> 00:12:44.463
storytelling and feminist themes.

235
00:12:46.290 --> 00:12:49.540
So here are a few contemporary artists using screen printing

236
00:12:50.730 --> 00:12:51.990
for graphic communication

237
00:12:51.990 --> 00:12:54.093
and contemporary fine art audiences.

238
00:12:56.550 --> 00:12:58.410
Comparing your prints with others

239
00:12:58.410 --> 00:13:01.470
can help you to learn more about screen printing techniques

240
00:13:01.470 --> 00:13:02.703
and how to improve them.

241
00:13:04.470 --> 00:13:06.420
Discuss with a partner or as a group

242
00:13:06.420 --> 00:13:09.360
how you could improve the quality of your screen prints.

243
00:13:09.360 --> 00:13:10.810
Pause here while you do this.

244
00:13:19.260 --> 00:13:21.460
Thanks for offering each other that support.

245
00:13:25.050 --> 00:13:26.700
Let's hear some of this feedback.

246
00:13:27.600 --> 00:13:29.880
Alex, "I noticed the edges of my print

247
00:13:29.880 --> 00:13:32.040
are a bit blurry in some areas.

248
00:13:32.040 --> 00:13:34.680
I'll try to make sure I use the right amount of ink

249
00:13:34.680 --> 00:13:37.647
and apply an even pressure throughout for the next ones."

250
00:13:38.940 --> 00:13:39.773
Good thinking.

251
00:13:39.773 --> 00:13:42.930
And Jacob, "I might experiment with using multiple colors

252
00:13:42.930 --> 00:13:44.760
by using different stencils,

253
00:13:44.760 --> 00:13:46.140
or by using the same stencil

254
00:13:46.140 --> 00:13:48.270
and carefully lining it up on the surface

255
00:13:48.270 --> 00:13:51.060
in different positions for variation."

256
00:13:51.060 --> 00:13:52.413
Sounds really interesting.

257
00:13:54.150 --> 00:13:57.543
Screens must be cleaned immediately with water and a sponge.

258
00:13:58.440 --> 00:13:59.670
This keeps mesh clear

259
00:13:59.670 --> 00:14:01.743
and ensures the equipment lasts longer.

260
00:14:04.230 --> 00:14:06.120
Let's have a check for understanding.

261
00:14:06.120 --> 00:14:08.250
Which of these will help keep screens

262
00:14:08.250 --> 00:14:09.813
and tools in good condition?

263
00:14:11.340 --> 00:14:14.823
A, washing with water and sponges after use.

264
00:14:16.320 --> 00:14:19.233
B, leaving ink to dry before cleaning.

265
00:14:20.790 --> 00:14:24.003
C, scraping off dried ink later.

266
00:14:25.530 --> 00:14:28.773
D, not cleaning, ink makes the mesh stronger.

267
00:14:31.440 --> 00:14:33.240
Pause here while you decide

268
00:14:33.240 --> 00:14:34.920
which of these will help keep screens

269
00:14:34.920 --> 00:14:36.393
and tools in good condition?

270
00:14:43.890 --> 00:14:45.660
Well done if you selected answer A.

271
00:14:45.660 --> 00:14:48.990
Indeed, it's washing with water and sponges after use

272
00:14:48.990 --> 00:14:51.790
that will help keep screens and tools in good condition.

273
00:14:54.900 --> 00:14:57.183
And now it's time for your next task.

274
00:14:58.350 --> 00:15:00.540
I would like you to use your stencil and screen

275
00:15:00.540 --> 00:15:02.523
to create at least two prints.

276
00:15:03.990 --> 00:15:06.270
Experiment with color, placement,

277
00:15:06.270 --> 00:15:08.793
and repetition to explore variation.

278
00:15:09.840 --> 00:15:10.900
So pause here

279
00:15:11.820 --> 00:15:14.010
while you have a go at this task,

280
00:15:14.010 --> 00:15:17.013
using your stencil and screen to create at least two prints.

281
00:15:17.880 --> 00:15:20.460
Enjoy your task. Enjoy your printing.

282
00:15:20.460 --> 00:15:22.103
I'll see you when you're finished.

283
00:15:30.540 --> 00:15:31.950
It's great to be back with you.

284
00:15:31.950 --> 00:15:33.790
So how did you get on with that task

285
00:15:34.950 --> 00:15:36.840
of using your stencil and screen

286
00:15:36.840 --> 00:15:38.910
to create at least two prints,

287
00:15:38.910 --> 00:15:41.820
experimenting with color, placement, and repetition

288
00:15:41.820 --> 00:15:43.173
to explore variation?

289
00:15:44.430 --> 00:15:46.200
You might have created something like this

290
00:15:46.200 --> 00:15:47.940
and you might have said something like this.

291
00:15:47.940 --> 00:15:49.083
Let's hear from Sofia.

292
00:15:50.197 --> 00:15:51.570
"I used a leaf stencil

293
00:15:51.570 --> 00:15:54.753
to create these variations of screen prints.

294
00:15:55.980 --> 00:15:58.680
I changed colors to evoke different seasons,

295
00:15:58.680 --> 00:16:01.917
and used both sides of the stencil to mirror the design."

296
00:16:02.850 --> 00:16:04.023
So wonderful.

297
00:16:06.330 --> 00:16:08.550
I would like you to share with someone your impressions

298
00:16:08.550 --> 00:16:11.520
of Sofia's prints and Sofia's process

299
00:16:11.520 --> 00:16:12.873
to achieve these outcomes.

300
00:16:14.160 --> 00:16:15.610
Pause here while you do this.

301
00:16:23.940 --> 00:16:25.230
Thanks for sharing.

302
00:16:25.230 --> 00:16:26.160
And now I would like you

303
00:16:26.160 --> 00:16:29.070
to share your prints with each other

304
00:16:29.070 --> 00:16:30.390
and to talk through your process.

305
00:16:30.390 --> 00:16:33.360
How did you come to your final outcome?

306
00:16:33.360 --> 00:16:34.810
Pause here while you do this.

307
00:16:41.940 --> 00:16:43.023
Thanks for sharing.

308
00:16:44.130 --> 00:16:47.100
Next, I'd like you to offer each other some feedback

309
00:16:47.100 --> 00:16:48.330
on your prints.

310
00:16:48.330 --> 00:16:50.490
What do you think has worked really well?

311
00:16:50.490 --> 00:16:51.930
And any suggestions

312
00:16:51.930 --> 00:16:54.153
for some changes or a different approach?

313
00:17:01.740 --> 00:17:03.660
Thanks for offering each other that feedback

314
00:17:03.660 --> 00:17:04.770
and those suggestions.

315
00:17:04.770 --> 00:17:06.930
Hopefully, they will be helpful.

316
00:17:06.930 --> 00:17:08.073
And finally,

317
00:17:09.270 --> 00:17:11.460
I would like you to share with each other

318
00:17:11.460 --> 00:17:14.493
any ideas you have for future screen prints.

319
00:17:15.870 --> 00:17:19.020
What might be a future design that you would like to print,

320
00:17:19.020 --> 00:17:21.600
and any ideas about colors or process

321
00:17:21.600 --> 00:17:22.950
that you'd like to explore?

322
00:17:30.540 --> 00:17:31.748
Thanks so much for sharing.

323
00:17:31.748 --> 00:17:33.510
I hope you're feeling inspired

324
00:17:33.510 --> 00:17:35.673
to continue your screen printing journey.

325
00:17:37.800 --> 00:17:39.900
In our lesson "Screen printing basics:

326
00:17:39.900 --> 00:17:41.640
from stencils to finished prints,"

327
00:17:41.640 --> 00:17:43.590
we've covered the following.

328
00:17:43.590 --> 00:17:47.580
Stencils are used to block and reveal areas of ink.

329
00:17:47.580 --> 00:17:50.550
Even pressure and consistent angle with the squeegee

330
00:17:50.550 --> 00:17:52.413
is vital for clean prints.

331
00:17:53.280 --> 00:17:56.520
Screen printing allows for repetition and variation

332
00:17:56.520 --> 00:17:58.383
through color and composition.

333
00:18:00.390 --> 00:18:03.570
Well done, everyone, for joining in with this lesson.

334
00:18:03.570 --> 00:18:04.980
Screen printing is really one

335
00:18:04.980 --> 00:18:07.080
of my most favorite things ever,

336
00:18:07.080 --> 00:18:10.170
so I'm so pleased to have shared this with you.

337
00:18:10.170 --> 00:18:12.240
It was great to go right into the detail

338
00:18:12.240 --> 00:18:15.360
of how to create stencils and screen prints

339
00:18:15.360 --> 00:18:19.590
and looking at ways in which we can explore

340
00:18:19.590 --> 00:18:21.813
some variation in our prints.

341
00:18:23.100 --> 00:18:25.380
I hope you'll continue on your screen printing journey

342
00:18:25.380 --> 00:18:27.693
and I'm wishing you all the best with that.

343
00:18:29.220 --> 00:18:30.570
Hope you've enjoyed this lesson.

344
00:18:30.570 --> 00:18:32.250
I've really enjoyed teaching you,

345
00:18:32.250 --> 00:18:33.600
and I'm looking forward to seeing you

346
00:18:33.600 --> 00:18:35.760
at another art lesson soon.

347
00:18:35.760 --> 00:18:37.533
Until then, stay creative.

lessons.lessonTitle: Deepening the understanding of the principles of printing

lessonKeywords.description: aligning layers of a print accurately when using multiple colours or block
the arrangement of visual elements within an artwork

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Printing methods share core principles but create different effects.
Registration and layering add complexity and precision to designs.
Compositional choices affect clarity and visual impact.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Printing is a creative process where choices about technique, layering, and texture produce unique outcomes - even when using the same plate or block.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Printing is only about copying or replicating an image.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can apply printing principles, including registration and composition, to produce layered prints with precision and creativity.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Encourage pupils to embrace "happy accidents" - unexpected textures or shifts in registration can be reframed as creative opportunities rather than mistakes, helping build resilience and experimentation in printmaking.

184

186

187
00:09:33.150 --> 00:09:36.663

189
00:09:42.690 --> 00:09:44.883
over-inking causes smudges,

00:09:45.870 --> 00:09:47.943
misaligned layers causing blur,

191
00:09:49.230 --> 00:09:51.903
imprecise marking of registration points,

192
00:09:52.830 --> 00:09:55.140
rushing through the process.

193

Pause here and share with someone,

lessons.lessonTitle: Digital printing: integrating technology in printmaking

lessonKeywords.description: a method of printing directly from a digital file to paper or fabric using inkjet or laser technology
graphics made up of paths defined by mathematical equations, scalable without losing quality
graphics composed of pixels, where quality decreases when enlarged
measured in dots per inch (DPI); the print clarity and detail

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Digital technology can expand traditional printmaking methods.
Image file types (vector vs raster) affect print quality.
Preparing digital files correctly ensures successful transfer to substrates.
Print resolution and scale impact clarity of final outcomes.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Resolution and image type matter - a raster image may pixelate when enlarged, while vector graphics remain sharp.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Any image from the internet will print clearly at large scale.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can prepare and create a digital design ready for high quality printing onto a chosen material.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Model the difference between raster and vector images live on screen - zooming in helps pupils see why resolution matters. Provide physical print examples so students can compare digital prep with real outcomes.

lessons.lessonTitle: Exploring intaglio: creating depth and detail in prints

lessonKeywords.description: a printmaking process where lines are incised into a surface to hold ink
the surface (metal, card, or plastic) used to incise a design for printing
a sharp engraving tool used to cut lines into a plate
the final printed image transferred from plate to paper

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Intaglio creates depth by holding ink in recessed lines in a plate.
Varying pressure and line quality impacts detail and tonal range.
Inking and wiping methods change the clarity and richness of print impressions.
Safe tool use with burins is essential when cutting plates.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: In intaglio printing, the recessed lines hold the ink - the surface must be wiped clean so only incised marks transfer ink to paper.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: The ink should be applied only to the raised surface of the plate.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can create an intaglio print that shows depth and detail through the use of line, tone, and inking techniques.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Demonstrate wiping slowly and exaggerate the difference between over-wiping and under-wiping so pupils clearly see how subtle changes affect the printed outcome.

lessons.transcript_sentences:
Hi, I'm Miss Blue, and I'm really excited to be learning with you today.
I hope you find our lesson as interesting as I do.
Let's get started.
The outcome of this lesson is: "I can create an intaglio print that shows depth and detail through the use of line, tone, and inking technique." Let's go over our keywords.
Intaglio: a printmaking process where lines are incised into a surface to hold ink.
Plate: the surface, metal, card, or plastic used to incise a design for printing.
Burin: a sharp engraving tool used to cut lines into a plate.
Impression: the final printed image transferred from plate to paper.
Let's start with an introduction to intaglio.
Intaglio is a printmaking technique where ink sits in incised recesses or inside carved lines rather than raised surfaces.
Here's an example of a horse intaglio on the left.
When paper is pressed into the plate, it picks up the ink from these grooves.
The process creates detailed and textured prints with fine, intricate lines.
While relief printing transfers ink from the raised surface of a block, intaglio transfers ink from the recessed lines.
This opposite process explains why intaglio prints can achieve such fine details.
Have a look at these birds on the left.
I love how it's captured the fine details of their feathers.
Intaglio printing allows artists to achieve precision, depth, and a wide tonal range.
Lines can be varied in thickness, and wiping techniques alter the richness of tones.
This makes it ideal for both artistic and graphic communication.
Does this process interest you yet? Intaglio is such a beautiful printmaking process to me because it allows for such rich and detailed prints.
I think it's loved by an array of different artists because it allows for this amazing level of control.
I love how you can make fine, delicate marks or bold, dark ones, depending on how deeply you cut or how much ink you leave on the plate.
The results seem to give such depth and texture that it feels almost three-dimensional, giving the image a special kind of life, like this bird on the left.
It's as if, through peering into its eyes, you could know its story.
Even though it's on a plain 2D background, it feels whole and real.
I'd argue that intaglio lends itself especially to graphic work because it captures all of these tiny gestures and marks, which will be eye-catching on a billboard or on a computer screen.
It's a process that communicates emotion, movement, and atmosphere through line alone.
Each print feels like a record of the artist's hand and energy.
Here you can see a selection of intaglio printmaking tools.
Do you recognize any of them? On the left, we have a burin.
Wiping tools: sponge, cotton bud, and cheesecloth.
On the right, we have a printing press and the plate.
An intaglio plate can be used multiple times if taken care of.
One of the most common plates is made of metal.
Which of the following describes intaglio printmaking? Is it: A, intaglio uses raised surfaces; B, intaglio uses incised recesses; C, intaglio plates can only be used once; or D, intaglio plates can be used multiple times? Pause the video while you decide on the correct answers.
If you said B and C, you would be correct.
Intaglio uses incised recesses, and the plates can be used multiple times.
Well done for paying attention.
Many artists have used intaglio to create dramatic and detailed works.
Looking at examples of intaglio prints shows how powerful line and tone can be in telling a story or creating atmosphere.
The portrait on the left seems to tell a mythological story.
The intaglio process lends itself to this mythic quality.
It seems dramatic and detailed.
Many artists and printmakers have explored intaglio.
Rembrandt van Rijn was one of the most influential printmakers in history.
He used intaglio to achieve dramatic light, shadow, and texture in his etchings.
Fay Pomerance was a mid-20th-century artist who worked with etching and printmaking.
She often used printmaking to explore mystical and symbolic imagery.
Ronnie Tjampitjinpa is known for his striking linear and geometric designs, which draw on sacred Dreamtime stories and cultural traditions.
He uses painting and printmaking to explore them.
When designing or sketching for an intaglio plate, it's important to experiment of line variation and tonal range.
Intaglio allows you to work with fine details and textures that are different to other printmaking methods, and this process will help you to create a visually interesting piece.
I would argue that intaglio is one of the best processes for capturing variation and tonal range.
I think it allows for a real contrast between light and dark, giving a rich tonal quality that's created by thicker or thinner lines.
It adds a layer of depth and emotion to the image.
Like the artwork on the left of the stones, it feels as if you could reach into the stones and touch them.
I can almost hear what they'd sound like through the print.
In my own experience of etching, I focused on capturing the delicate details of a dried leaf.
I was quite focused on the fine veins, soft folds, and any tiny imperfections I found by peering at it closely.
I realized that through using lighter or shallow lines alongside deeper, more defined ones, I was able to show both the fragility and the strength of its structure.
Once printed, those variations created a sense of movement and realism.
It felt as if the leaf was almost breathing.
You can transfer your design directly onto an intaglio plate by placing the drawing face down and running it through a printing press.
Using transfer paper.
Using transfer paper to trace the design onto the plate, or copying the drawing onto the plate.
Consider which method you will use before drawing, as you might transfer it directly onto the plate, which will need to be the same size.
Pause the video while you plan this out.
Let's test your knowledge.
Which quality is most important when sketching designs for an intaglio plate? Is it: A, line variation and tonal range; B, bright colors; C, symmetry and repetition; or D, large shapes without detail? Pause the video while you decide on the correct answer.
If you said A, you would be correct.
Line variation and tonal range are the most important things when sketching designs for an intaglio plate.
Your task now is to create a design for your intaglio plate that uses varied lines and tonal areas.
Focus on textures, patterns, and contrasts rather than large, flat shapes.
Pause the video here while you work on the task.
There are many possible outcomes.
You might have said something like Sam.
He says, "I created this design using a photo of a pepper as a reference picture.
I tried to build tonal areas up through hatched lines, and this will translate well as an intaglio print." This is a great outcome on the right.
I love the tonal quality of the light and dark areas.
It makes it look more three-dimensional and realistic.
Now let's focus on techniques for intaglio printing.
Intaglio printing traditionally uses metal plates to draw into, however, you might use: clear acetate or Plexiglass, or Tetra Pak juice cartons.
I wonder if you've got any of those around you.
One of my first experiments with intaglio stemmed from pure curiosity.
I'd found a leftover juice carton in the recycling bin at home and on a whim decided to turn it into a printmaking plate.
I wasn't expecting anything in particular, but after peeling it open and scratching a quick sketch into the metallic side with a blunt pencil, using the back of a spoon as a burin.
When I lifted the paper, the image was there: crisp, moody, and incredibly detailed.
My next experiment was more thought-through.
I wanted to create a city skyline onto the surface and made sure I pressed just hard enough to make grooves without tearing through and rubbed block printing ink into the etched lines, wiping off the excess.
I added different layers to create contrast and was amazed at how sharp and clear the lines were.
Trace your design onto an intaglio plate by drawing on top with firm pressure.
You can see how this person has traced around their design onto the back of a juice carton.
It looks like they've gone over it so that the recesses are deeper.
When working with sharp tools, it's important to handle them with care.
Keep hands away from the cutting line and work slowly to avoid slips.
Burins and lino carving tools are very sharp and can cause injury if misused.
I myself have been victim to a lino carving tool cut.
You definitely have to exercise patience and embrace the slow and meditative process.
Safety ensures precision and confidence in your work.
This intaglio print on the right-hand side looks quite simple at first.

I think the metallic quality lends itself well because it draws your eye to the magic of these lines.
It's even more eye-catching on the cardboard surface.
Use a burin or needle to carefully cut your design into the plate.
You can use a craft knife to peel away the darkest areas.
Deeper cuts hold more ink, creating darker lines, while shallow cuts produce finer detail.
Think about how line depth affects tone.
Pause the video while you think about this.
Many contemporary artists continue to experiment with intaglio printmaking.
Such as: Caledonia Curry, AKA Swoon, is a contemporary printmaker and street artist.
He uses large-scale woodcuts and intaglio-inspired techniques.
Her work often depicts social issues and personal storytelling.
Glenn Ligon's text-based etchings and prints explore race, language, and identity.
His intaglio works often blur legibility, forcing viewers to consider their meaning.
Sunnu Rebecca Choi combines printmaking with mixed-media approaches.
Choi explores identity, migration, and cultural memory through layered surfaces and experimental processes.
Why is safe handling of a burin or etching tool important? A, they're fragile and break easily; B, they must be kept clean for the ink to stick; C, they're sharp and can cause injury if misused; or D, they are expensive and hard to replace? Pause the video while you decide on the correct answer.

At this stage, the plate may look very messy, but don't worry, wiping will reveal your design.
The key to intaglio is wiping correctly using a rag or cloth.
You can see how the person is demonstrating on the left.
Too much wiping removes ink from the grooves, resulting in a faint print; too little wiping leaves the surface dirty.
It's important to use a clean rag or cloth, otherwise, your print could become contaminated.
Aim for a balance that preserves details and provides depth.
Intaglio prints work best on slightly dampened paper.
The moisture helps the fibers press deeply into the incised lines to pull out the ink.
Make sure you prepare the paper before printing.
You might find that a spray bottle can help, or perhaps a damp sponge.
To use the printing press and create your first impression, place your inked plate face-up on the press bed.
Lay the damp paper on top and cover it with blankets.
The pressure pushes the paper into the grooves, transferring the ink to create an impression.

Discuss with a partner if you need to change anything in your process before making another impression.

The printed image transferred onto paper through intaglio printing is known as: A, artifact; B, inkling; C, expression; or D, impression? Pause the video while you decide on the correct answer.

The printed image transferred onto paper through intaglio printing is known as an impression.

Pause the video while you work on this task.

To summarize, intaglio creates depth by holding ink in recessed lines in a plate.
Varying pressure and line quality impacts detail and tonal range.
Inking and wiping methods change the clarity and richness of print impressions.
Safe tool use with burins is essential when cutting plates.

I hope you had fun and learned something new along the way.
See you next time.

lessons.lessonTitle: Monoprinting techniques: unique and expressive prints

lessonKeywords.description: a one-off print created by pressing or drawing onto an inked surface
the flat surface (e.g. acrylic sheet) used to apply ink for printing
the surface quality (real or implied) in an artwork
a monoprint technique involving drawing into or removing ink from a plate before printing

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Monoprinting creates unique, non-repeatable artworks.
Expressive marks can be developed deliberately through line, pressure, and texture.
Techniques include direct drawing, subtractive methods, and textured surfaces.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Monoprints are valued for their unique, imperfect, and expressive qualities that cannot be exactly replicated.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Monoprints should look “perfect” and repeatable, like digital prints.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can create unique and expressive monoprints using both direct and subtractive techniques.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Encourage pupils to embrace unpredictability - remind them monoprints aren’t meant to be identical or flawless. Celebrate experimentation and “happy accidents” as part of the creative process.

lessons.lessonTitle: Mixed media printing: combining traditional and modern methods

lessonKeywords.description: a unique print made by drawing or inking on a surface and pressing onto paper
a print created using a textured collage plate
adding computer-generated imagery or text onto a traditional print
combining more than one artistic medium within a single artwork

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Mixed media printing integrates traditional methods (e.g. monoprint, collagraph) with modern digital techniques.
Printmaking benefits from both traditional techniques and digital edits through digital overlays and refinement.
Mixed media approaches encourage creativity, problem-solving, and new ways of working.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Digital tools enhance traditional methods by expanding creative possibilities - neither replaces the other.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Digital tools replace traditional printmaking.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can create a mixed media print that combines traditional printmaking techniques with digital overlays.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Encourage experimentation - mistakes often lead to creative breakthroughs. Remind pupils that layering and combining techniques is about trial, refinement, and risk-taking, not just a polished final outcome.

lessons.lessonTitle: Advancing relief printing: techniques and applications

lessonKeywords.description: aligning layers of a print accurately when printing multiple colours or blocks
a printmaking process where raised surfaces carry ink to create an image
a relief method where one block is progressively cut away to print multiple colours
a surface designed to add patterns or textures to a print

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Relief printing can be advanced using layering, reduction techniques, and texture plate applications.
Precision in registration is vital to produce professional multi-layered prints.
Experimentation with texture plates and surfaces enhances creative outcomes.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Too much ink causes smudging and loss of detail; even, thin layers produce cleaner and sharper results.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: More ink always produces stronger, better prints.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can apply advanced relief printing techniques, including layering, registration, and texture, to create a refined graphic print.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Model registration and reduction clearly with step-by-step visuals; encourage pupils to print test runs before final attempts to refine technique and reduce mistakes.

Hi, I'm Miss Blue and I'm really excited to be learning with you today.
I hope you find our lesson as interesting as I do.
Let's get started.
The outcome of this lesson is, I can apply advanced relief printing techniques including layering, registration and texture to create a refined graphic print.
Let's go over our keywords: Relief printing: A printmaking process where raised surfaces carry ink to create an image.
Registration: aligning layers of a print accurately when printing multiple colors or blocks.
Texture plate: a surface designed to add patterns or textures to a print.
Reduction printing: a relief method where one block is progressively cut away to print multiple colors.
Let's start with exploring printing techniques and applications.
Printmaking has a long and rich history with skills and techniques that have been refined and developed throughout this time.
To achieve an effective print, there are certain techniques which can be used to help advance the level of quality found in our own prints.
As someone who is a screen printer onto textile, I rely on correct technique to ensure a good print.
Some of the techniques I use include the way I handle the ink before printing, making sure it's properly mixed with no lumps to ensure proper pigment distribution onto my print.
I know what the correct consistency of the ink should look like.
If it's too thick, it won't print well, and if it's too thin, the same thing happens.
Being a printer means knowing your craft and what you should expect from each stage of the process.
I wonder if relief printing has any similarities to screen printing, let's have a look.
It's helpful to familiarize yourself with the tools you have available.
Depending on the methods you are using, you might have lino or soft-cut blocks, lino carving tools, brayers or ink rollers, baren, printing press.
Have you heard of this equipment before? Printmaking can involve lots of materials, but essentially you'll need a block for carving or painting onto, tools to carve or paint with, ink to roll it onto the block and paper to print onto.
To help transfer the ink from the block to the paper.
You might use a printing press a baren or the heel of your hand.
Check that you have these tools available.
You don't need access to lots of printmaking materials to make an effective print.
Establishing good technique takes time and is the priority to focus on even if only limited materials are available.
Printmaking lends itself to experimentation and can be practiced with minimal tools, especially with relief printing.
The principles of good technique include the pressure, consistency, registration, and surface preparation.

Registration means aligning each layer of your print so color doesn't overlap incorrectly.
Good registration ensures your design looks crisp, professional and intentional.

A common type of printmaking is relief printing.
In relief printing, only the raised surfaces carry ink to create an image.
This means that the areas of the block, which are carved away, will not carry or transfer ink when printing.
Relief printing is often regarded as an easy and quick process, which is thoroughly enjoyable because of its direct, tactile and wonderfully immediate prints.
Unlike other methods like screen printing, there's minimal setup.
You can carve ink and print within a few simple steps, and it's easy to do from home.
You can also often find materials from home.
I find it to be a very intuitive process.
I like the idea of carving away what you don't want.
It allows for such creativity to unfold between the positive and negative space.
Each print feels like a small discovery and it's a fun quick way to create different color experiments even with just one block.
Many colors can be used in a single print, a process known as reduction printing.
In reduction printing sections of the block are carved away after each color is printed.
This means that once an area has been carved away, it cannot be reprinted.
So careful and intentional planning is key.
For reduction printing, print the lightest color first, then carve away more areas for each subsequent layer.

Using a grid, tape, pins or a wooden corner jig can help

97
00:05:00.450 --> 00:05:02.340
with aligning paper and printing blocks

98
00:05:02.340 --> 00:05:04.083
for accurate registration.

99
00:05:05.970 --> 00:05:07.818
In professional screen printing rooms,

100
00:05:07.818 --> 00:05:11.409
print tables might have a metal bar that you rest on

101
00:05:11.409 --> 00:05:14.853
to ensure correct registration for repeat prints.

102
00:05:15.870 --> 00:05:19.410
There is a specific process for setting up these repeats

103
00:05:19.410 --> 00:05:21.063
as an industrial standard.

104
00:05:23.960 --> 00:05:26.943
A common type of printmaking is relief printing.

105
00:05:26.943 --> 00:05:30.990
In relief printing, only the raised surfaces carry ink

106
00:05:30.990 --> 00:05:33.120
to create an image.

107
00:05:33.120 --> 00:05:34.980
This means that the areas of the block,

108
00:05:34.980 --> 00:05:37.110
which are carved away, will not carry

109
00:05:37.110 --> 00:05:38.943
or transfer ink when printing.

110
00:05:39.960 --> 00:05:42.630
Relief printing is often regarded as an easy

111
00:05:42.630 --> 00:05:45.305
and quick process, which is thoroughly enjoyable

112
00:05:45.305 --> 00:05:47.580
because of its direct, tactile

113
00:05:47.580 --> 00:05:49.560
and wonderfully immediate prints.

114
00:05:49.560 --> 00:05:50.760
Unlike other methods

115
00:05:50.760 --> 00:05:53.545
like screen printing, there's minimal setup.

116
00:05:53.545 --> 00:05:57.541
You can carve ink and print within a few simple steps,

117
00:05:57.541 --> 00:05:59.521
and it's easy to do from home.

118
00:05:59.521 --> 00:06:02.957
You can also often find materials from home.

119
00:06:02.957 --> 00:06:05.911
I find it to be a very intuitive process.

120
00:06:05.911 --> 00:06:08.973
I like the idea of carving away what you don't want.

121
00:06:09.990 --> 00:06:12.018
It allows for such creativity to unfold

122
00:06:12.018 --> 00:06:14.893
between the positive and negative space.

123
00:06:14.893 --> 00:06:17.198
Each print feels like a small discovery

124
00:06:17.198 --> 00:06:19.110
and it's a fun quick way

125
00:06:19.110 --> 00:06:21.345
to create different color experiments even

126
00:06:21.345 --> 00:06:23.181
with just one block.

127
00:06:23.181 --> 00:06:26.436
Many colors can be used in a single print,

128
00:06:26.436 --> 00:06:29.850
a process known as reduction printing.

129
00:06:29.850 --> 00:06:33.240
In reduction printing sections of the block are carved away

130
00:06:33.240 --> 00:06:35.073
after each color is printed.

131
00:06:35.910 --> 00:06:38.760
This means that once an area has been carved away,

132
00:06:38.760 --> 00:06:40.650
it cannot be reprinted.

133
00:06:40.650 --> 00:06:43.443
So careful and intentional planning is key.

134
00:06:45.540 --> 00:06:49.170
For reduction printing, print the lightest color first,

135
00:06:49.170 --> 00:06:52.443
then carve away more areas for each subsequent layer.

136
00:06:53.430 --> 00:06:56.910
Each stage reduces the block further revealing only

137
00:06:56.910 --> 00:07:00.150
what remains raised, and these are the only areas

138
00:07:00.150 --> 00:07:02.910
which carry ink for the next pass of printing.

139
00:07:02.910 --> 00:07:04.800
From my point of view, I think

140
00:07:04.800 --> 00:07:06.510
that relief printing lends itself

141
00:07:06.510 --> 00:07:09.060
so beautifully to fluid and organic shapes

142
00:07:09.060 --> 00:07:10.980
like this one on the right.

143
00:07:10.980 --> 00:07:14.040
I always tend to think of flowing lines, leaves, waves,

144
00:07:14.040 --> 00:07:17.550
or abstract forms, maybe inspired by nature.

145
00:07:17.550 --> 00:07:19.890
The artwork on the right almost looks like an

146
00:07:19.890 --> 00:07:21.969
in depth study of a tree trunk,

147
00:07:21.969 --> 00:07:24.120
which has become more abstracted

148
00:07:24.120 --> 00:07:26.190
through the printing process.

149
00:07:26.190 --> 00:07:28.560
It's a great example of how you can have an idea

150
00:07:28.560 --> 00:07:31.650
or theme in mind and through making it transforms

151
00:07:31.650 --> 00:07:34.170
into something unique and playful.

152
00:07:34.170 --> 00:07:36.000
Each layer becomes a conversation

153
00:07:36.000 --> 00:07:39.240
with the last revealing unexpected harmonies

154
00:07:39.240 --> 00:07:42.810
between color, shape, and negative space, allowing

155
00:07:42.810 --> 00:07:45.780
for a richly expressive and intuitive outcome.

156
00:07:45.780 --> 00:07:47.310
Looking at this artwork,

157
00:07:47.310 --> 00:07:49.800
in which layer do you think they started with?

158
00:07:49.800 --> 00:07:53.400
What do you think their theme was or starting idea?

159
00:07:53.400 --> 00:07:55.350
Pause the video while you have a think.

160
00:08:01.004 --> 00:08:04.240
What is the main principle of relief printing?

161
00:08:04.240 --> 00:08:06.840
Is it A, ink is pressed through a stencil?

162
00:08:06.840 --> 00:08:10.560
B, ink is transferred from assessed lines?

163
00:08:10.560 --> 00:08:13.710
C, ink is painted directly onto paper?

164
00:08:13.710 --> 00:08:17.925
Or D, ink is applied to raised surfaces only?

165
00:08:17.925 --> 00:08:21.003
Pause the video while you decide on the correct answer.

166
00:08:27.780 --> 00:08:30.300
If you said D, you would be correct.

167
00:08:30.300 --> 00:08:32.405
The main principle of relief printing is

168
00:08:32.405 --> 00:08:36.104
that ink is applied to raised surfaces only.

169
00:08:36.104 --> 00:08:39.150
Your task now is to use two colors

170
00:08:39.150 --> 00:08:41.280
and make a simple test print focusing on

171
00:08:41.280 --> 00:08:43.620
registration accuracy.

172
00:08:43.620 --> 00:08:45.390
Don't worry about detail.

173
00:08:45.390 --> 00:08:48.060
Concentrate on precision in lining up layers.

174
00:08:48.060 --> 00:08:49.380
You could choose from the techniques

175
00:08:49.380 --> 00:08:51.961
that we've had a look at earlier in the lesson.

176
00:08:51.961 --> 00:08:54.723
Pause the video while you work on this task.

177
00:09:00.840 --> 00:09:03.228
There are many possible outcomes to this task.

178
00:09:03.228 --> 00:09:06.060
Let's hear from Sam who says,

179
00:09:06.060 --> 00:09:09.060
I made this print using two colors.

180
00:09:09.060 --> 00:09:11.220
The first layer was printed in yellow

181
00:09:11.220 --> 00:09:14.910
and the second layer was in a darker color to add contrast.

182
00:09:14.910 --> 00:09:17.760
You can see his outcome is very effective.

183
00:09:17.760 --> 00:09:19.884
I love the use of color theory.

184
00:09:19.884 --> 00:09:22.200
It's interesting working backwards

185
00:09:22.200 --> 00:09:24.330
from the lightest color to the darkest.

186
00:09:24.330 --> 00:09:26.680
It makes you think about the print differently.

187
00:09:27.690 --> 00:09:30.933
Now, let's go over applying advanced printing techniques.

188
00:09:32.550 --> 00:09:35.310
Texture plates can be made by pressing materials

189
00:09:35.310 --> 00:09:38.760
into inked blocks to great depth and variety.

190
00:09:38.760 --> 00:09:41.970
This technique is also known as planography.

191
00:09:41.970 --> 00:09:43.830
A texture plate adds richness

192
00:09:43.830 --> 00:09:46.233
and originality to your print outcomes.

193
00:09:47.070 --> 00:09:49.830
For me, texture plates are a fascinating way

194
00:09:49.830 --> 00:09:53.040
to bring depth and tactility into relief printing.

195
00:09:53.040 --> 00:09:55.560
I love the way it transforms a flat surface

196
00:09:55.560 --> 00:09:58.500
into something richly layered and more sensory.

197
00:09:58.500 --> 00:10:00.120
In the past, I've explored a range

198
00:10:00.120 --> 00:10:02.951
of different textured materials onto my plates, such

199
00:10:02.951 --> 00:10:07.951
as lace, sleeves, fabric string, or even recycled cardboard.

200
00:10:08.580 --> 00:10:10.979
I find that you can really capture the intricate patterns

201
00:10:10.979 --> 00:10:13.523
and irregularities of the material itself.

202
00:10:13.523 --> 00:10:16.380
And now so many possibilities when you begin

203
00:10:16.380 --> 00:10:18.810
to collage different textures together so

204
00:10:18.810 --> 00:10:20.760
that it becomes more abstract.

205
00:10:20.760 --> 00:10:23.228
The process is really organic and unpredictable.

206
00:10:23.228 --> 00:10:25.290
I think it's a lovely way for the artist

207
00:10:25.290 --> 00:10:27.028
to truly reveal the different layers

208
00:10:27.028 --> 00:10:29.201
of their interests in one print.

209
00:10:29.201 --> 00:10:32.250
With this dialogue between surface pressure

210
00:10:32.250 --> 00:10:34.892
and the memories of different materials.

211
00:10:34.892 --> 00:10:37.236
In this texture place on the left, it seems

212
00:10:37.236 --> 00:10:40.710
like perhaps cardboard and string has been used.

213
00:10:40.710 --> 00:10:43.848
I'd say there's a few different layers hidden within.

214
00:10:43.848 --> 00:10:46.774
Texture plates can be made using polystyrene

215
00:10:46.774 --> 00:10:49.080
by drawing into them of a sharp pen

216
00:10:49.080 --> 00:10:50.790
and cutting out the shape.

217
00:10:50.790 --> 00:10:53.992
How you ink these plates can change the resulting print.

218
00:10:53.992 --> 00:10:58.663
I love the effect of these prints and the simplicity of it.

219
00:10:58.663 --> 00:11:01.863
You get a real sense of detail because it's been cut out.

220
00:11:04.020 --> 00:11:05.790
To transfer an image onto a plate

221
00:11:05.790 --> 00:11:09.030
before carving, use a good quality photo printed

222
00:11:09.030 --> 00:11:12.210
in black and white on standard printer paper.

223
00:11:12.210 --> 00:11:14.403
Then draw over the top with a marker pen.

224
00:11:15.840 --> 00:11:17.568
Next turn the paper over.

225
00:11:17.568 --> 00:11:20.784
The pen should be visible through the paper in reverse.

226
00:11:20.784 --> 00:11:24.393
Go over the marker pen lines on this side of the paper.

227
00:11:27.313 --> 00:11:31.527
Now use graphite to trace the image onto the lino.

228
00:11:31.527 --> 00:11:34.140
If it's green or blue lino, then roll

229
00:11:34.140 --> 00:11:38.017
that a little ink on the photo to help with the tracing.

230
00:11:38.017 --> 00:11:40.860
You can see some examples below.

231
00:11:40.860 --> 00:11:43.674
Use a marker pen once more on top of the lino

232
00:11:43.674 --> 00:11:47.066
to stop the design rubbing off as you work.

233
00:11:47.066 --> 00:11:50.490
Use the lino carving tools to cut away

234
00:11:50.490 --> 00:11:52.350
and carve out the areas of the lino

235
00:11:52.350 --> 00:11:54.903
that are not in by your marker pen.

236
00:11:54.903 --> 00:11:57.169
You can also use graphite to make rubbings

237
00:11:57.169 --> 00:12:00.603
of the lino to see how it's going at this stage.

238
00:12:01.876 --> 00:12:05.010
Lino is one of my favorite processes.

239
00:12:05.010 --> 00:12:06.660
Forgetting texture.

240
00:12:06.660 --> 00:12:09.479
This depends on the type of carving tool that you use,

241
00:12:09.479 --> 00:12:12.063
whether it's fine or thick.

242
00:12:14.940 --> 00:12:17.520
Continue carving the lino until all areas

243
00:12:17.520 --> 00:12:19.560
around the design are removed.

244
00:12:19.560 --> 00:12:23.493
You can see how this turns into this, turns into this.

245
00:12:24.600 --> 00:12:26.250
Only the areas of your design, which

246
00:12:26.250 --> 00:12:28.539
of the printing should remain raised.

247
00:12:28.539 --> 00:12:31.680
Take your time of this process

248
00:12:31.680 --> 00:12:33.720
and make sure that you protect your fingers

249
00:12:33.720 --> 00:12:37.353
and hands as the carving tools can be quite sharp.

250
00:12:39.870 --> 00:12:43.918
Why is registration important in multilayered printing?

251
00:12:43.918 --> 00:12:47.430
Is it A, it helps the ink dry faster?

252
00:12:47.430 --> 00:12:49.888
B, it prevents smudges during printing?

253
00:12:49.888 --> 00:12:54.870
C, it ensures each color layer aligns correctly?

254
00:12:54.870 --> 00:12:57.990
Or D, it makes carving easier?

255
00:12:57.990 --> 00:13:00.813
Pause the video while you decide on the correct answer.

256
00:13:06.120 --> 00:13:08.580
If you said C, you'd be correct.

257
00:13:08.580 --> 00:13:11.580
Registration is important in multi layered printing

258
00:13:11.580 --> 00:13:14.973
because it ensures each color layer aligns correctly.

259
00:13:16.740 --> 00:13:19.890
Let's have a look at this piece in more detail.

260
00:13:19.890 --> 00:13:21.720
To advance your printmaking,

261
00:13:21.720 --> 00:13:23.910
consider combining different techniques

262
00:13:23.910 --> 00:13:26.550
like relief printing, reduction printing,

263
00:13:26.550 --> 00:13:28.260
and texture plates.

264
00:13:28.260 --> 00:13:32.670
Incorporating varied techniques requires thorough planning.

265
00:13:32.670 --> 00:13:35.100
Discuss with a partner the techniques you might use

266
00:13:35.100 --> 00:13:36.570
in your printmaking process.

267
00:13:36.570 --> 00:13:38.920
Pause the video while you have this discussion.

268
00:13:45.600 --> 00:13:48.720
With your linocut ready for print, you can experiment

269
00:13:48.720 --> 00:13:50.605
with different color combinations

270
00:13:50.605 --> 00:13:53.190
to create a series of prints.

271
00:13:53.190 --> 00:13:56.670
I love how the artist has used fluorescent colors here

272
00:13:56.670 --> 00:13:58.833
with a contrasting warm background.

273
00:14:00.960 --> 00:14:03.663
Notice how each print is slightly different.

274
00:14:04.680 --> 00:14:06.660
Which one is your favorite?

275
00:14:06.660 --> 00:14:08.610
Pause the video while you have a think.

276
00:14:14.490 --> 00:14:18.390
Laura says, I want to use multiple colors in my print,

277
00:14:18.390 --> 00:14:20.160
so I will use the reduction techniques

278
00:14:20.160 --> 00:14:23.370
to carve each layer away between prints.

279
00:14:23.370 --> 00:14:25.881
I will start with a light background color.

280
00:14:25.881 --> 00:14:29.694
Andeep says, I'd like to use a variety of textures

281
00:14:29.694 --> 00:14:33.035
to create a dynamic composition through printmaking.

282
00:14:33.035 --> 00:14:35.850
I'll wait for each layer to dry between prints

283
00:14:35.850 --> 00:14:37.380
to avoid them smudging.

284
00:14:37.380 --> 00:14:40.338
Historical and contemporary examples of print printmakers

285
00:14:40.338 --> 00:14:42.840
include Raduan Man:

286
00:14:42.840 --> 00:14:45.308
uses printmaking, particularly woodcut

287
00:14:45.308 --> 00:14:47.370
to create large scale works

288
00:14:47.370 --> 00:14:49.470
that merge traditional techniques

289
00:14:49.470 --> 00:14:53.253
with contemporary narratives on urbanization and memory.

290
00:14:56.340 --> 00:14:59.490
Sybil Andrews: produced bold linocuts

291
00:14:59.490 --> 00:15:03.540
that captured the dynamism of urban life, machinery

292
00:15:03.540 --> 00:15:07.590
and movement with strong colors and simplified forms.

293
00:15:07.590 --> 00:15:11.490
Sherrie York is a contemporary relief print maker working

294
00:15:11.490 --> 00:15:15.990
with woodblock and linocuts focusing on the environmental

295
00:15:15.990 --> 00:15:18.060
and ecological themes.

296
00:15:18.060 --> 00:15:21.480
Printmaking can also be used to provide social commentary,

297
00:15:21.480 --> 00:15:24.603
exploring identity, and developing narratives.

298
00:15:25.530 --> 00:15:28.425
Margo Humphrey uses vibrant color linocuts

299
00:15:28.425 --> 00:15:32.400
and lithographs to explore themes of family, faith

300
00:15:32.400 --> 00:15:34.320
and cultural identity.

301
00:15:34.320 --> 00:15:36.589
Ade Adesina: produces intricate,

302
00:15:36.589 --> 00:15:40.500
surreal linocut landscapes that fuses natural

303
00:15:40.500 --> 00:15:45.420
and human made elements reflecting environmental concerns

304
00:15:45.420 --> 00:15:47.407
and cultural journeys.

305
00:15:47.407 --> 00:15:49.890
Michael Mules is a print maker

306
00:15:49.890 --> 00:15:52.424
whose detailed linocuts use strong contrasts

307
00:15:52.424 --> 00:15:57.424
and precise carving to capture architecture, landscapes

308
00:15:57.660 --> 00:16:00.540
and narrative scenes with graphic intensity.

309
00:16:00.540 --> 00:16:02.310
Let's test your knowledge.

310
00:16:02.310 --> 00:16:04.856
What is the process of reduction printing?

311
00:16:04.856 --> 00:16:08.060
Is it A, using two blocks side by side?

312
00:16:08.060 --> 00:16:11.220
B, adding texture plates to one block.

313
00:16:11.220 --> 00:16:14.490
C, printing without using a brayer?

314
00:16:14.490 --> 00:16:18.783
Or D, cutting away parts of the block after each print run?

315
00:16:19.680 --> 00:16:22.380
Pause the video while you work out the correct answer.

316
00:16:28.380 --> 00:16:30.870
If you said D, you would be correct.

317
00:16:30.870 --> 00:16:33.540
The correct process of reduction printing is

318
00:16:33.540 --> 00:16:37.162
to cut away parts of the block after each print run.

319
00:16:37.162 --> 00:16:38.640
Your task now is

320
00:16:38.640 --> 00:16:41.524
to create a print combining at least one texture plate

321
00:16:41.524 --> 00:16:44.550
and one instance of reduction printing.

322
00:16:44.550 --> 00:16:47.130
Pause the video while you work on this task.

323
00:16:47.130 --> 00:16:49.380
Feel free to go back over the slides

324
00:16:49.380 --> 00:16:50.853
to get some inspiration.

325
00:16:56.880 --> 00:16:58.590
There are many possible outcomes.

326
00:16:58.590 --> 00:17:00.303
Let's have a look at Izzy's.

327
00:17:01.320 --> 00:17:03.630
I made this print by creating a texture plate

328
00:17:03.630 --> 00:17:05.920
with polyboard and expressive mark-making

329
00:17:05.920 --> 00:17:08.265
for a turquoise background.

330
00:17:08.265 --> 00:17:09.720
I then carved lino

331
00:17:09.720 --> 00:17:11.370
for the black sewing machine printed

332
00:17:11.370 --> 00:17:13.983
on top of orange to complete the composition.

333
00:17:15.210 --> 00:17:16.740
You can see in that image

334
00:17:16.740 --> 00:17:20.280
that the two different processes work effectively.

335
00:17:20.280 --> 00:17:22.740
The sewing machine is in the foreground

336
00:17:22.740 --> 00:17:25.871
and is a dynamic print thanks to the linocut.

337
00:17:25.871 --> 00:17:29.220
The background is more subtle and delicate.

338
00:17:29.220 --> 00:17:32.130
This is thanks to the poly board technique.

339
00:17:32.130 --> 00:17:33.390
To summarize,

340
00:17:33.390 --> 00:17:35.970
relief painting can be advanced using

341
00:17:35.970 --> 00:17:37.775
layering reduction techniques

342
00:17:37.775 --> 00:17:40.620
and texture plate applications.

343
00:17:40.620 --> 00:17:43.454
Precision and registration is vital to produce,

344
00:17:43.454 --> 00:17:46.612
to produce professional, multi layered prints.

345
00:17:46.612 --> 00:17:48.870
Experimentation with texture plates

346
00:17:48.870 --> 00:17:52.499
and surfaces enhances creative outcomes.

347
00:17:52.499 --> 00:17:54.210
Thank you so much for listening

348
00:17:54.210 --> 00:17:56.580
and paying attention in this lesson.

349
00:17:56.580 --> 00:17:59.730
I hope you had fun and learn something new along the way.

350
00:17:59.730 --> 00:18:00.843
See you next time.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Digital art is built on key visual principles, including composition, contrast, layering and resolution.
Understanding how these principles interact strengthens technical and creative outcomes.
Layer control and editing decisions affect the mood, clarity and effectiveness of digital artwork.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Higher resolution increases detail but may not improve design choices; strong composition and contrast matter more for impact.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Higher resolution always makes digital artwork better.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can apply principles of composition, layering and contrast to refine and enhance digital artwork.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Model the digital process step by step using a projector. Encourage pupils to experiment, but stress that purposeful editing choices (composition, layering, contrast) matter more than effects for their own sake.

00:10:57.240 --> 00:10:58.410

00:11:00.690 --> 00:11:03.120

00:11:10.110 --> 00:11:12.813

231
00:11:55.200 --> 00:11:58.650

232
00:11:58.650 --> 00:12:01.293

233
00:12:02.370 --> 00:12:03.930

234
00:12:03.930 --> 00:12:06.570
refers to the image's detail and quality,

235
00:12:06.570 --> 00:12:09.963
measured by the number of pixels or dots per inch, DPI.

236
00:12:11.280 --> 00:12:13.740

00:12:13.740 --> 00:12:16.350

238
00:12:16.350 --> 00:12:18.210

239
00:12:18.210 --> 00:12:20.370
which limits the number of available layers

and can lead to lagging.

241
00:12:22.890 --> 00:12:24.150

and will allow high-quality printing of the artwork

but may not improve design choices.

255

256
00:13:22.110 --> 00:13:25.473
Opacity controls how solid or see-through a layer is.

257
00:13:26.640 --> 00:13:29.850
Opacity can be applied to each line, shape, and color

258
00:13:29.850 --> 00:13:32.823
used in a digital artwork or an entire layer.

259
00:13:34.170 --> 00:13:36.000
Lowering the opacity of the layer

260
00:13:36.000 --> 00:13:37.770
allows you to softly blend images

261
00:13:37.770 --> 00:13:39.213
or visual elements together.

262
00:13:42.090 --> 00:13:43.890

263
00:13:43.890 --> 00:13:46.470
layers can interact with each other in varied ways

00:13:46.470 --> 00:13:48.813
to create a range of visual outcomes.

265
00:13:49.920 --> 00:13:52.173

00:13:53.130 --> 00:13:56.250

00:14:00.810 --> 00:14:03.120

standard, obscures layers below;

00:14:06.210 --> 00:14:09.390
darken, emphasizes darker pixels;

271
00:14:09.390 --> 00:14:12.690
lighten, emphasizes lighter pixels;

multiply, darkens shadows;

00:14:15.450 --> 00:14:17.493
screen, brightens the image;

274
00:14:18.330 --> 00:14:20.910
color, recolors a layer;

275
00:14:20.910 --> 00:14:24.390
overlay, adjusts contrast and brightness.

276
00:14:24.390 --> 00:14:27.480
You can experiment with layer opacity and blending modes

277
00:14:27.480 --> 00:14:29.310
to create a range of special effects

00:14:29.310 --> 00:14:31.053
within your digital artwork.

lessonKeywords.description: an image made by combining two or more separate photographs
hiding or revealing parts of an image without permanently erasing
a digital setting that controls how layers interact visually

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Transformation goes beyond enhancement; it creates entirely new visual outcomes.
Masks and blending modes enable complex, non-destructive edits.
Composite images can communicate imaginative or surreal concepts.
Opacity adjustments allow subtle control over transformations.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Transformation in digital art includes combining, masking, blending, and reimagining images - not just changing size or shape.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Transforming an image always means stretching or resizing it.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can transform images by combining, masking, and blending to create new compositions with altered meaning.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Demonstrate masking slowly and narrate your steps; it’s often the hardest concept. Remind pupils that transformation is about creativity as well as technique - encourage imaginative risk-taking while maintaining technical accuracy.

Let's explore each keyword in turn and find out what they mean.
Composite.
An image made by combining two or more separate photographs.
Masking.
Hiding or revealing parts of an image without permanently erasing.
Blending mode.
A digital setting that controls how layers interact visually.
Opacity, the transparency level of a layer or effect.

Composite, masking, blending mode, and opacity.

lessonKeywords.description: altering or adjusting an image to achieve a desired effect
a digital workspace element allowing parts of an image to be edited separately
a tool-based change to an image’s brightness, contrast, colour, or tone

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Photo manipulation can be used to adjust and enhance the original image.
Contrast, brightness, and saturation can be used to enhance photographs effectively.
Selection and clone tools can be used for targeted layer editing and specific elements in a photo.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Filters are quick presets, but artful digital manipulation involves purposeful use of tools (layers, selections, cloning, adjustments) to control outcome and meaning.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Photo manipulation is just applying filters.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can enhance and manipulate digital images using layers, adjustments, and editing tools to improve their quality and meaning.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Demonstrate tool use live while narrating your thinking; emphasise non-destructive editing with layers. Remind pupils to zoom in/out frequently to check detail and overall impact. Encourage experimentation, but link edits back to intention and meaning.

lessons.lessonTitle: Introduction to animation: bringing digital art to life

lessonKeywords.description: the process of creating the illusion of movement by displaying a sequence of images or frames
a single still image in an animation sequence
a frame that marks a significant change in movement or design
a digital workspace showing the order and duration of frames

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Animation is created by sequencing images over time.
Frames and keyframes are the building blocks of digital animation.
Timelines help animators to create the structure and sequence of an animation.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Animation is carefully planned, using frames, keyframes, and digital tools to control timing, pace, and movement.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Animation is just drawing moving pictures quickly.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can create a short digital animation loop using frames, keyframes, and a timeline to bring my artwork to life.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Keep demonstrations short and visual, show frame-by-frame changes clearly. Encourage pupils to test their animations frequently; seeing movement unfold motivates learners and helps them self-correct pacing and flow.
