94
00:05:17.280 --> 00:05:20.103
Great animation requires planning and preparation.

95
00:05:21.210 --> 00:05:23.700
It can also be a time consuming process.

96
00:05:23.700 --> 00:05:26.430
Creating each frame and making believable transitions

97
00:05:26.430 --> 00:05:29.820
between frames can require a dedicated animator

98
00:05:29.820 --> 00:05:31.653
or team of animators.

99
00:05:32.910 --> 00:05:35.370
The next time you watch a film with animated elements

100
00:05:35.370 --> 00:05:38.100
or special effects in it, check the credits to notice

101
00:05:38.100 --> 00:05:40.110
how many animators worked on it.

102
00:05:40.110 --> 00:05:41.793
It might be more than you think.

103
00:05:45.895 --> 00:05:50.895
A frame is one single still image in an animation sequence.

104
00:05:51.180 --> 00:05:54.513
So we can see six different frames here.

105
00:05:55.710 --> 00:05:58.983
And when we run them together, we get this animation.

106
00:06:00.420 --> 00:06:02.640
Think of frames like pages in a flipbook,

107
00:06:02.640 --> 00:06:04.800
when turned quickly, the images move

108
00:06:04.800 --> 00:06:06.000
and are brought to life.

109
00:06:08.550 --> 00:06:10.200
Pause here and share with someone your impression

110
00:06:10.200 --> 00:06:11.913
of this animation sequence.

111
00:06:18.990 --> 00:06:19.940
Thanks for sharing.

112
00:06:22.740 --> 00:06:25.350
Often animators will use a storyboard to get a sense

113
00:06:25.350 --> 00:06:28.113
of the pace, flow, and direction of the animation.

114
00:06:29.220 --> 00:06:31.620
A storyboard should feature the most important moments

115
00:06:31.620 --> 00:06:32.523
in the animation.

116
00:06:33.690 --> 00:06:36.930
Even if your animation idea does not use a narrative format,

117
00:06:36.930 --> 00:06:38.880
such as if the animation will feature

118
00:06:38.880 --> 00:06:42.390
moving geometric shapes, a storyboard is still useful

119
00:06:42.390 --> 00:06:45.210
to create before getting immersed into the process

120
00:06:45.210 --> 00:06:46.743
of animating each frame.

121
00:06:48.510 --> 00:06:49.500
Pause here and share with someone.

122
00:06:49.500 --> 00:06:51.333
Have you used a storyboard before?

123
00:06:58.680 --> 00:07:00.830
Thanks for sharing your use of storyboards.

124
00:07:01.770 --> 00:07:04.620
A storyboard does not need to be made up of highly detailed

125
00:07:04.620 --> 00:07:06.273
and beautifully rendered images.

126
00:07:07.410 --> 00:07:10.080
It can be rough sketches that indicate an intention

127
00:07:10.080 --> 00:07:13.485
for the animated sequence, featuring descriptive annotations

128
00:07:13.485 --> 00:07:15.333
to explain your idea more clearly.

129
00:07:16.410 --> 00:07:20.283
You can see a great example of a visual storyboard here.

130
00:07:23.790 --> 00:07:26.040
There are different possibilities for animations

131
00:07:26.040 --> 00:07:28.790
depending on the tools and software you have available.

132
00:07:29.730 --> 00:07:31.440
When starting out, it can be helpful

133
00:07:31.440 --> 00:07:34.440
to keep your ideas simple and use minimal technology.

134
00:07:34.440 --> 00:07:38.460
For instance, stop motion animation requires only a camera,

135
00:07:38.460 --> 00:07:41.793
a stable surface or tripod, and a movable object.

136
00:07:43.800 --> 00:07:45.870
Discuss with the partner an idea you have

137
00:07:45.870 --> 00:07:47.490
for a short animation.

138
00:07:47.490 --> 00:07:48.963
Pause here while you do this.

139
00:07:57.420 --> 00:07:59.970
Thanks for sharing your idea for a short animation.

140
00:08:01.047 --> 00:08:02.010
Here is Aisha.

141
00:08:02.010 --> 00:08:04.110
I'd like to make a stop motion animation

142
00:08:04.110 --> 00:08:07.530
of a plasticine character jumping up and down in the air.

143
00:08:07.530 --> 00:08:09.420
I'll use thin wire to move it slightly

144
00:08:09.420 --> 00:08:11.013
before taking each photo.

145
00:08:12.210 --> 00:08:13.050
And Alex.

146
00:08:13.050 --> 00:08:14.250
Using digital software,

147
00:08:14.250 --> 00:08:17.340
I'm going to create a short animation of a bouncing ball,

148
00:08:17.340 --> 00:08:19.560
changing its roundness as it bounces,

149
00:08:19.560 --> 00:08:21.810
and adding an elliptical shadow underneath

150
00:08:21.810 --> 00:08:23.640
to make it look more realistic.

151
00:08:23.640 --> 00:08:24.873
I love these ideas.

152
00:08:27.810 --> 00:08:29.910
Let's have a check for understanding.

153
00:08:29.910 --> 00:08:32.190
What is a frame in animation?

154
00:08:32.190 --> 00:08:35.250
Is it A, the border around an image;

155
00:08:35.250 --> 00:08:38.730
B, the tool used to crop a picture;

156
00:08:38.730 --> 00:08:42.540
C, a still image that is part of a sequence;

157
00:08:42.540 --> 00:08:45.900
or D, a folder where animations are stored?

158
00:08:45.900 --> 00:08:47.100
Pause here while you decide,

159
00:08:47.100 --> 00:08:48.933
what is the frame in animation?

160
00:08:57.240 --> 00:08:59.490
Well done if you selected answer C.

161
00:08:59.490 --> 00:09:02.010
Indeed, a frame in animation is a still image

162
00:09:02.010 --> 00:09:03.573
that is part of a sequence.

163
00:09:05.400 --> 00:09:07.563
And now it's time for your first task.

164
00:09:08.760 --> 00:09:11.340
I would like you to sketch or digitally design

165
00:09:11.340 --> 00:09:13.140
a short animation storyboard,

166
00:09:13.140 --> 00:09:17.040
which includes three to four frames with annotations.

167
00:09:17.040 --> 00:09:20.313
So pause here while you have a go at this task.

168
00:09:21.480 --> 00:09:23.180
I'll see you when you're finished.

169
00:09:30.420 --> 00:09:31.530
It's great to be back with you.

170
00:09:31.530 --> 00:09:33.660
How did you get on with that task of sketching

171
00:09:33.660 --> 00:09:36.660
or digitally designing a short animation storyboard,

172
00:09:36.660 --> 00:09:39.660
which includes three to four frames with annotations?

173
00:09:39.660 --> 00:09:41.063
You might have said something like this.

174
00:09:41.063 --> 00:09:42.600
Here is Alex.

175
00:09:42.600 --> 00:09:44.100
So in this first image, we've got,

176
00:09:44.100 --> 00:09:45.570
the shadow gets lighter

177
00:09:45.570 --> 00:09:47.913
when the ball is further from the ground.

178
00:09:49.650 --> 00:09:51.690
In the next image, the ball lands on the ground

179
00:09:51.690 --> 00:09:54.513
and Alex has made that ball wider.

180
00:09:56.070 --> 00:09:58.860
Next, the ball lengthens when bouncing back up

181
00:09:58.860 --> 00:10:01.113
and we can see the shadow is lightened again.

182
00:10:02.220 --> 00:10:03.420
And then in the final image,

183
00:10:03.420 --> 00:10:06.123
the ball steadily comes to a stop on the ground.

184
00:10:07.410 --> 00:10:09.720
My storyboard shows the key features and frames

185
00:10:09.720 --> 00:10:12.063
for an animated bouncing ball sequence.

186
00:10:14.790 --> 00:10:16.410
I think this is gonna be really effective.

187
00:10:16.410 --> 00:10:17.643
Great job, Alex.

188
00:10:20.280 --> 00:10:22.320
And now we're onto our next learning cycle;

189
00:10:22.320 --> 00:10:24.753
creating and refining a short animation.

190
00:10:25.890 --> 00:10:29.460
All animators, including those in games, films, and adverts,

191
00:10:29.460 --> 00:10:32.343
rely on the same basic principles of animation.

192
00:10:33.390 --> 00:10:36.420
Even complex animation start with storyboards,

193
00:10:36.420 --> 00:10:38.403
simple keyframes and loops.

194
00:10:39.630 --> 00:10:41.880
Pause here and share with someone your impressions

195
00:10:41.880 --> 00:10:44.583
of this storyboard that we can see on the screen.

196
00:10:52.650 --> 00:10:53.600
Thanks for sharing.

197
00:10:55.620 --> 00:10:58.563
A keyframe marks a change in the movement or design.

198
00:10:59.700 --> 00:11:02.490
They are important because they guide the in-between frames

199
00:11:02.490 --> 00:11:05.463
and shape the overall flow of the animation sequence.

200
00:11:06.685 --> 00:11:08.160
Your keyframes might be created

201
00:11:08.160 --> 00:11:11.160
by referring to a storyboard and making sure they exist

202
00:11:11.160 --> 00:11:12.390
in your animation timeline

203
00:11:12.390 --> 00:11:15.663
before creating the subtler transitional frames.

204
00:11:17.520 --> 00:11:20.490
If you're making a hand drawn animation of a blinking eye,

205
00:11:20.490 --> 00:11:22.930
then the two keyframes would be an open eye

206
00:11:24.137 --> 00:11:25.800
and a closed eye.

207
00:11:25.800 --> 00:11:28.320
So you've got keyframe 1, the closed eye

208
00:11:28.320 --> 00:11:30.483
and keyframe 2, the open eye.

209
00:11:31.380 --> 00:11:32.630
And here's our animation.

210
00:11:34.860 --> 00:11:37.050
With these two key frames in the timeline,

211
00:11:37.050 --> 00:11:38.280
you would create more frames

212
00:11:38.280 --> 00:11:40.140
to fill the in-between moments of the eyelid,

213
00:11:40.140 --> 00:11:43.773
gradually opening and closing to create a natural blink.

214
00:11:46.350 --> 00:11:49.380
Loops can be used in an animation to create repetition

215
00:11:49.380 --> 00:11:52.503
or reverse a sequence to save time re-animating.

216
00:11:53.580 --> 00:11:55.290
Social media GIFs are often loops

217
00:11:55.290 --> 00:11:57.660
that run endlessly without stopping.

218
00:11:57.660 --> 00:11:59.160
There may be a clear beginning and end

219
00:11:59.160 --> 00:12:01.830
that jumps between frames or a loop can be made

220
00:12:01.830 --> 00:12:04.170
to end the sequence in the same way it begins

221
00:12:04.170 --> 00:12:06.153
for a seamless timeline transition.

222
00:12:09.090 --> 00:12:10.940
Let's have a check for understanding.

223
00:12:12.150 --> 00:12:15.330
A frame that marks a significant change within an animation

224
00:12:15.330 --> 00:12:16.507
is known as a...

225
00:12:18.054 --> 00:12:19.143
A, key frame;

226
00:12:20.640 --> 00:12:22.473
B, sequence shifter;

227
00:12:23.910 --> 00:12:25.443
C, key point;

228
00:12:26.730 --> 00:12:28.383
or D, moment maker.

229
00:12:29.940 --> 00:12:33.840
Pause here while you decide what a frame that marks

230
00:12:33.840 --> 00:12:36.933
a significant change within an animation is known as.

231
00:12:45.180 --> 00:12:47.370
Well done if you selected answer A.

232
00:12:47.370 --> 00:12:49.860
Indeed, a frame that marks a significant change

233
00:12:49.860 --> 00:12:52.533
within an animation is known as a key frame.

234
00:12:55.950 --> 00:12:59.010
Artists approach making animations in different ways

235
00:12:59.010 --> 00:13:00.480
to creatively tell stories

236
00:13:00.480 --> 00:13:03.690
and communicate their ideas to audiences.

237
00:13:03.690 --> 00:13:07.440
Hayao Miyazaki is a co-founder of Studio Ghibli,

238
00:13:07.440 --> 00:13:10.500
renowned for hand-drawn animation that blends fantasy

239
00:13:10.500 --> 00:13:12.450
with real-world themes.

240
00:13:12.450 --> 00:13:14.340
His films showcase rich storytelling

241
00:13:14.340 --> 00:13:17.280
and imaginative character designs demonstrating

242
00:13:17.280 --> 00:13:20.523
how traditional 2D animation brings art to life.

243
00:13:21.690 --> 00:13:24.360
Matt Partridge works with hand-drawn frames

244
00:13:24.360 --> 00:13:26.580
and character animation showcasing

245
00:13:26.580 --> 00:13:28.413
classic animation techniques.

246
00:13:29.550 --> 00:13:33.720
Emily Howells is a 2D mixed-media animator and illustrator.

247
00:13:33.720 --> 00:13:35.190
Her style shows expressive

248
00:13:35.190 --> 00:13:37.683
and achievable possibilities with animation.

249
00:13:40.200 --> 00:13:42.990
Yasmine Djedje-Fisher-Azoume's work

250
00:13:42.990 --> 00:13:46.740
blends digital 2D animation with analog techniques,

251
00:13:46.740 --> 00:13:48.690
drawing inspiration from textures,

252
00:13:48.690 --> 00:13:50.793
traditions, and cultural memory.

253
00:13:52.440 --> 00:13:55.800
Ishu Patel is known for experimental short animations

254
00:13:55.800 --> 00:13:59.460
using paint on glass and innovative digital techniques.

255
00:13:59.460 --> 00:14:01.410
His films reveal cultural symbolism

256
00:14:01.410 --> 00:14:03.363
and creativity through animation.

257
00:14:04.680 --> 00:14:06.840
And Sarah Ezekiel creates artwork

258
00:14:06.840 --> 00:14:09.720
using assistive technology, EyeGaze.

259
00:14:09.720 --> 00:14:12.330
She highlights how tools and technology can be used

260
00:14:12.330 --> 00:14:15.123
to enable expressive animations and artworks.

261
00:14:17.640 --> 00:14:19.680
A common mistake when making animations

262
00:14:19.680 --> 00:14:23.193
is using too few frames, which makes movement look jumpy.

263
00:14:24.510 --> 00:14:27.090
Whilst animating, check the flow and transitions

264
00:14:27.090 --> 00:14:30.120
of your images by scrolling through the image gallery

265
00:14:30.120 --> 00:14:31.683
or moving through the timeline.

266
00:14:32.910 --> 00:14:35.730
Animation takes time and practice to master.

267
00:14:35.730 --> 00:14:38.610
With each animation you make, you'll learn more techniques

268
00:14:38.610 --> 00:14:40.620
to help create convincing sequences

269
00:14:40.620 --> 00:14:42.273
that captivate your audience.

270
00:14:43.920 --> 00:14:45.870
There's more to animation than simply drawing

271
00:14:45.870 --> 00:14:47.940
moving pictures quickly.

272
00:14:47.940 --> 00:14:50.977
It requires planning, storyboards, frames,

273
00:14:50.977 --> 00:14:54.603
keyframes and timelines to carefully control movement.

274
00:14:55.620 --> 00:14:58.620
Keyframes outline important moments.

275
00:14:58.620 --> 00:15:01.290
Frames gradually build movement.

276
00:15:01.290 --> 00:15:03.930
And timelines and loops can be used to organize the pace

277
00:15:03.930 --> 00:15:05.703
and smoothness of the animation.

278
00:15:08.430 --> 00:15:10.280
Let's have a check for understanding.

279
00:15:11.310 --> 00:15:13.260
Which of the following is a common mistake

280
00:15:13.260 --> 00:15:14.763
when making animations?

281
00:15:16.200 --> 00:15:18.783
A, testing the animation frequently;

282
00:15:20.220 --> 00:15:23.073
B, planning the sketches before animating;

283
00:15:24.630 --> 00:15:27.453
C, adjusting timing on the timeline;

284
00:15:28.860 --> 00:15:32.283
D, using too few frames, making movement look jumpy.

285
00:15:33.540 --> 00:15:34.800
Pause here while you decide

286
00:15:34.800 --> 00:15:38.673
which of these is a common mistake when making animations.

287
00:15:46.290 --> 00:15:48.210
Well done if you selected answer D.

288
00:15:48.210 --> 00:15:51.660
Indeed, using two few frames making movement look jumpy

289
00:15:51.660 --> 00:15:54.603
is a common mistake when making animations.

290
00:15:58.410 --> 00:16:00.510
And now it's time for your next task.

291
00:16:00.510 --> 00:16:03.183
I would like you to create a short loop animation.

292
00:16:04.350 --> 00:16:05.550
You should:

293
00:16:05.550 --> 00:16:07.590
select a simple movement to animate,

294
00:16:07.590 --> 00:16:10.740
such as a blinking character, a bouncing ball,

295
00:16:10.740 --> 00:16:12.783
waving hand, or a moving object.

296
00:16:14.910 --> 00:16:16.350
Plan and use key frames

297
00:16:16.350 --> 00:16:18.633
to mark changes in movement or design.

298
00:16:21.270 --> 00:16:23.463
Apply loops to smooth your animation.

299
00:16:25.200 --> 00:16:26.700
So pause here while you have a go

300
00:16:26.700 --> 00:16:29.073
at creating a short loop animation.

301
00:16:31.710 --> 00:16:34.313
Enjoy your task and I'll see you when you're finished.

302
00:16:41.850 --> 00:16:43.110
That's good feedback with you.

303
00:16:43.110 --> 00:16:44.700
How did it get on with that task

304
00:16:44.700 --> 00:16:46.773
of creating a short loop animation?

305
00:16:48.101 --> 00:16:51.660
We might have created something like this. Here's Alex.

306
00:16:51.660 --> 00:16:54.270
I made an animated bouncing ball sequence

307
00:16:54.270 --> 00:16:55.980
through digital software.

308
00:16:55.980 --> 00:16:58.740
I widened and lengthened the shape of the ball

309
00:16:58.740 --> 00:16:59.970
to make it look bouncier

310
00:16:59.970 --> 00:17:02.673
and applied a loop to make a continuous animation.

311
00:17:04.590 --> 00:17:07.110
Pause here and share with someone your impressions

312
00:17:07.110 --> 00:17:08.943
of Alex's animation.

313
00:17:17.880 --> 00:17:19.710
Thanks for sharing those impressions

314
00:17:19.710 --> 00:17:22.920
and now sharing your short animations with each other,

315
00:17:22.920 --> 00:17:26.463
offering each other some feedback on your animations.

316
00:17:28.110 --> 00:17:29.580
Can you spot the keyframes?

317
00:17:29.580 --> 00:17:33.510
Can you spot any little touches like Alex?

318
00:17:33.510 --> 00:17:36.510
Change the shape of the ball and also the lightness

319
00:17:36.510 --> 00:17:38.490
or darkness of the shadow.

320
00:17:38.490 --> 00:17:40.173
What things can you spot in each other's animation

321
00:17:40.173 --> 00:17:43.353
that have really helped them to be effective and successful?

322
00:17:45.510 --> 00:17:47.510
Take some time to share with each other.

323
00:17:54.960 --> 00:17:55.910
Thanks for sharing.

324
00:17:57.060 --> 00:17:59.280
And finally, I'd like you to share with each other

325
00:17:59.280 --> 00:18:02.040
what's an idea that you have for a future animation?

326
00:18:02.040 --> 00:18:03.790
What might you like to create next?

327
00:18:04.770 --> 00:18:08.133
Take some time to share your future animation aspirations.

328
00:18:14.370 --> 00:18:15.363
Thanks for sharing.

329
00:18:17.550 --> 00:18:19.950
In our lesson, "Introduction to Animation:

330
00:18:19.950 --> 00:18:21.450
Bringing Digital Art to Life,"

331
00:18:21.450 --> 00:18:23.280
we've covered the following.

332
00:18:23.280 --> 00:18:26.553
Animation is created by sequencing images over time.

333
00:18:27.630 --> 00:18:29.700
Frames and keyframes are the building blocks

334
00:18:29.700 --> 00:18:31.143
of digital animation.

335
00:18:32.310 --> 00:18:34.800
Timelines help animators to create the structure

336
00:18:34.800 --> 00:18:37.410
and sequence of an animation.

337
00:18:37.410 --> 00:18:39.600
Well done everyone for joining me with this lesson.

338
00:18:39.600 --> 00:18:42.360
It was so great to explore animation together,

339
00:18:42.360 --> 00:18:46.050
your experience of it, your enjoyment of it,

340
00:18:46.050 --> 00:18:47.880
and to then have the go

341
00:18:47.880 --> 00:18:51.180
at creating your own sequence of animation.

342
00:18:51.180 --> 00:18:52.860
I hope you've enjoyed this lesson,

343
00:18:52.860 --> 00:18:54.630
and I hope you're excited

344
00:18:54.630 --> 00:18:57.280
about where you're going to take your animation next.

345
00:18:58.770 --> 00:19:00.360
And run to look out for the credits

346
00:19:00.360 --> 00:19:02.700
on the next animation that you watch.

347
00:19:02.700 --> 00:19:04.770
Check out how many animators were involved

348
00:19:04.770 --> 00:19:06.153
in that piece of work.

349
00:19:08.220 --> 00:19:09.390
I've really enjoyed teaching you

350
00:19:09.390 --> 00:19:10.530
and I'm looking forward to seeing you

351
00:19:10.530 --> 00:19:12.000
at another art lesson soon.

352
00:19:12.000 --> 00:19:13.683
Until then, stay creative.

lessons.lessonTitle: Digital painting techniques: brushstrokes and beyond

lessonKeywords.description: the transparency level of a digital brush or layer
the rate at which paint is applied when a brushstroke is made
building up visual effects by stacking elements in separate digital layers
the technique of merging colours or tones smoothly

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Digital brushes can mimic traditional media whilst offering flexibility and control.
Opacity and flow settings control subtlety and intensity of brushstrokes.
Brush customisation can be used to express a personal artistic style.
Layering and blending allows digital artists to gradually build up elements and create smooth transitions between them.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Realism depends on how brush settings, layering and blending are applied - not the tool itself. Technique and practice are crucial.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Using digital brushes automatically makes artwork look realistic.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can apply digital brush techniques, including opacity, flow, layering and texture, to create expressive and realistic digital paintings.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Encourage pupils to experiment with brush settings rather than aiming for a “perfect” outcome - confidence with tools develops through play, not just replication.

The outcome for today's lesson is I can apply digital brush techniques, including opacity, flow, layering, and texture, to create expressive and realistic digital paintings.
We have some keywords in our lesson.
Let's go through them.
Opacity, flow, layering, and blending.
What do these keywords mean? Opacity is the transparency level of a digital brush or layer.
Flow, the rate at which paint is applied when a brushstroke is made.
Layering, building up visual effects by stacking elements in separate digital layers.
And blending, the technique of merging colors or tones smoothly.
These are our keywords: opacity, flow, layering, and blending.
Let's look out for them.
Let's listen out for them.
They will be coming up in our lesson today.
Our lesson is called Digital Painting Techniques: Brushstrokes and Beyond, and it has two learning cycles, digital brush tools and developing digital art techniques.
Let's begin by exploring digital brush tools.
Digital paintings are created using digital brushes.
How do you think digital brushes differ from traditional paint brushes? Pause here and share with someone.
Thanks for sharing.
While we're here, pause for a moment longer and share with someone your impressions of this digitally created painting that we can see on the screen.
Thanks for sharing.
Digital brushes are powerful tools for artists.
They can mimic a range of traditional art materials like pastels, pencils, and paints, and they can be used to create custom textures like rocky mountains, flowing clouds, or luminous stars.
How artists use digital brushes influences how expressive these tools can be, and a lot can be achieved even with a few simple brushes.
We can see an example of a digital brush on the screen there.
Pause here and share with someone, have you seen one of these digital brushes before or used one? Thanks for sharing.
Brush settings can be changed to alter the appearance and effect of digital brushstrokes, including their opacity, flow, size, pressure sensitivity.
Opacity controls how transparent a brushstroke is.
Lower opacity makes marks lighter and more subtle, while high opacity creates bold, solid strokes.
When opacity is reduced, brushstrokes can be layered to gradually create depth and soft transitions.
Flow determines how much paint is applied with each stroke.
A low flow setting is like having a small amount of paint on a traditional brush, while a high flow setting carries a lot of paint, so it'll be instantly noticeable.
When flow is reduced, each brushstroke builds up color slowly and can allow for smooth blending.
Pause here and share with someone your impressions of the painting we can see on the screen.
What kind of flow of paint do you think has been applied? Thanks for sharing.
It seems to me like quite a high flow of paint has been used there.
Let's have a check for understanding.
What happens if the flow of a brush is set very low? Is it a, the brushstroke appears darker, b, the brushstroke builds up gradually, c, the colors automatically blend, d, the brush texture disappears.
Pause here while you decide, what happens if the flow of a brush is set very low? Well done if you selected answer b.
Indeed, if the flow of a brush is set very low, the brushstroke builds up gradually.
Changing the size of a brush allows you to cover larger or smaller areas of the canvas.
Adding a color wash to the background will benefit from using a larger brush, while adding smaller details will be easier with a smaller brush.
Use the zoom function to focus in on sections of a digital artwork, but remember to zoom out and view the whole artwork regularly.
Pressure sensitivity is a setting available for some tablets, stylus, and digital art software tools.
When applied to a brush, you can use different pressures whilst drawing to change the opacity, flow, or size of the brush to further mimic the effects of traditional materials.
Digital visual effects can be made by using different brush settings or by erasing and blending with them.
You can also apply different brush settings to the eraser and blend tool.
Erasing in this way can build textures into an artwork or layer.
Blending can be used to create smooth transitions between tones, colors, shapes, and layers.
Many artists experiment with digital art tools.
David Hockney has increasingly used digital tools to make art through his career.
In his vibrant landscape artworks, he shows how traditional mark-making effects can be simulated and extended digitally.
Tishk Barzanji is a digital painter inspired by architecture, surrealism, and texture.
His richly symbolic work show layering and the stylized ways that digital mark-making can be used.
And Vince Fraser combines illustration, photography, and layered textures through digital tools.
His work explores Afrofuturism and cultural identity through digital experimentation.
So these are just some of the many artists experimenting with digital art tools.
Pause here and share with someone, do you know of any other artists experimenting with digital art tools? Thanks for sharing.
Let's have a check for understanding.
Which tool helps create smooth transitions between colors? Is it a, eraser, b, layer mask, c, blending, or d, zoom? Pause here while you decide, which tool helps create smooth transitions between colors? Well done if you selected answer c.
Indeed, it's blending that helps create smooth transitions between colors.
And now it's time for your first task.
I would like you to create a digital sampler sheet of digital brush experiments.
You should explore different types of opacity, flow, and texture settings, label each example with the brush settings used, explore and build confidence through play.
So pause here while you have a go at this task.
Have fun and create a digital sampler sheet of digital brush experiments.
I'll see you when you're finished.
It's great to be back with you.
How did you get on with that task of creating a digital sampler sheet of digital brush experiments? You might have created something like this and said something like this.
Here's Laura.
"I experimented with different digital brush settings, mimicking textures for watercolor, acrylic, pastels, and graphite." And great to see those recordings of opacity and flow used each time.
And now we're onto our next learning cycle, developing digital art techniques.
Layers allow artists to separate parts of their work.
What do you think are the advantages of creating a digital work using layers? Pause here and share with someone, what do you think? Thanks for sharing.
Using layers makes it easier to edit and refine without disturbing other elements.
For example, one layer might hold the background, another the subject, and another the details.
This approach to making digital artworks makes the process more controlled and editing more flexible.
I wonder if you had some answers like these.
Blending merges any two visual elements together smoothly, such as tones, colors, shapes, and layers.
Blending can be used to create realistic transitions for skin tones, shadows, or skies.
Pause here and share with someone your impressions of the blending in this digital artwork.
Thanks for sharing.
Texture brushes can imitate surfaces like fabric, stone, glass, or fur.
They help digital artworks to feel tactile and expressive.
Pause here and share with someone your impressions of this artwork.
Thanks for sharing.
Layers, textures, and blending effects are commonly used by artists to create a range of explorative art forms. Toyin Ojih Odutola is known for highly textural portraiture using digital and traditional media, exploring identity and storytelling through layered, intricate mark-making.
Riva Lehrer is a painter and digital illustrator exploring identity, disability, and the body.
She uses layered, traditional, and digital media to develop textured mark-making effects in her work.
And Anthony Azekwoh is a digital painter who explores folklore, mythology, narrative, and expressive digital brushwork.
He uses texture, depth, vibrant color, and layered techniques in his digital compositions.
Let's have a check for understanding.
Why is layering important in digital painting? A, it separates elements for easier editing.
B, it makes files smaller for easier editing.
C, it automatically adds shadows when editing.
D, it saves the image as a JPEG after editing.
Pause here while you decide why is layering important in digital painting.
Well done if you selected answer a.
Indeed, layering is important in digital painting because it separates elements for easier editing.
Using digital brushes doesn't automatically make an artwork look realistic.
Realism depends on consideration of the elements, and principles of art, and a thoughtful use of settings and techniques, like layering or blending.
Pause here and share with someone your impressions of this painting.
Thanks for sharing.

Thanks for sharing.

Sophie Kahn works with 3D scanning and digital media, exploring imperfection and texture.

These works are often layered in material and meaning, exploring identity and cultural memory.

Thanks for sharing.

Pause here while you do this.
Thanks for having a go at that.

Digital brushes can mimic traditional media whilst offering flexibility and control.
Opacity and flow settings control subtlety and intensity of brushstrokes.
Brush customization can be used to express a personal artistic style.
Layering and blending allows digital artists to gradually build up elements and create smooth transitions between them.

It was great to look at layering and blending and building up those elements of our digital artwork to create hopefully something that you're feeling quite proud of.
I hope you've enjoyed this lesson.
I've really enjoyed teaching you.
I'm looking forward to seeing you at another art lesson soon.
Until then, stay creative.

lessons.lessonTitle: Cyanotype: using the power of the sun

lessonKeywords.description: a photographic printing process that produces a cyan blue image using sunlight and light-sensitive chemicals
the amount of light allowed to hit the light-sensitive surface to create an image
an image made without a camera by placing objects directly on a light-sensitive surface and exposing it to light
the difference between light and dark areas in an image

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Cyanotype is an early photographic process using UV light to create blue toned images.
Light exposure and object placement affect the final result of a cyanotype.
Photograms explore composition through shape, light, and shadow.
Contrast can be manipulated by exposure time and material transparency.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: The image develops gradually and deepens in colour after rinsing and drying; exposure time and sunlight intensity affect results.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Cyanotype images always appear instantly after sun exposure.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can create a cyanotype print and refine it digitally to explore composition and contrast.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Encourage pupils to test different exposure times and object transparencies - remind them that unpredictability is part of the creative process. Link back to photography’s history to deepen understanding.

lessons.lessonTitle: Mixed-media digital art: combining traditional and digital methods

lessonKeywords.description: using more than one artistic medium in a single artwork
placing different visual elements on top of each other to create depth and complexity
the arrangement of visual elements within an artwork

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Traditional and digital methods can be combined in art to create a range of visual outcomes.
Analogue and digital media can be merged effectively by using composition principles.
Textures and surfaces can be used in digital media to create images which look handmade.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Digital tools expand, rather than replace, creativity. Artists can blend hand-drawn, painted, or textured work into digital layers to achieve unique results.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Digital art lacks the creativity or authenticity of traditional methods.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can combine traditional and digital methods to create a mixed-media artwork.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Encourage pupils to see digital art as an extension of traditional methods. Remind them to experiment boldly, save versions frequently and reflect on how analogue textures enhance digital compositions.

lessons.lessonTitle: Deepening the understanding of the principles of textile design

lessonKeywords.description: the starting point of inspiration (e.g. flower)
how an artist/designer changes or adapts a source
methods such as embroidery, appliqué, or sewing

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Motifs can be developed from a source such as a flower and transformed through textile techniques.
The principles of textile design balance, contrast, repetition, and emphasis guide creative choices.
Different techniques change the outcome: appliqué, embroidery, or printing can make the same motif look different.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Using different techniques can change your textile work. A motif may look flat when printed, detailed with embroidery, or bold and layered in appliqué. Your choice of textile technique changes the way a motif is interpreted.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: If I use the same motif, my work will always look the same.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can develop a textile design from a source by using balance, contrast, repetition, and emphasis with different techniques.

teacherTips.teacherTip: It is useful to teach pupils to apply the principles of textiles as a system, giving them a strong starting point to carry forward into a successful outcome.

lessons.lessonTitle: Embroidery skills: creating detailed and decorative stitching

lessonKeywords.description: advanced embroidery techniques that add texture, detail, and depth.
the decoration or enhancement applied to the surface of a fabric through techniques like embroidery.
a test piece to trial and experiment with ideas before final work.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Artists identify strong sources from their research and sketchbooks to inspire embroidery designs.
Artists apply complex stitching techniques to add depth, texture and visual interest.
Choices in surface design including placement, colour and stitch variety help capture the essence of the theme.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Using a variety of embroidery stitches when creating a refined sample creates visual interest, contrast, texture and depth to the design.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Stitching is for securing fabric pieces together so the type of stitch should be uniform.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can identify suitable sources from my sketchbook and use complex stitches to create detailed, decorative embroidery samples.

teacherTips.teacherTip: This project will suit pupils who already have knowledge of embroidery stiching. Pupils can also develop their samples later on to use in final outcomes.

lessons.lessonTitle: Exploring dyeing methods: colour and pattern creation

lessonKeywords.description: a cut-out shape used to apply paint or dye in a specific pattern
adding colour to fabric by soaking it in dye
a method that prevents dye from colouring certain parts of the fabric

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Artists simplify designs into bold motifs so they can be cut and used as stencils.
Combining dyed backgrounds with stencil printing allows artists to create layered, textured effects.
Combining printing with resist techniques helps control where dye or ink is absorbed, adding contrast.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Different dyeing methods produce different effects, techniques like dip-dyeing, tie-dye, or resist create uneven or patterned results, while immersion dyeing can give a more uniform colour.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: All dyeing methods colour fabric evenly across the whole surface.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can experiment with dyeing and stencil printing techniques to create a patterned fabric design.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Model safe use of a craft knife through practical demonstration and ensure close supervision of pupils.

lessons.lessonTitle: Thematic development: designing cohesive and expressive textile art

lessonKeywords.description: relating to a unifying idea or subject
how well the elements of a design link together
showing feelings, identity, or ideas through design.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Artists use themes to guide and connect their textile designs.
Cohesion comes from repeating motifs, colours and materials in a deliberate way.
Expressive qualities emerge through choices in texture, colour and composition.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Actually, thematic development is about refining ideas so your motifs and techniques feel connected. Too many unrelated ideas can make a design look chaotic — repeating and varying motifs from one clear theme helps create cohesion.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Thematic development means I have to use as many different ideas as possible to make my work interesting.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can develop a textile artwork that is both cohesive and expressive by exploring a theme and combining techniques thoughtfully.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Encourage students to limit themselves to one strong theme and develop it in depth rather than collecting too many unrelated sources. Remind them that cohesion comes from repetition and variation of a few key motifs, not from cramming in lots of ideas.

lessons.lessonTitle: Mixed-media textiles: combining materials and methods

lessonKeywords.description: improving and adjusting your work to make it stronger
changing and repeating a design idea to make it more effective
in textiles combines different materials and techniques, like print, embroidery, or appliqué, in one piece

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Artists use motif development to explore, adapt and strengthen design ideas before applying them to textile techniques.
Refining designs helps ensure motifs work effectively in stitch or appliqué, balancing detail with clarity.
Mixed-media combines print, embroidery and fabric techniques to create layered, textured textiles.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Drawing motifs and sketching developmental ideas during the initial stages in design work helps to consolidate ideas.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: You don't need drawings in a textile project.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can review my project and develop ideas to create a mixed-media motif development sample.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Allow pupils to practise with the technique they would like to use before they start working on motif development. The smaller motif development piece can be developed into a more complex textile final outcome.

lessons.lessonTitle: Weaving techniques: crafting textures and patterns

lessonKeywords.description: woven fabric where the weft forms the pattern or image
the surface quality created through weaving
fabrics made by interlacing fibres through techniques like weaving or knitting

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Artists use constructed textiles in diverse ways, from functional design to large-scale installations.
Cultural background and personal identity often influence an artist’s choice of materials, colours and techniques.
Experimentation with texture and form allows artists to push the boundaries of traditional weaving and tapestry.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Constructed textiles include any fabric created by interlacing, knotting, looping, or bonding fibres such as weaving, knitting, crochet, macramé and even non-woven techniques, not just loom weaving.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Constructed textiles are only made by weaving on a loom.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can design and create a woven sample that uses shape and texture to produce a clear pattern.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Spend some time teaching students how to draw their grid out on grid paper. They should count their warp threads and then count their weft threads and try to mark them on their grid. It is a good idea to also add colour at this stage.

lessons.lessonTitle: Fabric manipulation: techniques for texture and form

lessonKeywords.description: changing or altering fabric to create new shapes, textures, or forms.
gathering fabric with stitches so it creates ripples, folds, or pleats.
The surface quality of fabric, which may feel smooth, rough, soft, or structured.
when fabric is bent or doubled to form ridges, pleats, or layers that add structure and texture.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Artists use fabric manipulation to transform flat textiles into sculptural surfaces with depth and movement.
Techniques such as ruching, layering, and folding create different textures that can change the look of the piece.
Fashion designers and textile artists use these methods to explore ideas, add expression & how fabric is used in design.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Fabric manipulation does add decoration, but it can also change the structure of fabric. Techniques like ruching, folding, or layering can give garments shape, volume, and movement, not just surface detail.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Fabric manipulation is only used to make clothes look more decorative.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explore fabric manipulation techniques and create a textile sample using ruches, layers, or folding.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Pupils should be encouraged to be experimental and intuitive when using these fabric manipulation techniques.

lessonKeywords.description: to show or represent something in a picture, drawing, or description.
a work of art that can be seen in the round, is three dimensional or as a relief.
the outline or shape of something, especially the curves of a surface.
the process of shaping and forming clay, often by hand.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Depicting a person in 3D has been done for hundreds of years using materials such as marble, clay and stone.
Clay is a malleable material and has been used by artists to create portrait forms.
Clay can be used in many ways and an artist's style can be seen through how they manipulate the clay.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: 3D portraits can be created in various sizes and forms, not just large figurative sculptures. They can include small, detailed works or abstract representations.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Only large, figurative sculptures are considered 3D portraits.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can manipulate clay to model 3D portraits.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Encourage students to experiment with the clay’s malleable qualities when creating 3D portraits. Advise them not to have a fixed idea of the final result, but to let the material guide them. This will help foster creativity and allow unexpected forms to emerge during the process.

lessonKeywords.description: a representation of a person, usually focussing on their face, expression and identity
to show or stand for something, often in a visual or symbolic way
the application of media in free sweeping gestures

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: A portrait is a representation of a person, usually focusing on their face, expression, and identity.
Portraits are found across art, craft, and design celebrating individuality.
Artists often use a multidisciplinary approach when creating portraits.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: A portrait can also include symbolic representations, like objects that reflect the person’s personality or even something as unique as a sample of their DNA.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Portraits must always show the person directly.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain how artists use a range of creative tools to represent themselves and other people.

teacherTips.teacherTip: For Learning Cycle 1, you’ll need to find or take a photo for your portrait. This could be of yourself, a loved one, someone you admire, or an everyday person. This task can be pre-prepared or split across two lessons.

lessonKeywords.description: the focus, topic, or image of an artwork, e.g. in a portrait, the subject is the person who has been painted
the feeling or emotion a piece of art gives you (like happy, calm, or sad)
the size of one part of something compared to another part, especially how facial features, body parts or objects fit together

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: The painted portrait is understood to have originated in Ancient Egypt, over 5,000 years ago
Paint allows artists to explore texture, colour, and form, capturing emotion and personality
The versatility of paint enables both realistic and abstract interpretations of a subject

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: While many portraits aim for realism, painting also allows for abstract and emotional interpretations, capturing the subject's personality, mood, and deeper meaning beyond just physical appearance.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: The painted portrait only focuses on realism and accuracy in depicting the subject.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use a limited colour palette to paint a portrait.

teacherTips.teacherTip: You may wish to tailor the artists to your context or use the slide deck in the broad manner planned here. Guidance on facial proportion can be found in the additional materials.

lessonKeywords.description: groups which have been included in artworks and/or have made artworks
a person’s level of importance, rank, or social standing
the way someone stands or sits, especially in to show a certain feeling, attitude, or idea
how the subject’s eyes are directed—whether they are looking directly at the viewer, or in a different direction

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Portraits have historically been used to convey power and use composition to do this
The history of the portrait also highlights a lack of representation, artists are changing this narrative
Portraits are personal representations and can include other elements to help tell a person's story

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Artists use paper, cardboard, silhouettes and even walls to create bold, powerful and expressive figures. You do not need to only paint a face to create a portrait.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Making a portrait always means painting a face.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can create a cut out figure that shows power and presence.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Encourage students to think of this task as performing power through portraiture. It’s not about creating perfect drawings — it’s about collaborating, taking creative risks and owning space in a way that challenges traditional portrait rules.

contentGuidance.contentGuidanceLabel: Depiction or discussion of discriminatory behaviour
contentGuidance.contentGuidanceDescription: Discriminatory behaviour or images, whether on the grounds of race, gender, disability, religion or belief or sexual orientation, or otherwise.

contentGuidance.contentGuidanceLabel: Depiction or discussion of sensitive content
contentGuidance.contentGuidanceDescription: Subjects which particular individuals may be sensitive to, eg, adoption, migration, bereavement or death, divorce, poverty, deprivation.

contentGuidance.contentGuidanceLabel: Depiction or discussion of violence or suffering
contentGuidance.contentGuidanceDescription: Depiction of war, threats of war, death or the aftermath of war.

lessonKeywords.description: is the purposeful arrangement of type to enhance readability, communication and visual impact
the message or idea that is communicated by something, whether it's words, images, or actions
art that is based on an idea or message, not just how it looks

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Artists use text in their work as a powerful tool to convey thoughts and feelings
Typography can be added onto an art work, or be an artwork in its own right
We can use typography to inform our art work and discuss our identity

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Words can express things a face alone might not show — like beliefs, experiences, or emotions. The style of the text also adds meaning.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Words don’t matter that much — it’s the drawing that tells the story.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can understand the power of typography in art, and how it can be used to tell our stories and form the design of a portrait.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Encourage pupils to read their chosen words or quotes aloud before adding them to their portrait. Hearing the words can help them think about tone, emotion, and how the visual style (font, size, placement) can match the feeling behind the words.

lessons.lessonTitle: Using portraiture to reveal and conceal identities

lessonKeywords.description: to hide or obscure parts of something
to show or uncover something that might not be obvious
the area occupied by the main subject
the empty area around or within a subject in an artwork
a dark shape or outline usually filled with black

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Portraits often reveal how a person looks, but artists can also create portraits that conceal their physical appearance.
Portraits can challenge us to look at people from different perspectives rather than traditional representations.
Negative space portraits can help to reveal other aspects of identity.
Playing with materials to express emotions can bring our feelings to the forefront of our portraits.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Negative space may look ‘empty,’ but artists use it intentionally to draw attention elsewhere — it helps us focus on shape, emotion, or story without showing everything. It’s a powerful choice, not a mistake.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Negative space just means there’s nothing there — it’s empty or unfinished

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can play with negative space and mark-making to create an expressive portrait.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Encourage students to focus on shape over detail when working with silhouettes and negative space — this helps shift their thinking from “drawing a person” to “observing shapes,” which can improve observation and creativity.

lessons.lessonTitle: Exploring 3D art materials with casting (paper and plaster)

lessonKeywords.description: a sculpture making technique where a malleable material is formed in mould
a hollow container used to shape the malleable material
a part of the mould that curves around the object or cast in a way that makes it hard to remove the object from the mould. It can trap the cast inside the mould if not designed carefully

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Casting is a sculpting process that allow us to create replicas or translate modelled sculptures into durable materials.
Hands-on experimentation with materials fosters a deeper understanding of their properties.
Exploring different casting methods supports informed choices and more intentional outcomes in future projects.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Plaster and paper have very different properties. Plaster sets quickly and picks up fine details. Paper air dries more slowly and shrinks more as it dries. It might not show fine texture as clearly.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Plaster and paper will behave the same way in a mould.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explore casting techniques through hands-on experimentation to create casts using plaster and paper.

teacherTips.teacherTip: The Additional materials has deeper context on artists. Be mindful of the health and safety around plaster (exothermic reaction & dust).

lessons.lessonTitle: Responding to organic forms with card, papers and modroc

lessonKeywords.description: the process of building or assembling materials to create a structure
a three-dimensional shape that has height, width, and depth, like a cube or sphere
a structure that stays upright without support from walls or other objects

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Artists turn to nature to find shapes, textures, and colours which could inspire sculptural forms
By experimenting with various materials, like clay, paper, or fabrics, we can create unique shapes and forms
We can use sculptural features and designs to express culture, history and emotions

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Artists can employ a range of shapes and forms to create their sculptural works.

lessons.lessonTitle: Exploring biomorphic sculptures using papier mâché

lessonKeywords.description: shapes that look like forms found in nature, such as plants, animals, or the human body
a material made from paper and glue or paste, used to create 3D models and sculptures
connecting two or more parts of a sculpture or structure using glue, tape, staples or other methods

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: A biomorphic sculpture is an art form inspired by organic shapes found in nature.
Artists use various materials including clay, metal, wood, stone, thread, wire or found objects to create organic forms.
We can sketch from nature and simplify the structure to create an idea for a sculpture.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Some sculptures are delicate and light. Sculptural works can be presented in a range of ways including hung, free standing, stacked or in relief.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Sculptures have to be heavy, strong objects which are fully free standing.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can develop biomorphic sculptures through drawing and taking inspiration from nests and eggs.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Greater depth of context around artists as well as source imagery can be found in the Additional materials.

lessonKeywords.description: the structure of an object, referring to three dimensional space
cutting or chipping away from a solid material like wood or stone to shape a 3D form
a sculpture where shapes are raised from a flat background, not fully 3D
the early stage of a sculpture where the basic shape is formed before adding detail

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Thinking in 3D is a valuable skill in fields like architecture, design, and art.
Sketching 3D objects from different angles helps in understanding depth and form.
Breaking down complex forms into simpler shapes makes the object easier to understand.
When carving, removing small amounts at a time helps achieve a more refined and detailed result.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Soap is a soft material, and carving too deeply can cause unintended breakage. It’s important to carve in gradual layers, starting with rough shaping before adding finer details.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: If the surface is carved too deeply, layers can be glued back on later.

lessonKeywords.description: when an artist expresses personal perspectives, emotions, identity, or experiences in their work, rather than striving for objective representation
the artist’s purpose or motivation behind creating a piece of work

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Some artists only make art as pure self-expression - there is no intention to share with an audience.
Some artists intend to make art as pure self-expression, but eventually do share their work with an audience.
Some artists start by creating art as self-expression and with the intention of sharing with others.
In many cultures, creative self-expression is woven into daily life.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Some art is made as an act of pure self-expression. Even deeply personal works are shaped by history, identity, and society, meaning they can take on wider meanings even if the artist did not intend them to.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: All artists make art with the intention of sharing with an audience.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can engage in thinking, making and discussion about art as self-expression.

teacherTips.teacherTip: You could lead by sharing examples of the final task so that pupils understand what the making aspect of the lesson is building up to.

lessons.lessonTitle: Curating identity: choosing what to show in art

lessonKeywords.description: The way an artist represents themselves or others through art.
When an artist hides or obscures parts of their identity, maybe through using abstraction, symbolism, or selective representation.
When an artist intentionally shares aspects of identity, history, or emotions through choices in their work.
The use of objects, colours, or imagery in art to represent deeper meanings or ideas beyond their literal appearance.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Identity is multifaceted and can change over time.
Artists explore and express identity in their work, and they do not always do this through traditional portraits.
Artists make selections about what to conceal or reveal in their work.
You don’t need to share the same identity as an artist to understand and appreciate their work.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Artists make selections about what to conceal or reveal in their work.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: When artists make work about identity, they reveal all aspects of themselves.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can analyse and create artwork that explores how artists choose to conceal or reveal aspects of identity.

teacherTips.teacherTip: This lesson encourages self-exploration and personal reflection, which may bring up strong thoughts or emotions for some pupils.

lessons.lessonTitle: Personal to universal: art as connection

lessonKeywords.description: an emotional reaction
when people, places, or things feel linked together through feelings, experiences, memories, or relationships.
a way of sharing something that happened whether real or imagined.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Art can transcend language, geography and time to communicate ideas or emotions.
Universal themes can be understood globally, even when expressed in different ways.
Artists create spaces or artworks to promote shared feelings or experiences creating connection among their audiences.
Discussing an artwork helps us to make connections and deepen our understanding.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Art connects people because it sparks emotions and ideas, even if everyone sees it differently. It’s the shared experience, not exact understanding, that brings people together.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Art only connects people if everyone understands it the same way.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I understand how art can share ideas and emotions that connect people, even if they are from different places or times.

teacherTips.teacherTip: This lesson has options for either using a camera or drawing a design. If there is computer access, students could print their own imagery to place the figure over.

conflict, or joy.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Craftspeople across cultures play essential roles in creating art that holds spiritual or symbolic meaning.
Craftspeople have created objects used for rituals or ceremonies, such as altarpieces, prayer flags, or ceremonial masks

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Religious art isn’t just paintings or sculptures, it includes architecture, textiles, calligraphy and even temporary creations like Rangoli and sand mandalas, all used to express and connect with the spiritual.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Religious art only includes paintings or sculptures.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can make an artwork inspired by religious practice.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Task  A – You may consider incorporating music to enhance the meditative environment.

the use of objects, colours, or imagery in art to represent deeper meanings or ideas beyond their literal appearance

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Artists might use mapping through literal geography, map-like work or more subjective or abstract representations.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: In Western art history, the roles of men and women are often depicted in traditional ways.

lessons.lessonTitle: 3D Design: form, structure and surface texture

lessonKeywords.description: the 3D shape of an object (its height, width and depth)
how a form is built and supported so it holds together
a container – something that can hold or carry things

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Form can be geometric, organic, or abstract.
Form influences impact and interaction with space and light.
Surface can communicate story, identity, or texture.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Surface texture plays a key role in communicating meaning, mood, or identity in sculpture.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Surface texture is just decoration and doesn’t really matter.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explore how form, structure and surface work together to shape a vessel.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Remind students to keep the armature removable. Encourage them to experiment with form, structure and surface, and prompt them to reflect on what worked well and what they would improve next time.

lessonKeywords.description: the method of building or assembling parts to form a 3D structure
a sculptural technique where raised elements are built up from a flat surface
the shape and structure of a 3D object, including its volume and mass

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Knives or scissors to cut cardboard into desired shapes. Pieces can be bent or folded to create dimensional forms.
Stacking multiple layers of cardboard adds depth and dimension. Layers can be cut differently creating unique profiles.
Roll cardboard into cylinders or fold into angular shapes; origami techniques can also be used.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Cardboard becomes structurally strong when layered, folded or rolled. It is even used in architecture and furniture design for its surprising durability.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Cardboard is too weak to build strong structures.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can cut, shape and build 3D forms with cardboard, using folding, layering and rolling techniques.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Pre-score fold lines lightly to guide students in bending clean, sharp edges. Emphasise test folding first; ensure students plan their shapes before cutting to minimise waste and errors.

lessons.lessonTitle: 3D design: the influence of sources on your investigations

lessonKeywords.description: the starting point or inspiration for design
the cultural, historical, or social background of a source
the process of changing a source into a new textile design

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: By utilising a wide range of source materials, sculptors enrich their creative processes, resulting in dynamic designs.
Exploring sources introduces sculptors to various styles, concepts, and cultural influences, fostering creativity.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Sources are not meant to be copied. They act as a starting point for creativity. Designers explore a source’s shapes, patterns, colours, or meanings and reinterpret them to create original work that reflects their own ideas and context.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: A source is just something to copy.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can identify and apply influences from sources to create original 3D work.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Encourage pupils to see their source as a springboard, not a template. Many pupils may feel they need to copy their chosen image or object directly. Model how to extract shapes, textures, forms, or patterns from the source.

lessonKeywords.description: a sculpture made by combining different found objects
materials that have not been bought or created for the purpose of making art, but have been collected from more random sources
to gather and group objects that link to an idea or theme

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Found materials let artists explore new forms, textures and ideas not possible with traditional sculpture.
Using found objects supports recycling, sustainability and an eco-friendly approach to making art.
Found materials bring history and meaning, letting artists comment on culture, history, or social issues.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Found materials bring unique textures and personal or cultural meaning to a sculpture.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Found materials are just junk and don’t belong in real artwork.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can create a sculpture using found materials that reflect a theme or concept.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Ask pupils to bring in a few found objects linked to a theme (e.g. memory, home, personal choice). Include one “surprise” object that doesn’t fit within the theme. This helps explore contrast, create unexpected links and develop understanding of how meaning shifts when objects are curated.

lessonKeywords.description: the outside of a clay form that can be carved, built up, stamped, or moulded to add texture and meaning
adding patterns, colours, or details to make something more attractive
the idea or message that guides your design

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Carving into the surface of a leather hard piece to create designs, often reveals a contrasting colour underneath.
Scoring the surfaces of clay pieces and applying slip (liquid clay) helps to bond them when joining.
Using pre-made molds to shape clay, allows for intricate designs and uniformity.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Surface design should be planned and integrated to reflect and enhance the sculptural idea.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Surface decoration should be added at the end and doesn’t need much thought.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explore and apply surface decoration techniques on clay, linking them to a chosen theme.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Model how to use everyday objects (toothbrush, fork, lace, leaves) as tools for stamping and texture—this makes the process accessible and sparks creativity. Remind pupils to always score and slip when joining clay to prevent pieces from breaking off when dry.

lessonKeywords.description: a hollow form used to shape plaster
prevents plaster sticking to the model
pouring a liquid material (like plaster) into a mould, where it hardens into the shape of the mould to form a replica

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: When casting, plaster is poured directly over a model to create a mould.
When casting, the model is coated with a release agent to prevent sticking.
A mould can be created in two halves, allowing for more complex shapes.
Applying a thin layer of plaster (poured or brushed) to a model and building up several layers creates a solid shell.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Plaster heats as it sets and pouring too much at once can trap air, cause cracks or damage the model. Layering ensures detail and structure.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: I can just pour all the plaster at once and it will work.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can experiment with three plaster casting methods and show how form, surface and construction interact.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Have clearly labelled example stations for each technique. Use small, manageable forms for faster drying. Demonstrate the proper mixing ratio of plaster to water and health and safety, including wearing face masks and gloves.

lessonKeywords.description: shaping clay by pressing with fingers and thumb
rolling and stacking long strands of clay
flattening clay sheets and joining them to build forms

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Forming clay by pinching and shaping it with fingers is typically used for small bowls or decorative objects.
Rolling out, stacking and joining coils (long strands of clay) can be used to build up the walls of pots and sculptures.
Slabbing involves flattening clay into sheets (slabs) and assembling them to create structures like boxes or walls.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Simple clay techniques can be used to build complex and expressive sculptural forms.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Basic clay techniques like pinch or coil are only for beginners.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explore different methods of clay construction to build a sculptural form.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Encourage pupils to talk about their choices while making. Asking “Why did you choose that shape/angle?” helps them link their practical work to themes (identity, imagination, emotions) rather than focusing only on technique.

lessons.lessonTitle: 3D Design: introduction to the principles of sculpture

lessonKeywords.description: a three-dimensional art form
a small-scale model used to visualise and test a sculpture before making it.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Sculpture is a three-dimensional art form.
Principles include form, space, balance, texture, proportion, and movement.
Traditional and modern sculpture transform materials into expressive forms.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Sculpture can be abstract or symbolic, focusing on space, balance, and movement rather than realism.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Sculpture must be realistic or life-like to be considered good.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explore and apply the core principles of sculpture to create a maquette.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Adapt artists and subject matter to reflect student interests. Model how to describe sculpture using the core principles. Emphasise that there’s no single ‘right’ answer—individual interpretation and experimentation are part of the process.

lessons.lessonTitle: 3D design: an introduction to the areas of study

lessonKeywords.description: the physical substances artists use to make a sculpture — like clay, wood, metal, paper, or fabric
the main idea or message behind a sculpture
the features or characteristics of a material, such as texture, weight, flexibility, or strength, that affect how it feels and behaves

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Materials affect aesthetics and tactile qualities.
Techniques vary with each material: carving, modeling, casting, assembling.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Any material can be powerful in sculpture if it supports the concept or message being expressed.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Expensive or traditional materials are better for making sculptures.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explore how different materials influence the making and meaning of a sculpture.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Model how to test and observe materials. Emphasise that there are no ‘best’ materials, just ones that work for your idea. Let students explore freely before refining.

lessonKeywords.description: the use of two or more artistic materials or techniques in a single artwork
texture that can be physically felt (e.g., rough, bumpy, soft)
the illusion of texture created using techniques like shading, pattern, or collage

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Combining different materials and techniques can allow artists to convey complex ideas and emotions.
Mixing media creates interesting textures and dimensions that can enhance the visual and tactile experience of a piece.
Artists can break away from traditional boundaries by experimenting with unconventional combinations.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Mixed media is intentional. Each material or technique is chosen for a reason, either to add texture, create contrast, or express an idea or emotion. Artists think carefully about how the materials work together to enhance the artwork.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Mixed media just means using any random materials together, it doesn’t really matter what you choose.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can combine different materials and techniques to create a mixed media artwork.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Greater contextual information on the artists' work can be found in the additional materials. You may wish to alter the imagery to better fit your project themes.

lessonKeywords.description: a printmaking technique where only the raised parts of a surface are inked
a method where the same block is carved and printed in layers, reducing it each time
the surface (like lino or wood) from which a print is made

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Relief printing is a technique where the raised surfaces of a plate are inked and pressed onto paper, creating an image.
Relief printing dates back to ancient times and was essential for reproducing images before modern printing existed.
Printing gives opportunity for a wide range of experimentation and discovery.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Artists can experiment with texture, layering, colour and materials; like using different surfaces to print onto or combining different printing methods, to develop unique and expressive outcomes.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Printmaking has to follow strict rules and can’t be creative or experimental.

lessonKeywords.description: art materials that do not use water to activate (e.g. pencil, charcoal, chalk, pastel)
the difference between light and dark areas in a drawing
a technique used to blend charcoal to create soft edges or smooth transitions
to go back into an artwork to change, improve, or fix parts of it

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Charcoal can create expressive, bold lines and rich blacks which is effective for dramatic contrasts and blending.
Dry media, like charcoal, allows for loose and expressive marks, making it ideal for capturing movement and emotion.
Techniques such as smudging (with fingers or tools) can create smooth gradients and depth, particularly with charcoal.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: While charcoal can be loose and expressive, with practice it can also be controlled for fine detail. Artists often use different types of charcoal (e.g. vine for light sketching, compressed for deep blacks) to achieve a full range of effects.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Charcoal is messy and hard to control, so it's not suitable for detailed or serious artwork.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use charcoal to create expressive drawings that show contrast, texture, and emotion using a range of techniques.

teacherTips.teacherTip: The Additional materials contains further context and support about artists. You could adapt the subject drawn from to meet the themes and interests of students. When applying fixative or hair spray to the drawings, use a well ventilated space such as an outdoor area.

lessonKeywords.description: a technique used to block out areas of the paper you want to keep white or light using a barrier that stops paint from soaking into those areas
a technique where a thin, transparent layer of paint is added over a dry wash. It builds up colour and depth without covering the details underneath
the act of gently lifting wet paint from the paper using a tissue, sponge, or dry brush
a smooth, even layer of watered-down paint applied across a large area
a technique where you add wet paint into another area of wet paint. The colours mix and spread naturally on the paper, creating soft edges, blends and interesting effects.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Watercolour is transparent, so artists paint the lightest areas first and build up gradually to darker tones.
Watercolour allows you to blend colours and tones softly to create smooth gradients and natural-looking colour shifts.
Artists can use masking fluid to mask and protect areas of their work to protect or preserve lighter areas.
Glazing involves painting thin, transparent layers over dry paint. It adds depth or shadow without covering the details.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: In watercolour, layering too many dark colours can muddy the painting. It’s better to plan ahead, work from light to dark and use clean water and controlled layers to avoid errors.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: You can paint over a mistake with a darker colour to fix it.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use masking, glazing and blending techniques to create a layered watercolour painting.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Greater contextual information on the artists' work can be found in the additional materials. You may wish to alter the imagery to better fit your project themes. When using masking fluid, care should be taken as some students could be sensitive to the latex in some masking fluids.

lessonKeywords.description: a printmaking process where only one strong impression can be made, making each print unique
a lighter second print made from leftover ink on the plate after the first print; it creates a soft, faint image, like a shadow of the original. Artists may use ghost prints to create layered effects

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Each monotype is singular rather than a reproducible copy, which creates a unique artwork with only one edition.
Artists use mark-making to express tone and texture in monotype.
Artists can use less formal tools like cotton buds and wooden forks to experiment in monotype.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Monotypes create a single, original image. You can sometimes pull a faint ghost print after the first, but it’s never identical. The unique nature is what makes monotype special.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: You can make multiple identical prints from one monotype plate.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Acrylic or oil paints can produce vibrant, opaque colours that enhance visual impact and depth in artwork.
