lessonKeywords.description: a technique where ink is diluted with water to create lighter values
the process of mixing ink with water to lighten its intensity
a smooth transition from one shade or colour to another
lines, marks or details that are clean, exact, and carefully made

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Inks are excellent for creating precise lines, making them ideal for illustrations, comic art, and detailed drawings.
Inks can be diluted with water to create washes and gradients, adding dimension to artwork.
For a more expressive style, splattering or dripping ink or adding bleach can create dynamic textures and effects.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: While ink is permanent when dry, it can be diluted with water whilst wet to create lighter values, washes, and gradients.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Once ink is applied it can't be lightened as it is permanent.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explore and exploit the creative possibilities of ink by controlling its properties and applying a range of expressive techniques to develop artwork.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Greater contextual information on the artist's work can be found in the additional materials. You may wish to alter the imagery to enhance your own project themes.

lessons.lessonTitle: Experiment with dry media: fine liner

lessonKeywords.description: how thick or thin a line is. Artists use different line thickness to show depth, importance, or to add interest to a drawing.
a line made up of small dashes or gaps instead of being solid. Artists use this to suggest lightness, softness, or something that isn’t fully visible.
the use of different elements to create visual interest and complexity in an artwork. Achieved by using different colours, shapes, sizes, textures, lines.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Fine liners come in various sizes for different line weights. Thin for detailed work and thicker to create bold lines.
Fine liners excel in creating clean, crisp lines. They’re ideal for intricate details and precise illustrations.
Fine liners can be used in conjunction with other media allowing for rich textures and layered effects.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Nib size changes line weight and impacts detail and clarity; thinner nibs are better for intricate details, thicker nibs for bold outlines.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: All fine liners produce the same effect, regardless of nib size.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use fine liners with different nib sizes to create clean, detailed lines and combine them with other media to enhance my artwork.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Greater contextual information on the artist's work can be found in the additional materials. You may wish to alter the imagery to better fit your project themes.

lessonKeywords.description: the perceived "heaviness" of an element in the artwork, which is influenced by its size, colour, or placement
a layout where elements are not mirrored but still balanced through visual interest
the arrangement of elements in an artwork

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Experiment with overlapping materials to create depth. Layers can add complexity and intrigue to the artwork
Use contrasting colours, textures, and shapes to create visual interest and draw the viewer’s eye
Consider visual weight, symmetrical or asymmetrical balance when arranging elements to achieve a harmonious composition

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: The photograph should interact with the background, not overpower it. The transparency of acetate or digital opacity allows the viewer to still appreciate the layers beneath. The photograph should complement the painted background, not mask it.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: The main subject photo should completely dominate the composition.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can create a layered collage with contrasting textures, shapes, and colours, while incorporating black and white photography to enhance depth and composition.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Greater contextual information on the artists work can be found in the additional materials. You may wish to alter the imagery to better fit your project themes.

lessons.lessonTitle: The basic principles of graphic communication

lessonKeywords.description: the distribution of visual weight in a work of art
the arrangement of opposite elements to create visual interest
the part of the design that catches the viewer's attention
the arrangement of elements to show importance, guiding the viewer’s eye
the feeling of harmony between all parts of the artwork

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Graphic communication involves the use of visual elements to convey messages.
Key principles include balance, contrast, hierarchy, emphasis, unity, variety and movement.
Understanding how different elements can be arranged to create effective communication.
Ability to critique and improve designs based on principles of graphic communication.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: While aesthetics are important, graphic communication focuses on conveying information effectively through visual principles like balance, hierarchy and alignment.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Graphic communication is mainly about making things look pretty.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can identify and apply the basic principles of graphic communication in my designs.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Use real-world examples that pupils can relate to, like social media graphics or product packaging, to illustrate key principles. This helps connect theory to practice and help to keep pupils engaged.

lessonKeywords.description: the arrangement of visual elements on a page or design to guide the viewer’s eye and convey information effectively
the way elements such as images, text, and shapes are combined and placed within a design
the visual order of elements, guiding viewers from the most important to least important using size, placement, or colour
the visual distribution of elements in a design to create harmony (can be symmetrical or asymmetrical)
the grouping of related elements close together to create a visual connection

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Layout and composition help to create effective, engaging and visually appealing designs.
A well-structured layout helps guide the viewer’s eye through the design, making it easier to understand information.
Considered composition ensures a pleasing arrangement of elements, enhancing the overall attractiveness of the design.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: More elements can overwhelm the viewer. Effective use of empty space and a clear hierarchy can increase impact and readability.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: A more crowded layout makes the design look more informative or detailed.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can create a clear and effective layout using composition principles to communicate ideas in a graphic design.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Model the principles live using a shared screen or printed example - move elements around and ask students how each change affects clarity, balance and focus. This helps to deconstruct abstract ideas by making them visual and concrete.

lessonKeywords.description: altering or adjusting an image using digital tools to change its appearance or message
using stacked image components or elements in software to edit non-destructively
the intensity or purity of colour; higher saturation = brighter, lower = muted or greyed
placing contrasting images or elements next to each other to create meaning or tension

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Image manipulation allows designers to adjust colours, contrast and brightness for visually striking compositions.
Tools like layers, filters and cropping can drastically change image tone and meaning.
Manipulated images can convey complex ideas that resonate with the audience, enhancing the message of a design.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Digital art is a legitimate medium, just like painting or drawing. It requires creative decisions and skill - manipulation is a method of artistic expression, not a shortcut.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Digital manipulation is cheating or inauthentic art.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use digital tools to manipulate an image and change its message or emotional impact.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Demonstrate one technique live before setting tasks - seeing a tool used in context helps demystify digital software for beginners and boosts confidence, especially for pupils unsure of their IT skills.

lessons.lessonTitle: Hand rendered working methods: dry media

lessonKeywords.description: non-liquid materials such as pencils, charcoal, pastels, and graphite sticks, used to create marks on paper
a drawing technique where parallel lines are used to create shading or texture
a method of shading or texture that uses intersecting sets of parallel lines to build up tones and create depth
the technique of using fingers, blending stumps, or tissue to blur and soften the edges of marks to create smooth tonal transitions
the range of light to dark tones that can be achieved in a piece of artwork, essential for creating depth and volume

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Dry media techniques such as hatching, cross-hatching and smudging can be used to create varied textures and tones.
Different dry materials such as pencils, pens, markers and pastels can be used to convey texture and mood.
Dry materials are ready to use immediately, making them beneficial for quick sketches and on-the-go work.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Dry media is highly versatile and can be used for bold, expressive textures and atmospheric effects, not just for precision.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Dry media can only be used for fine, detailed work.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explore dry media techniques to create varied textures, tones, and expressive graphic designs.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Encourage pupils to experiment with different pressures and techniques. Show how light pressure creates subtle gradients, while heavy pressure brings out bold, dramatic textures. Remind them that dry media is not just for detail - bold, expressive work is just as valuable!

lessonKeywords.description: the art and technique of arranging type to make written language legible, readable, and visually appealing
a symbol made up of text and/or images used to identify a brand or organisation
a small decorative stroke or extension at the end of a letter's main strokes, often seen in traditional fonts
a typeface without the small projecting features called "serifs", known for a clean and modern look
the spacing between individual letters in a piece of text, adjusted for better visual balance

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: A simple design is easily recognisable and memorable. Complex logos can be difficult to reproduce and may lose clarity.
Organising text in a way that creates a clean, professional look. Consistent alignment helps guide the reader's eye.
The design should reflect the brand's identity and values, resonating with its target audience.
A strong logo should be distinctive and easy to recall, helping to create brand recognition.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Fonts are like voices - each has a different tone. Choosing a bold, heavy font versus a thin, elegant one can completely change how a brand is perceived by the viewer.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: All fonts communicate the same message - it’s just about how the letters look.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain how typography influences logo design and create my own typographic logo to represent a brand.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Use real world examples to make typography relevant. Link font and typography choices to pupils’ favourite brands and encourage discussion around their emotional impact before starting tasks.

lessons.lessonTitle: Digital working methods: combining images and type

lessonKeywords.description: the style, arrangement and appearance of text used in design to convey tone and message
the positioning of text or elements in relation to each other, which affects clarity and balance
the difference between elements (e.g. colour, size, weight) that helps important parts stand out
how easily text can be read, affected by font choice, size, spacing and background
the arrangement of elements to guide the viewer’s eye and highlight the most important information

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Manipulating images, or combining them with type, allows designers to create unique visuals that capture interest.
Images and type may need to be resized or reformatted for various media to ensure they look good across all platforms.
Image and text manipulation allows designers to experiment with different styles, colours and layouts.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Typography must be chosen and placed purposefully to support the tone, audience and message - readability is just the starting point.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Any text will work as long as it’s readable.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can combine images and typography using digital tools to create clear and impactful visual communication.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Model the thought process of placing a text out loud. Explain why you might choose a font, why it’s placed there and how it changes the meaning. This helps to teach design thinking and not just tool use.

lessons.lessonTitle: Hand rendered working methods: wet media

lessonKeywords.description: liquid-based art materials such as ink, watercolour, or gouache used for mark-making
applying one wash of colour over another once dried to create depth and richness
the technique of smoothly merging two or more colours while wet
using brushstrokes, splatters, and drips to convey emotion or movement

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Develop an understanding of the properties and behaviour of wet media by exploring a range of wet media techniques.
Develop control over brush handling and water-to-paint ratios to create different effects.
Create graphic outcomes that communicate moods or themes through wet media techniques.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Expressive, loose, or even accidental marks can be intentional and valued in graphic communication, depending on the project's aims.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Wet media must always be fully controlled and neat to look professional.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can experiment with wet media techniques to create expressive graphic designs that communicate a theme.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Demonstrate and encourage fearlessness with wet media - mistakes and spontaneous effects are valuable learning moments. Model how to adapt 'happy accidents' into creative graphic solutions.

00:06:14.250 --> 00:06:16.830

00:06:23.592 --> 00:06:26.610

118
00:06:26.610 --> 00:06:29.673

119
00:06:32.910 --> 00:06:35.730

120
00:06:35.730 --> 00:06:38.010

121
00:06:38.010 --> 00:06:40.650

00:06:40.650 --> 00:06:43.365

00:06:43.365 --> 00:06:46.020

00:06:46.020 --> 00:06:48.393

125
00:06:50.850 --> 00:06:54.540

126
00:06:54.540 --> 00:06:57.510

127
00:06:57.510 --> 00:06:59.103

00:07:00.960 --> 00:07:03.645

129
00:07:03.645 --> 00:07:07.743

130
00:07:10.080 --> 00:07:12.930

131
00:07:12.930 --> 00:07:14.823

132
00:07:16.350 --> 00:07:17.700

135
00:07:24.060 --> 00:07:25.743
to the same central point.

136
00:07:28.830 --> 00:07:31.800

137
00:07:31.800 --> 00:07:33.270

lessonKeywords.description: a symbol made up of text and/or images used to identify a brand or organisation
a set of letters that share a similar shape and design
the visual elements (such as logo, colours, and fonts) that create a company's public image

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Ensuring that text is easy to read at various sizes. Choosing appropriate typefaces and sizes is crucial for legibility.
Adjusting the space between lines of text for readability. Proper leading can improve the overall flow of text.
A well-balanced logo feels visually stable and pleasing. Proportion helps maintain harmony among design elements.
The logo should be effective in both small and large formats, maintaining clarity and recognition at any size.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: The most successful logos are often simple as clear designs are more memorable and versatile across different media, formats and sizes.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Logos have to be complicated and detailed to look professional.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can design a typographic logo that communicates a brand identity effectively through font choice and simple imagery.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Model your design thinking aloud as you sketch - verbalising choices around font, balance, and simplicity helps students internalise professional creative decision-making processes.

lessons.lessonTitle: Graphic Communications: the influence and application of sources

lessonKeywords.description: original materials or objects used as direct references in artwork, such as photographs, objects, or life studies
indirect references that influence a work, including images from books, the internet, or artworks of other artists
the use of visual elements (e.g. line, shape, colour) to communicate meaning or ideas in a design or artwork
investigating the background, cultural, or social relevance of a source to inform how it may influence design choices

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Sources of inspiration play a key role in shaping the direction of creative work as it develops.
Using a range of sources allows graphic designers to create more dynamic, relevant, and compelling designs.
Exploring a range of sources introduces designers to various styles, concepts, and cultural influences.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Influence means taking inspiration and transforming it into something new, adding your own creative input rather than directly copying.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Copying or replicating an image is an appropriate way to use a source.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can identify and apply influences from primary and secondary sources to create original graphic communication work.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Encourage students to look at sources critically, not just visually. Ask them what the source communicates beyond the surface level - its context, its mood, or its cultural significance. This will help them develop deeper and more personal connections to their design ideas.

lessons.lessonTitle: Digital processes: using digital media to manipulate an image

lessonKeywords.description: changes you can add to an image to create a certain look or style, like making it black and white or adding contrast
changing or improving an image using software to adjust things like colour, brightness, or composition
a feature in the software that lets you do a specific job, such as selecting part of an image, drawing, or adding text

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: There are different types of photo editing software.
Most photo editing software has a toolbar where you can find the tools you need.
You can use the lasso tool to select areas of an image.
Creating a selection allows you to selectively edit part of an image.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: In reality, edits can be extremely subtle and still have a significant impact on the final image.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Photo editing is always obvious or “fake”.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use use filters, effects, and the lasso tool in digital editing software to manipulate images.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Use Select > Inverse in the top menu when you want to edit the opposite area of your current selection, particularly useful for background edits.

lessons.lessonTitle: Photography: the influence of sources on photographic investigations

lessonKeywords.description: investigation into and study of information to establish facts and reach conclusions
a place from which something, in this instance images or information, originates
the circumstances that form the setting of an idea, event or photographic work
notes and comments that accompany work

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Researching photographers helps us understand their ideas, style, techniques, and context.
Context can include cultural, historical, material, and social influences on a photographer’s work.
Annotation means describing, analysing, interpreting, and making a personal response to images.
Research should inspire our own photography, not by copying, by adapting techniques and linking them to our themes.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Research feeds directly into experimentation and outcomes.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Research is separate from making work.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can research, record, and annotate a photographer’s work, and show how their ideas, style, or techniques connect to my own.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Keep reminding students to link back to their own theme. That way, research never feels separate from making, and students avoid description with no connection.

lessonKeywords.description: how light illuminates the subject of a photograph
the source of light identified in a picture, including natural and artificial light
the feeling or atmosphere a photo creates.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Lighting is one of the most important elements in photography.
Photography can be in a studio or outdoors, and a major difference between these two strands is the light source.
The direction of light plays a big role in how an image looks and feels.
Subject, composition and lighting in a photograph can have a big impact on the mood.
In early photography, artists relied entirely on light, shadow, contrast, and tone.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Lighting has the power to transform a photograph, shaping its mood, tone, and clarity.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Lighting is just a technical tool in photography.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I understand how lighting affects photographs and can experiment with using light creatively

teacherTips.teacherTip: Encourage pupils to reflect on how lighting feels, not just how it looks.

lessonKeywords.description: how far away a subject is when referring to an image
the hole that lets light into the camera, controlling depth of field
how sharp or blurred a subject appears

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Subjects at different distances from the camera appear at different depths.
The higher the f-stop, the greater depth of field, meaning more of our picture is in focus.
Lower f stop settings produce a narrower depth of field, meaning more of the picture appears out of focus.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Depth of field is mainly controlled by adjusting the aperture (f-stop).
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Depth of field is only controled by moving the camera nearer or further away from the subject.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain and use depth of field to take pictures

teacherTips.teacherTip: Prepare a selection of photographs and images that demonstrate varied depths of field and/or provide means for pupils to research their own.

lessons.lessonTitle: Darkroom processes: using an enlarger and developing a print

lessonKeywords.description: a room for developing photographs, in which normal light is excluded
device used to project an image from a negative onto light-sensitive paper
act of allowing light to reach photographic paper during printing
process of combining exposed prints with chemicals to produce an image

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: In film photography, darkrooms are used to develop pictures that are taken on a physical roll of film.
Photographs are produced using light-sensitive paper that is exposed to light that passes through the negative.
Chemicals are then used to develop the image.
Contact sheets can be used to easily see all of the pictures on a roll of film.
Test strips are used to measure how much exposure each picture should have.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: The safelight is not a “free pass” for unlimited light exposure and that all light exposure must be controlled and time-sensitive.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: The safelight allows any kind of light to be on in the darkroom without damaging prints.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I understand how to develop a contact sheet and a print in a darkroom using an enlarger.

teacherTips.teacherTip: When teaching the process of making test strips, emphasise that this step is not just a formality, it’s a critical tool for quality control.

lessonKeywords.description: movement, specifically of a subject within a photograph
the effect caused by moving either the camera or the subject whilst a photo is being taken

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Motion in photography refers to the way movement is captured or conveyed.
European and American photographers began using motion photography to analyse and capture motion scientifically.
Many visual cultures have long used motion to express meaning.
Motion is no longer just about technique, it’s a form of visual storytelling.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Photographers can freeze action sharply or blur it creatively, depending on the photographer’s intent.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Photographers can't control the way movement is depicted in their photographs.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can capture moving subjects in my photographs.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Encourage students to reflect on how motion can communicate mood or cultural meaning, not just technical skill.

lessons.lessonTitle: Picture taking: aperture and shutter speed settings

lessonKeywords.description: The hole through which light travels in a camera lens
The part of the camera that opens to allow light through the aperture

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Cameras work by allowing light to pass into a camera and onto a light sensitive surface.
The f-stop or aperture controls allow us to change the size of the opening.
The shutter speed allows us to control how long the aperture is open.
By using both of these, we can control how light or dark our photographs are, and can reduce or manipulate blur.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: While both aperture and shutter speed do affect exposure (how light or dark a photo is), they also have creative effects on how the photo looks, such as blur.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Changing the aperture or shutter speed only affects how bright the photo is.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use aperture and shutter speed settings to control light and blur in my photographs.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Use addtional side-by-side visual examples to show not just exposure changes, but also creative effects.

lessons.lessonTitle: Digital processes: using digital media to layer an image

lessonKeywords.description: the main concept in digital editing, used to control and separate parts of an image
a type of layer used to edit colour, tone, or effects without changing the original image
the part of an image that is furthest away. In digital editing, this refers to the layer placed behind all others

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: In digital editing, layers are used to give greater control and flexibility when editing.
When different images are layered together to make a single image, we call this a composite image.
Using adjustment layers and layer masks are examples of non-destructive editing

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: By using adjustment layers and layer masks, edits are non-destructive.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Editing an image always changes or damages the original file.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use digital photo editing software to layer images for different purposes.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Highlight that digital layering isn’t just about technical skill, it’s about storytelling and imagination, whether making something surreal, humorous, or visually striking.

a shape or pattern used as a guide for cutting fabric.
placing fabric pieces on top of each other to add depth, texture, or detail to a design.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Appliqué is a way of drawing with fabric and stitch techniques.
It is important to choose the correct fabric for the appliqué to help describe the surface textures.
Stitch can be turned into a design feature, for example using a bold colour which will stand out against the fabric.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Stitching fabric shapes onto a background is a common way to attach pieces in appliqué. However, appliqué can also involve using fabric glue or PVA glue to attach smaller pieces of fabric to a larger background.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Appliqué must involve stitching.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can design and make an appliqué using fabric shapes and stitches.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Many people think appliqué is embroidery or stitch. It is worth taking the time to teach students the difference between all of these disciplines.

lessons.lessonTitle: Textile design: the influence of sources on investigations

lessonKeywords.description: the starting point or inspiration for design
the cultural, historical, or social background of a source
the process of changing a source into a new textile design

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Artists analyse sources and identify shapes, patterns, textures, and meanings that can inspire textile designs.
Understanding the cultural, historical, and social context of a source adds depth and relevance to a design.
Sources can be reinterpreted and transformed into original textile outcomes.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Sources are not meant to be copied. They act as a starting point for creativity. Designers explore a source’s shapes, patterns, colours, or meanings and reinterpret them to create original work that reflects their own ideas and context.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: A source is just something to copy.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can identify and apply influences from sources to create original textile work.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Pupils will start their textile sample in this lesson. The sample will be inspired by their chosen source but they will need to finish the textile work over the course of another lesson.

lessonKeywords.description: a frame with fine mesh used to press ink through a design onto fabric or paper
a tool with a flat rubber edge used to pull ink across a screen for printing
a liquid mixed with paint to make it flexible and washable on fabric

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Painting onto the silkcreen will only produce one, singular print not multiple prints.
The silkscreen technique allows versatility to produce an art piece or a wearable piece.
Artists can use other techniques, like hand stitch embroidery, to develop their design or artwork.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: It will only produce one singular print.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: You can make multiple identical prints from one hand painted silkscreen.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can draw, paint and print my design using colour mixing on a silkscreen.

teacherTips.teacherTip: The painting process should be quick as the ink and dyes can dry on the screen. Students should put enough printing ink on the screen to be able to create a vibrant print.

lessons.lessonTitle: Introduction to the principles of textile design

lessonKeywords.description: a specific method used to create or decorate fabric, such as weaving, printing, or embroidery
materials made from fibres that are woven, knitted, felted, or bonded to create fabrics
a distinct area of practice within textiles, such as embroidery, knitting, printing, or technical textiles

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Textiles involve the use of fabrics, fibres, and techniques to create designs.
Key principles include texture, surface design, structure, function, and fibre and materials.
Understanding how these elements combine helps create effective and meaningful textile outcomes.
Developing the ability to analyse and improve designs based on the principles of textiles is an important skill.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: The principles of textiles apply to interiors, art, and technical textiles.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: The principles of textiles only apply to fashion

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain the principles of textiles and create a research page exploring one textile discipline.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Pupils can photocopy the sample they would like to use for their research page, rather than use the real thing, as they will need it in a specific place in their sketchbook.

a substance used to colour materials.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Batik has deep cultural roots, and artists use batik to honour and preserve these traditional techniques and motifs.
The dyeing process in batik produces rich, vibrant colours that can be layered and blended.
Wax is applied to fabric before dyeing, preventing dye from reaching certain areas and creating patterns.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: If you don't iron off the wax after dyeing, the fabric will look unfinished and waxy.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: You don’t have to iron off the wax after dyeing.

lessonKeywords.description: decorative designs applied to the surface of materials like fabric, paper, or ceramics
a design that is copied and arranged over and over to cover a surface
the size of a design or motif in relation to its surface or surrounding space

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Repeat patterns create a sense of rhythm and continuity, making the fabric visually appealing and harmonious.
Designers often scale the motif up or down to change its size and add variety in a repeat pattern.
Many textile traditions repeat patterns, allowing artists to connect their work to cultural heritage.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Surface pattern can be applied to many materials, including ceramics, wallpaper, furniture, and architecture.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Surface pattern decoration is only used in textiles.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explore surface pattern by designing a motif and experimenting with scale to create repeat patterns.

teacherTips.teacherTip: This project can work well if you have a photocopier or printer in the classroom or near the classroom so that pupilss can photcopy their work once they are ready.

lessonKeywords.description: a sewing machine attachment that lets you move the fabric freely to draw with thread
a tool that stitches fabric together using thread
a long, thin strand of fibre used for sewing. It connects pieces of fabric together or can be used decoratively to draw or create texture.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Artists use sewing machines to draw with thread, creating expressive portraits by layering line, tone, and texture.
Understand how to set up and control a sewing machine for freehand stitching, using the correct tool and techniques.
Experiment with thread, colour, and layering to develop stitched, thread drawings in response to a project theme

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: With a freehand arm, you can move the fabric in any direction to draw curves, lines, and patterns with thread. Artists use this to stitch portraits, text, and textures, guiding the fabric by hand like drawing with a pencil.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: You can only use a sewing machine for straight lines or joining fabric.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can create a thread drawing by using a sewing machine to draw with freehand stitching.

teacherTips.teacherTip: It is much easier to draw with a sewing machine if you have a freehand arm so it is worth investing in a few. Students who are not that confident with the sewing machine can put their base fabric into an embroidery hoop. This will create tension on the fabric and make it easier for them to control.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Set design is the art of designing environments and atmospheric spaces.
Colour combinations and different mark- making techniques can be used to represent different atmospheres.
Card brackets are useful in constructing temporary three dimensional spaces.
To test and show the scale of space, silhouettes of actors can be placed in the space.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Set design is used in many different contexts, including theatre, film, fashion, art and music.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Set designers work only in theatre and film.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use paper techniques to develop a set design.

teacherTips.teacherTip: You could also encourage pupils to use small-scale props to place in the scene.

a symbol is a picture, shape, or object that stands for an idea or meaning

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Fashion design is the art of designing clothing and accessories.
Individual fashion is personal and links to time, place and culture.
Fashion designers are challenging our understanding of fashion.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Fashion design is more than trends; it can challenge our understanding of fashion.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Fashion design is solely about trends and superficial appearances.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explore how fashion design is influenced by identity, culture, and self expression.

teacherTips.teacherTip: All pupils works will be different due to the nature of experimentation, nothing should be deemed as incorrect. Teacher can consider the list of references suggested for the lesson. Pupils would benefit from having computers or tablets available to search for images.

lessonKeywords.description: the art of using visual elements to communicate messages
the arrangement of text and images on a surface

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Graphic design is the art of using visual elements to communicate messages.
Designers often push traditional boundaries of graphic design through ways such as using different mediums.
Graphic designers consider the target audience, the purpose and the message of the design piece.
Designers can use colour, imagery and layout to communicate their message.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Many graphic designers push traditional boundaries and shift the focus from creating purely aesthetically pleasing works to communicating messages about social justice.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: The main role of graphic designers is to make work that is pleasing to the viewer’s eye.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use colour, images and layout to create a piece of graphic design.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Having a range of posters advertising locations from the mid century will support pupils when creating their own.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Printed textiles are fabrics with designs or patterns created by printing techniques.
Printed textiles takes many forms and can be found in our homes through furnishings, clothing, wallpapers.
Incorporting motif designs is a big part of printed textiles

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Architecture is the art and science of designing and constructing buildings.
Architects create a sense of community through their designs.
Architects can incorporate patterns in their design both through the structure and literal patterns.
Patterns can represent communities in architecture.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Architects use many different patterns in their designs, both literal patterns and patterns through their use of form.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Architecture is plain and without details.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can create a poly block print inspired by patterns in architecture.

teacherTips.teacherTip: All students' works will be different due to the nature of experimentation; nothing should be deemed as incorrect. Teacher can expand on the list of references suggested for the lesson for more local examples.

Theaster Gates is an artist and architect who came from an area in Chicago in the United States.

This arts project designed and build affordable housing and community and arts centers.
Gates wanted to design architecture where people come together, to congregate and share stories, read and express themselves.
Other architects who design spaces for people to congregate are: Tamara Eagle Bull designed the Gila River Indian Community Governance Center to honor Indigenous values and traditions and serve as the central hub for the Community's tribal government.
Kazuyo Sejima's floating design center in Puyuan, China, uses lightweight steel structures to create a lattice-shaped dome.
It functions as a venue for exhibitions, gatherings and cultural events.
Sharon Davis designed the Women's Opportunity Center in Rwanda, empowering 300 women to develop income skills while offering sanctuary and hope.

A pattern is a repeated decorative design.

decorative design.
Pause here and share with someone.

The patterns are carved into concrete panels with handmade, vibrant ceramic star tiles crafted by artist Lubna Chowdhary.
Dylan Brady's use of repeating geometric patterns on the outside of the Pixel Building not only creates a striking visual identity, but also helps optimize natural light and ventilation, reducing energy consumption and enhancing sustainability.
Pattern can also be achieved in architecture through the different forms and structures used to create the building.
Kate Macintosh designed the London social housing project, Dawson Heights.
The forms used to create the building give it the appearance of a cruise ship floating on the horizon at night.
Chamberlin, Powell and Bon designed the Barbican Center in London.

A section can then be drawn onto poly block using a biro.

Check for understanding.

The roller is then used to cover the polyblock with the ink.
Paper is placed over the polyblock and a weight can be used to press it firmly together.
The paper is removed and a mirror print is revealed.

In our lesson: architects who build communities, we've covered the following: Architecture is the art and science of designing, planning and building structures.
Architects from across history have designed architecture to proved public spaces for people to congregate in.
Architects may be inspired by the patterns and forms that are part of their heritage or that occur in their culture.
Poly block printing is an effective way to capture patterns used in the form and structure of buildings as well as patterns added as decoration.
Well done, everyone, for joining in with this lesson.
It was great to explore architecture and, especially, architecture that brings people together.
I'm all for that, and I loved how you explored public spaces and the kind of space that you would like to create, and then, of course, getting down to your own poly block printing.
And I hope you enjoyed that moment when your print was revealed.
I really enjoyed this lesson, and I hope you did too, and I look forward to seeing you at another art lesson soon.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Design is the process of planning and creating things to solve problems or to meet a need.
Designers use design principles to help them in their work and to design solutions.
Design principles include aesthetics, function and interactivity.
Curiosity about the world around us is vital in design and designers use this to push boundaries.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Design is about making things that have never been made before.

lessons.lessonTitle: Street art: power to the people

lessonKeywords.description: a strong hope or desire to achieve something great in the future. It’s like a dream or goal you want to work towards
how various groups, cultures, or issues are visually portrayed in art to reflect their experiences and viewpoints
art in public spaces, including commissioned works such as murals and non-permitted works such as graffiti

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Street art can bring attention to important social issues such as social justice, inequality, and the environment.
Street art draws on diverse cultural influences, fostering appreciation for various traditions and backgrounds.
When communities engage in street art projects, it can create a sense of ownership and pride in local spaces.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Street art is a legitimate and powerful form of artistic expression that addresses important social issues.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Street art is primarily an illegal activity or act of vandalism.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can create a street art design that represents my aspirations and explain how street art has been used to address exclusion

teacherTips.teacherTip: The additional materials have greater support and ideas for developing and personalising the tasks.

lessonKeywords.description: to make something stronger, louder, or more noticeable. For example, if you amplify an idea or message, you make it more powerful or easier for people to notice or understand.
when you repeat an action, phrase, or image multiple times
an simple image or phrase that represents or stands for something else

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Art can bring awareness to social issues from around the world and can be about anything.
Art activism can amplify the voices of those who are under represented and anyone can be an activist.
Repetition in activism reinforces messages, using techniques and events to amplify impact and create change over time.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Art can also be used to activate social change and is a process that can helps spark conversation and raise awareness. The act of creating and sharing the work is powerful in itself.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Artwork is often seen as a passive object that hangs on a wall.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can employ repetition to raise awareness of social issues and amplify underrepresented voices.

teacherTips.teacherTip: More support for this lesson can be found in the Additional materials.

lessonKeywords.description: when people work together to make their community or the world better
an exchange of thoughts, ideas, or information between two or more people
a connection we make in our minds between ideas or things, based on something they have in common
a sheet of material with a design, shape, or letters cut out. Used to apply a pattern or image by painting, drawing, or spraying over the cut-out areas, leaving the design on the surface underneath.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Social action is about coming together to improve lives and solve problems important to communities.
Social action projects encourage discussion, conversation and heightened awareness.
Artists select materials to communicate more clearly with their audience.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Social action art might make tangible improvements to an issue but might focus instead on sparking conversation or raising awareness.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Social action art must always make tangible improvements to an issue.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Collaborative art is when artists and communities working closely together to make art.
Collaborative art can bring communities together and make connections.
Art can be a tool for helping people share experiences, confront challenges, and see new possibilities.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Collaborative art is a collective process of co-creation where ideas and efforts are deeply intertwined.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Collaborative art is just a group project with a leader.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can contribute to a collaborative artwork, which highlights the importance of community.

teacherTips.teacherTip: It is suggested that student groups should be approximately 4-6 students. Student photos may be used for the task and should be printed before the lesson, alternatively pupils could bring in images.

lessons.transcript_sentences:
Hello, my name is Mrs. Carter, and I'm gonna be guiding you through today's lesson on the power of collaboration.
We're going to be looking at how we can work together effectively, which means that we are gonna need to collaborate effectively together.
I'd like you to engage really as much as you can with every single task, give each task a really good go, and I'm sure we're gonna have some fantastic learning today.
Let's get started.
By the end of today's lesson, you're going to be able to say that I can contribute to a collaborative artwork, which highlights the importance of community.
In order to understand our learning today, there are a few keywords we need to be able to use fluently.
Starting with collaborative: working together with others to achieve a common goal or complete a task, that's how we're going to be working today.
Participants: people who take part in an activity, event, or competition.
Community: a group of people who share common interests, goals, experiences, or values.
I'm sure you can think of quite a few communities that you participate in.
Through our lesson today, we're going to have three learning cycles, starting with planning our collaborative artwork, we're then going to move on to making individual portraits, and finally combining portraits together to make a collaborative artwork.
Let's get started planning our collaborative artwork.
So what is collaboration? A collaboration is when a group of people work together to achieve a common goal.
Collaboration can involve sharing ideas, helping each other, and combining strengths and experiences.
I wonder if you can think of any collaborations you've participated in.
Check for understanding: True or false? A collaboration is when a group work together to achieve a common goal, sharing ideas, helping each other, combining strengths and experiences.
Pause the video and decide if you think that that is True or False.
How did you get on? Well done if you said that was True.
Working together to achieve a common goal through the sharing of ideas, helping each other, and combining strengths and experiences is a collaboration.
Artists create community spaces for dialogue and creativity, enabling the participants to share experiences, confront challenges, and see new possibilities.
Establishing a collaborative framework is key to this process.
The process of creating collaborative frameworks might look like this.
Defining your topic; so that would be deciding what the topic of your artwork would be about.
Assembling your participants; so who needs to be part of that community that you're going to work together with? Who are those participants? And depending on your topic might depend on who you select as a participant.
Setting goals together, facilitating engagements; so working out how we're gonna work together, how we're gonna keep people excited about working together.
Creating the artwork, and then showcasing and reflecting on the project and what that's been able to achieve.
So that's defining the topic, assembling the participants, setting goals together, facilitating engagement, creating art, and showcasing and reflecting.
So second check for understanding.
which is the missing step? So we've got defining the topic, a missing step, setting goals, facilitating engagement, creating art, and showcasing and reflecting.
Pause the video and identify which step has been missed off this list.
How did you get on? Well done if you said assembling the participants.
Assembling the participants is a crucial step in collaborative art.
It shapes the goals and the outcomes.
Some people believe that the participants in the project are less important than the artist.
They think participants are just making what the artist tells them.
In a collaborative project, the experiences and contributions of all the individuals is vital to the work.
Working collaboratively can mean working together on one artwork, so all at once, or it can mean working in parallel and bringing those ideas together.
It can also be a combination of the two processes.
And you can see here we've got some students working collaboratively, all on the same artwork, and we've got some students working in parallel.
There are many ways that artists collaborate on projects to share the experiences of individuals and their communities.
Some examples are: "Culture for a Changing City Community Mural" by Paint the Change, Halima Khanom and Rich Mix, "The Leap" are a Bradford-based action learning program who run community art projects and they have all sorts of different types of projects, and "There's no Place" from 2024 led by Jakkau Siributr, Taco Action is led by artist Holly Graham that make public anti-racist community-led actions in Thamesmead.
Here, Jun shares, "We are making a collaborative portrait, and I think it should focus on our friendship." Izzy adds, "As we are all connected by our school, I want to adapt to the school logo and add in the idea of growing up." The collaborative framework for this project looks like this.
So we've got the topic, portraits to celebrate our school, the participants, being our class, the goals are to celebrate unity and friendship, the engagement is working individually and coming together to create the mural, the artwork is a series of portraits that are joined together with patterns and symbols, and then presenting will be where we showcase and reflect at the end.
So, let's get started on making our decisions about our collaborative framework.
So for Task A-1, I would like you to work as a group to decide the goals for the task.
You need to decide the main concept for the artwork, and how that will be symbolized.
So in that prior example, they were looking at friendship and community, and they were employing their school logo as a symbol not only of growth, but also of friendship.
So this for you could include the meaning behind the colors you choose, the size that you're gonna work, and any extra imagery that you would like to add to layer in meaning.
Pause the video and have those conversations as a group to make the decisions about your collaborative artwork.

lessonKeywords.description: the human-made spaces around us that create our local environment
an important place or thing that is recognisable and stands out. It could be a building, artwork or natural feature that helps people know where they are or what a place is known for.
built elements such as buildings, streets, roads, parks, and bridges

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Built environment can create a sense of pride in a community through shared histories or experiences.
Landmarks and structures can connect us to our communities.
Architects play with materials to help inspire interesting designs.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Architects consider the built environment, the local area's history and needs and think outside the box to create connections between communities in their work.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Architects only consider one building, not the wider area.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can design built environments which foster community pride and connection.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Additional materails have more support and further ideas for developed or divergent tasks. There is lots of scope to make local links in this lesson.

lessons.lessonTitle: The elements of art: shape and form

lessonKeywords.description: a two-dimensional, flat form defined by a line around the outer edge, limited to height and width.
a three-dimensional element that has height, width and depth (either real or perceived)

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Shape is 2D and flat, whereas form is 3D and relates to the actual or perceived mass of an object
We can use shape in our work to create interesting compositions
Sculptures are a 3D form and can be made from a variety of interesting materials
We can build larger forms by using repetition of shape.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Shape is flat and 2D, like a drawing. Form is 3D and has depth — you can see or feel it from different angles.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Shape and form are the same thing.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can turn flat shapes into three-dimensional forms by folding, cutting and building a paper sculpture.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Encourage experimentation! Let students test different paper techniques (folding, curling, layering) before starting their final sculpture. Provide examples but avoid over-directing — this helps build confidence and creativity.

lessonKeywords.description: what we see when light reflects off an object. Colour helps us describe how things look and can also make us feel different emotions.
the idea of how colours work together. It includes the colour wheel, primary and secondary colours, and how colours can mix or contrast.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Colours can carry different meanings, and these can vary across people, places and cultures.
We can use colour to convey emotion in our work.
Artists and designers can use colour theory and personal preference in their work.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Colours can carry different meanings, and these can vary across people, places and cultures.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Colours carry the same meaning for everybody.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use colour theory and personal preference to make a collage

teacherTips.teacherTip: Engage pupils in looking and discussing the use of colour in a range of art and design.

lessonKeywords.description: a design in which lines, shapes, forms or colours are repeated
making a copy of a design by pressing it onto a surface like fabric or paper
characterised by regular lines and shapes like squares, triangles, or circles
when a shape or design is copied again and again to make a pattern

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Patterns often involve designs made using printing techniques.
Printed patterns are often seen in everyday items like clothing, furnishings and wallpapers.
Block printing is a process where a design is transferred from a material onto a surface using  pressure.
Patterns often use geometric shapes and are built through repeat and print techniques.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: While repeating the same shape is one way to create a pattern, artists and designers use a variety of methods to make repeated patterns more dynamic, engaging and sophisticated.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: A repeated pattern is just the same shape copied over and over again.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use block printing to create a repeated pattern design.

teacherTips.teacherTip: You could break the lesson into two parts: Lesson 1 – Create backgrounds and build polytile stamps. Lesson 2 – Print onto backgrounds. Demonstrate how to ink up tiles clearly, keep working areas tidy and encourage creating repeat patterns in different ways. Pre-cut tiles and paper to save time.

lessonKeywords.description: there are two types of texture: actual texture and implied texture
suggested or shown indirectly, not actually there but made to look like it is
in art, to press a tool, object, or texture into a soft material (like clay) to leave a mark or pattern

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Texture can be either physical where we can touch and feel it or visual where there is the illusion of a surface.
We can create texture by using mark making and materials in different ways.
We can create texture through using mixed media and layering different materials onto a surface to create a composition.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Texture can mean how something feels, and we call that physical texture. But artists can also create the illusion of texture in drawings or paintings — that’s called visual texture.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Texture is only about how something feels, not how it looks.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can understand how texture can be created and translated in both 2D and 3D forms.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Encourage students to explore animal textures through research. Provide a variety of textured tools (combs, forks, found objects) and pre-cut clay to save time. Focus on building confidence with pinch moulding and shaping simple forms to create expressive, tactile animals.

lessons.lessonTitle: The role of a sketchbook in developing your 3D practice

lessonKeywords.description: a tool for artists to experiment, record ideas and develop their creative process
a creative journey is the ongoing process of exploring, developing, and expressing ideas

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: A sketchbook is a space to think, plan, collect, and test ideas.

Experimental sketchbooks help you take creative risks and reflect.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Sketchbooks are a personal record of your own creative journey, but in the GCSE course they also allow you to gain marks, so sometimes we recommend working in a certain way to help you achieve.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can create an exploratory sketchbook that reflects my artistic voice

lessonKeywords.description: the unique expression, style, and perspective an artist brings to their work
a distinctive visual language or way of working
something that inspires or shapes your creative choices

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: A 3D design style is shaped by influences, materials, and ideas.
Artists develop their style through experimentation, repetition, and reflection.
A personal style is not fixed—it can grow and change over time.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: A designer will grow and develop and so their distinctive style will evolve over time as they experiment more and engage with new ideas.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: A designer's style is fixed and remains constant.

lessons.lessonTitle: Refining your artistic voice by experimenting with techniques and skills

lessonKeywords.description: methods or approaches used to create art, such as layering, texturing, or blending
working in art with no fixed outcome or predetermined goal
in art can be an opportunity for discovery and growth, often leading to unexpected and innovative results

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Experimenting with new techniques expands artistic possibilities.
Many artists experiment. They rule-break and turn mistakes into opportunities for developing their artistic voice.
Open-ended experimentation allows artists to make mistakes that could lead to unexpected ideas and new techniques.

lessonKeywords.description: to show or illustrate through practical application or examples e.g. through sketchbook work
the final stage or result of a process e.g. a final piece
occurring repeatedly e.g. themes of interest or preferred techniques and materials

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: An artist's final piece or outcome is often a culmination of ideas and work.
When studying art, there are specific requirements about how to plan and demonstrate planning for a final piece.
Artists often identify recurring themes, materials and techniques as they look back at their developing ideas.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: A final piece represents the culmination of an artist's themes, materials and techniques, and artistic voice, at a particular moment in time.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: A final piece represents the culmination of an artist's whole life's work, all their ideas and all the materials they have ever used.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can plan a final piece that demonstrates my artistic voice and a culmination of my ideas.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Some pupils may benefit from more or less scaffolding around planning a final piece.

lessons.lessonTitle: Creating and presenting an artist research page

lessonKeywords.description: the process of examining the elements or structure of something
adding notes to explain, analyse, or share your thoughts about a piece of artwork
the circumstances or setting surrounding an event or idea, especially in art

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Analysing key themes and techniques used by an artist deepens our understanding of their art.
By studying the work of other artists, artists enrich their art and develop their own artistic voice.
Inspirational art can be found in many places offering diverse opportunities for research and discovery.
Artist research can be recorded visually and with annotations.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Recording and analysing an artist’s work is essential for developing your understanding of techniques, concepts, and creative processes. We don't need to copy an artist's work but can take and apply knowledge and ideas inspired by relevant artists.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Artist research is about making your work like another artist's artwork.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can research artists and present my findings and analysis.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Where possible, it is a good idea to use past sketchbooks and the pupils' own sketchbooks for discussion and feeback.

lessons.lessonTitle: The role of the sketchbook in developing your artistic voice

lessonKeywords.description: to improve and refine artistic skills, ideas, or techniques through practice and experimentation.
a way to document ideas, observations, and creative processes for future reference or reflection.
a personal space for artists to explore, experiment, and develop their skills and artistic voice.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Despite diverse backgrounds and approaches, common threads emerge in how artists engage with sketchbooks.
Using a sketchbook can help you develop your artistic skills and voice
Sketchbooks can document the progression of an artist’s skills and style over time.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Sketchbooks capture not only the final outcomes but also the processes and innovations behind more finished works.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Sketchbooks capture final outcomes and perfect work

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use my sketchbook to refine my artistic voice and guide my artistic choices

teacherTips.teacherTip: Task 1 will require pupils' own sketchbooks or examples from other pupils/artists .

lessons.lessonTitle: Designing in response to a specific theme

lessonKeywords.description: the specific subject or content that the artwork focuses on
a collection of images, colours and textures used to explore and develop visual ideas
artwork or design that communicates an idea through images and design elements

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Designers respond creatively to a given theme through research and experimentation.
Mood boards and thumbnail sketches help develop and refine visual ideas.
A successful graphic design communicates a concept clearly and creatively.
The creative process involves multiple iterations and decision-making.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Themes are open to interpretation - good design often uses symbolism, abstraction and personal meaning to create deeper, more thoughtful responses.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Designing in response to a theme means drawing something direct or literal.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can generate and develop visual ideas in response to a specific theme through research and sketching techniques.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Encourage students to think beyond the literal - model your own quick mind map to show how varied and personal a theme response can be and remind them that their initial ideas are a starting point, not a finished product.

lessonKeywords.description: the deliberate use of uniform elements such as colour, typography, imagery, and layout across a project or a body of work to create a cohesive and harmonious visual experience.
deals with the principles of beauty and artistic taste. It refers to the principles and elements that define the visual appeal and beauty of a work.
the distinctive visual characteristics and methods that define a creatives work, encompassing elements like form, colour, composition, and technique.
the process of creating a unique visual identity for a business or product, encompassing elements such as logos, colour schemes, typography, and imagery.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Graphic design is deeply integrated into our daily lives, we encounter examples frequently and in many ways.
A designer's style is a visual approach that reflects their unique perspective, creativity, and technical skills.
A designer creates a brand for a client by conducting thorough research to understand the client's mission and audience
The designer’s experiences, interests, and aesthetic preferences play a role in shaping a designer's unique style.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: The designer’s individual experiences, interests, and aesthetic preferences play a role in shaping a designer's unique style.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Unlike artists, a graphic designer's personal experiences and preferences have no influence on their work and style.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can understand and reflect on what shapes a graphic design style.

teacherTips.teacherTip: It is advisable to look at and discuss iconic and relatable examples of design and branding.

lessonKeywords.description: a central idea or theme that drives the visual direction and message of a design
the quality of being new, unique, or different from others’ work
a collection of visual elements (e.g. colour, imagery, typography) that express a designer’s or brand’s personality

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Design concepts reflect personal identity, values, and influences.
A unique design concept begins with self-reflection and intentional visual choices.
Personal experiences can inspire original and meaningful graphic design.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: A strong design concept isn’t just about appearance - it reflects a deeper idea or message you want to communicate. What you choose to show should connect to your personal voice and purpose.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: A design concept is just choosing what looks good.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can generate unique design concepts that reflect my identity, interests and influences.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Encourage students to dig deeper than surface aesthetics - ask probing questions like "Why is this meaningful to you?" to guide them toward a more authentic and personal design concept.

lessonKeywords.description: studying and copying the style of another designer to learn their techniques
taking existing styles, images, or ideas and changing them by adding your own twist to create something new and unique
smoothly combining colours, shapes, textures, or images to create a seamless and visually harmonious effect

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Graphic designers might use a combination of traditional and digital approaches.
By experimenting with ways of working and the design elements, designers can develop their graphic design style.
Nothing is 100% original! Every artist and designer is influenced by something.
Designers often take inspiration from other work and places and remix them adding their own twist.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Traditional approaches to graphic design existed before digital tools and are still widely used today.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Graphic desingers only use digtial tools.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use traditional and digital approaches and remix work in my own design style.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Show and discuss a range of tradional and digital, contemporary and historic approaches to graphic design.

lessonKeywords.description: the purpose or message behind a design; what the artist wants to communicate
the impact that a designer or movement has on a creative work
the specific stylistic choices (colours, shapes, layout) used by a designer or artist
the process of repeatedly refining and improving a design idea through drafts or versions

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Researching and analysing key visual features used by other designers is key to developing final ideas.
Familiarity with basic graphic design principles like balance and alignment is needed to develop a final idea.
Articulating how a final idea communicates design choices is an important part of the process.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: While your chosen designer should influence your work, the final piece should show your own creative voice. Think about what you want to communicate, and how the designer’s style can help you do that - not just replicate it.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: The final piece should just copy the designer’s style.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can create a final graphic design piece that reflects my personal style and shows influence from other designers.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Encourage students to justify every design choice by linking it to their designer research or personal intention. Use targeted questioning to draw out their thinking and help them move from imitation to innovation.

lessonKeywords.description: a set of principles guiding the visual style or artistic appearance of a piece of work
a written explanation or comment added next to images or designs to clarify or analyse them
the impact that one artist, designer, or style has on another’s work or creative process

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: A research page is a curated, creative presentation of a designer’s work and aesthetic, not just a collection of images.
Effective layout and annotation help communicate analysis and personal interpretation.
Design choices on the page may reflect the influence of another artist, designer, or style.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Research pages are not about collecting facts - they’re about showing how you understand and respond to a designer’s work through layout, analysis, and visual interpretation.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: A research page is just a collection of pictures and facts.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can create a research page that creatively presents a designer’s work using visual choices and annotations.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Model your thinking aloud as you place images and annotations - explain why you're making each visual decision to reinforce that the process is as important as the outcome.

lessons.lessonTitle: Using a graphic design sketchbook in experimental ways

lessonKeywords.description: the specific subject or content that the artwork focuses on
the process of exploring new and unconventional tools, materials, and techniques
the process of experimenting with different ideas, styles, and techniques to discover new creative possibilities

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Both artists and graphic designers use sketchbooks for creative exploration.
Graphic design is often based on themes and concepts rather than just aesthetics.
Experimental media play is a process where graphic designers push beyond their usual media or conventional tools.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Both artists and graphic designers use sketchbooks for creative exploration. The way they use them may differ in purpose, content, and process.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Only artists use skectchbooks.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use a sketchbook as a space for playful and expressive experimentation.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Looking at and discussing examples of graphic design sketchbooks will help to inspire.
