keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Landscapes offer a rich tapestry of colours, textures and forms that designers can take inspiration from.
Landscapes let graphic designers explore scale, perspective and composition from vast vistas to intimate details.
Designers can use landscapes to celebrate nature’s beauty and foster appreciation for ecological diversity.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: In graphic communication, the goal is to communicate visually, not replicate reality. Stylised or abstracted landscapes can be more impactful and expressive.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Graphic design landscapes must look realistic to be effective.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can review the range of ways graphic designers have been inspired by landscapes.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Greater contextual information on each designers work can be found in the additional materials. You may wish to alter the imagery to better fit your project themes.

more traditional composition and perspective,

211
00:10:24.840 --> 00:10:26.460
warm, rich colours.

212
00:10:26.460 --> 00:10:28.680
And what they have in common is they create connection

213
00:10:28.680 --> 00:10:31.443
to places by altering scale and composition.

214
00:10:32.850 --> 00:10:34.620
Now, we're onto our next learning cycle,

215
00:10:34.620 --> 00:10:36.783
design deconstruction: landscapes.

216
00:10:37.770 --> 00:10:39.900
What do you notice first about this design?

217
00:10:39.900 --> 00:10:41.600
Pause here and share with someone.

218
00:10:47.220 --> 00:10:48.183
Thanks for sharing.

219
00:10:49.770 --> 00:10:51.480
Graphic designers use various techniques

220
00:10:51.480 --> 00:10:53.190
to develop a distinct visual language

221
00:10:53.190 --> 00:10:55.230
and communicate in their work:

222
00:10:55.230 --> 00:10:58.290
the principles of design, balance, contrast, hierarchy,

223
00:10:58.290 --> 00:11:01.470
alignment, proximity, unity, and colour;

224
00:11:01.470 --> 00:11:04.470
the elements of art, line tone, colour, pattern,

225
00:11:04.470 --> 00:11:06.720
shape, form, and texture;

226
00:11:06.720 --> 00:11:09.090
text, imagery, and subject.

227
00:11:09.090 --> 00:11:10.680
We can deconstruct these techniques

228
00:11:10.680 --> 00:11:12.573

229
00:11:14.100 --> 00:11:15.810

230
00:11:15.810 --> 00:11:18.330

00:11:18.330 --> 00:11:21.210

232
00:11:21.210 --> 00:11:23.190

00:11:23.190 --> 00:11:26.490

234
00:11:26.490 --> 00:11:28.080

235
00:11:28.080 --> 00:11:31.050
B, it helps us see the techniques the designer used

236
00:11:31.050 --> 00:11:33.660
to express ideas and emotions,

237
00:11:33.660 --> 00:11:37.290
C, it only matters if the designer explains their work,

238
00:11:37.290 --> 00:11:39.750
or D, it tells us exactly what the designer

00:11:39.750 --> 00:11:43.020

240
00:11:43.020 --> 00:11:44.463
Pause here while you decide.

241
00:11:51.810 --> 00:11:54.213
Well done if you selected answers A and B.

242
00:11:55.770 --> 00:11:58.020
How are the principles of design used in this work?

243
00:11:58.020 --> 00:11:59.720
Pause here and share with someone.

244
00:12:06.570 --> 00:12:07.980

245
00:12:07.980 --> 00:12:11.133

246
00:12:12.060 --> 00:12:13.440
Straight lines are in perspective,

247
00:12:13.440 --> 00:12:15.003

248
00:12:16.050 --> 00:12:18.363

249
00:12:19.560 --> 00:12:22.653

250
00:12:23.850 --> 00:12:26.350

251
00:12:27.990 --> 00:12:30.330

252
00:12:30.330 --> 00:12:32.313

253
00:12:33.180 --> 00:12:35.370

254
00:12:35.370 --> 00:12:36.840

255
00:12:36.840 --> 00:12:38.910

256
00:12:38.910 --> 00:12:40.203
helps to achieve this.

257
00:12:41.550 --> 00:12:42.750
Check for understanding.

258
00:12:42.750 --> 00:12:44.640
How might a graphic designer create depth

259
00:12:44.640 --> 00:12:46.650

00:12:46.650 --> 00:12:50.190

00:12:50.190 --> 00:12:53.010

262
00:12:53.010 --> 00:12:55.980

00:12:55.980 --> 00:12:57.660
and simple backgrounds,

00:12:57.660 --> 00:13:01.320
D, only working with digital tools and techniques.

00:13:01.320 --> 00:13:02.720
Pause here while you decide.

266
00:13:10.170 --> 00:13:12.000

00:13:12.000 --> 00:13:14.610
Indeed, layering compositions with detailed foregrounds

268
00:13:14.610 --> 00:13:15.903
and simple backgrounds.

269
00:13:17.340 --> 00:13:20.010
How has this design achieved a sense of depth?

270
00:13:20.010 --> 00:13:21.710
Pause here and share with someone.

271
00:13:29.310 --> 00:13:30.990
Thanks for sharing.

272
00:13:30.990 --> 00:13:33.150

273
00:13:33.150 --> 00:13:34.893

274
00:13:36.000 --> 00:13:37.530
Objects and forms in the foreground

275
00:13:37.530 --> 00:13:38.980

276
00:13:40.620 --> 00:13:43.110

277
00:13:43.110 --> 00:13:44.820

278
00:13:44.820 --> 00:13:46.830

279
00:13:46.830 --> 00:13:49.230
and more detailed than layers in the background.

280
00:13:51.210 --> 00:13:53.130

281
00:13:53.130 --> 00:13:55.203
in their landscapes in a range of ways:

282
00:13:56.910 --> 00:13:58.950

283
00:13:58.950 --> 00:14:00.933

284
00:14:02.970 --> 00:14:05.100

285
00:14:05.100 --> 00:14:07.789

286
00:14:07.789 --> 00:14:10.200
or eye level in their landscape works.

287
00:14:10.200 --> 00:14:12.543
Pause here and decide, is this true or false?

288
00:14:18.390 --> 00:14:19.650

289
00:14:19.650 --> 00:14:20.790

00:14:20.790 --> 00:14:21.900

lessonKeywords.description: a physical form that can be seen or felt
the use of opposing elements (such as light vs dark) to create visual interest
the placement or arrangement of visual elements in a design

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Everyday objects can be used to convey meaning, messages, emotions and ideas in graphic communication.
Designers use composition and layout techniques to guide the viewer’s attention.
Contrast enhances visual communication by emphasising key elements.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Graphic design often begins with hand-drawn ideas, including observational drawing. Understanding shape, form, and composition from real objects improves digital outcomes.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Graphic design is only done on computers and doesn’t involve drawing or observational skills.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can observe and draw everyday objects to explore composition and layout in graphic design.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Use real-life objects with distinct shapes to support pupils in observing form and negative space - this helps bridge traditional drawing skills with digital layout awareness.

lessons.lessonTitle: Portraits and figures in Graphic Communication

lessonKeywords.description: artwork that represents a person’s likeness, often focusing on the face and expression
the qualities, beliefs, personality, or expressions that make a person or group unique, often reflected in art
the deliberate simplification or exaggeration of visual elements in an artwork to create a distinctive or expressive effect
the combination of design elements (line, shape, colour, etc.) used to communicate ideas visually
the process of breaking down an artwork into its basic components for analysis

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Portraits and figures can be powerful tools in graphic design to express messages, emotion, or identity.
Graphic designers often stylise figures to enhance meaning and create a signature visual style.
Deconstructing design helps us understand how the elements of art contribute to visual impact.
Personal identity can inform meaningful visual design choices.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Graphic design often relies on abstraction and stylisation to communicate more clearly and powerfully than realism - effective portraits use design choices to enhance meaning, not replicate reality.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Portraits in graphic design must look realistic to be effective.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explore and analyse how designers use portraits and figures, and begin creating my own design that communicates personal meaning through stylisation.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Use side-by-side comparisons to help students spot stylisation and design choices. Reinforce that design is intentional - encourage students to explain why they’ve made visual decisions as part of their planning and reflection.

lessons.lessonTitle: Light and dark in Graphic Communication

lessonKeywords.description: a dark shape or outline of something against a lighter background, showing only the outline with no internal detail
the difference between elements (like light and dark or rough and smooth) that makes parts of a design stand out

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Designers can use light and dark to create mood, atmosphere and contrast in graphic design.
We can find symbolic meanings of light and darkness across different cultures and art movements.
Designers can experiment with using light and shadow to define form, space and focus in their designs.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: This overlooks how contrast can be used to suggest emotion, tension, calm, or drama, not just realism.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Light and dark are only used to make things look realistic, not to create mood.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can review the range of ways designers have been inspired by light and dark in graphic design.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Greater contextual information on the designers work can be found in the additional materials. You may wish to alter the imagery to better fit your project themes.

lessons.lessonTitle: Inside and outside in Graphic Communication

lessonKeywords.description: the area around, between and within objects. It can be physical, like a room, or it can be visual
a point of change, a space between two different areas
things that block, separate, or divide spaces, people, or ideas
how an artist chooses to surround or crop a subject in an artwork

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Designers can represent physical and psychological boundaries through interior and exterior spaces.
Designers might use framing, perspective and scale to connect or separate inside and outside spaces.
Designs can explore the relationship between personal, private spaces and wider, public or natural settings.
Some graphic designers explore the boundary between external appearance and internal experience.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: In design, "inside" and "outside" can mean more than places — they can show how someone feels on the inside, how people hide emotions, or the contrast between personal and public life.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: "Inside" and "outside" in design always refers to physical spaces, like buildings or rooms.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can review the range of ways designers have been inspired by inside and outside.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Greater contextual information on the designer's work can be found in the additional materials. You may wish to alter the imagery to better fit your project themes.

a lack of symmetry; when two sides of something are not identical but still balanced visually

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: The inherent beauty of natural forms provides graphic designers with endless inspiration.
The diversity of colours, textures, and shapes found in nature can lead to visually striking designs.
Natural forms often use flowing, asymmetrical elements that contrast geometric rigidity, enabling dynamic compositions.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Graphic design often draws from organic, natural inspiration - many professional designs use textures, forms, and concepts from nature to create emotional or symbolic meaning.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Graphic design is mostly digital, so nature isn’t really relevant.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can review the range of ways designers have been inspired by natural forms in graphic design.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Encourage students to talk through their design breakdowns  - verbalising their thinking helps develop their visual literacy and deepens contextual understanding.

lessonKeywords.description: a dark shape or outline of something against a lighter background, showing only the outline with no internal detail
the difference between elements (like light and dark or rough and smooth) that makes parts of an image stand out

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Photographers can use light and dark to create mood, atmosphere and contrast in photography.
We can find symbolic meanings of light and darkness across different cultures and art movements.
Photographers can experiment with using light and shadow to define form, space and focus in their photographs.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: This overlooks how contrast can be used to suggest emotion, tension, calm, or drama, not just realism.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Light and dark are only used to make things look realistic, not to create mood.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can review the range of ways photographers have been inspired by light and dark in photography.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Greater contextual information on the photographer's work can be found in the additional materials. You may wish to alter the imagery to better fit your project themes.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Objects often carry symbolic weight, allowing artists to convey complex themes and narratives.
Photographers can choose objects that hold personal significance, creating works that resonate emotionally.

lessonKeywords.description: shapes, patterns, and structures found in nature (e.g. leaves, shells, plants)
a lack of symmetry; when two sides of something are not identical but still balanced visually

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: The inherent beauty of natural forms provides photographers with endless inspiration.
The diversity of colours, textures, and shapes found in nature can lead to visually striking photographs.
Natural forms often use flowing, asymmetrical elements that contrast geometric rigidity, enabling dynamic compositions.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: While some natural forms show symmetry, most have irregular, flowing shapes. Even symmetrical forms often have variations, this is part of what makes nature interesting to photographers.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Natural forms are always perfectly symmetrical, like leaves or flowers.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can review the range of ways photographers have been inspired by natural forms in photography.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Greater contextual information on the artists' work can be found in the additional materials. You may wish to alter the imagery to better fit your project themes.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Landscapes offer a rich tapestry of colours, textures and forms that photographers can take inspiration from.
Landscapes let photographers explore scale, perspective and composition from vast vistas to intimate details.
Photographers can use landscapes to celebrate nature’s beauty and foster appreciation for ecological diversity.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: While landscapes often show beautiful scenery, they can express powerful ideas, like climate change, migration, culture, or even identity. Photographers use landscapes not just to show what they see, but to say something about how they feel or value.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Landscapes are just pretty pictures of nature – there's not much meaning behind them.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can review the range of ways photographers have been inspired by landscapes.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Greater contextual information on each photographer's work can be found in the additional materials. You may wish to alter the imagery to better fit your project themes.

lessonKeywords.description: the focus, topic or image of an image e.g. in a portrait the subject is the person who has been photographed
the story or message that a photograph communicates about the subject
the use of objects, colours, or imagery to suggest deeper meanings

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Portraits can show a person’s identity, including culture, gender, age, social status and background.
Portraits can tell stories about people’s lives and experiences, suggesting relationships, emotions or history.
Photographers often use their work to share views on society, culture, or important issues.
Portraits can go beyond what someone looks like; they can show who they are and what they stand for.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: While capturing someone’s physical appearance can be part of a portrait, photographers often go much deeper. Portraits can reveal who someone is, exploring culture, identity, relationships, life experiences and even social or political themes.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Portraits are just about what someone looks like on the surface with no deeper meaning.

lessons.transcript_sentences:
Hello, my name is Ms. Tipping, and I'm really looking forward to learning with you today about portraits and figures in photography.
We're going to do lots of thinking, talking, and exploring together in this lesson.
So, shall we get started? Let's go.
By the end of today's lesson, you'll be able to review the range of ways photographers have been inspired by portraits and figures in photography.
Before we start, I would like to introduce you to some keywords we'll be using during the lesson.
A subject is the focus, topic, or image of an image.
For example, in a portrait, the subject is the person who has been photographed.
Narrative refers to the story or message that a photograph communicates about the subject, and symbolism is the use of objects, colors, or imagery to suggest deeper meanings.
Pause the video here to make a note of these keywords, and when you're ready to continue, press play.
These are the learning cycles we'll be working through together in today's lesson, looking at a photographer spotlight in portraits and figures, photographic deconstruction in portraits and figures, and also personal connection in portraits and figures.
So, in this first learning cycle, we're going to explore a photographer spotlight within portraits and figures.
Why do you think people have always been such a powerful subject in photography? Pause the video here and have a discussion with your partner and press play when you're ready to continue.
Well, photographers across history and cultures have been inspired to create portraits and depictions of people.
Photographers take different approaches to the exploration of portraits and figures in their work using different techniques and themes.
Some themes and techniques artists might use are documenting socio-cultural histories, symbolism, life experiences and social commentary, abstraction, and narrative and storytelling.
Some photographers focus on the accuracy of their work, aiming to achieve a highly recognizable likeness of their subject using natural lighting and choosing not to digitally edit the photographs.
This kind of representation is common when documenting social histories, cultures, or specific people.

lessonKeywords.description: the area around, between and within objects. It can be physical, like a room, or it can be visual
a point of change, a space between two different areas
things that block, separate, or divide spaces, people, or ideas
how an artist chooses to surround or crop a subject in a photograph

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Photographers can represent physical and psychological boundaries through interior and exterior spaces.
Photographers might use framing, perspective and scale to connect or separate inside and outside spaces.
Photographs can explore the relationship between personal, private spaces and wider, public or natural settings.
Some photographers explore the boundary between external appearance and internal experience.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: In photography, "inside" and "outside" can mean more than places - they can show how someone feels on the inside, how people hide emotions, or the contrast between personal and public life.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: "Inside" and "outside" in design always refers to physical spaces, like buildings or rooms.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can review the range of ways photographers have been inspired by inside and outside.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Greater contextual information on the photographers' work can be found in the additional materials. You may wish to alter the imagery to better fit your project themes.

lessonKeywords.description: a dark shape or outline of something against a lighter background, showing only the outline with no internal detail
the difference between elements (like light and dark or rough and smooth) that makes parts of an artwork stand out
often used in art to create contrast, highlight textures, and set moods

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Textile artists use light and dark to create mood, contrast, and atmosphere through fabric, texture, and tone.
Light and dark in textiles can carry symbolic meanings across cultures, styles, and design traditions.
Artists use shadows, highlights, and tone in textiles to shape form, suggest depth, and direct focus.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Silhouette is essential in textiles — it defines shape, structure and how a garment or piece interacts with light and contrast. Designers use silhouettes to make bold visual statements, create mood and control how the textile is seen in space.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Silhouette just means a shadow or outline — it doesn’t really matter in textile design.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can review the range of ways artists and designers have been inspired by light and dark in textiles.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Greater contextual information on the artists' work can be found in the Additional materials. You may wish to alter the imagery to better fit your project themes.

lessonKeywords.description: a view of natural scenery, often used as inspiration in textile art
a technique to show depth and distance using scale or spatial arrangement
a textile method of building up surface with fabric, stitch, or embellishment

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Artists translate nature’s colours, textures, and forms into textiles that capture the feel of landscapes.
Textiles can reflect cultural ties to place, exploring history, tradition, and people’s links to the land.
Many artists use eco materials and methods to highlight the need to protect landscapes and work sustainably.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: While landscapes often show beautiful scenery, they can express powerful ideas, like climate change, migration, culture, or even identity. Artists use landscapes not just to show what they see, but to say something about how they feel or value.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Landscapes are just pretty pictures of nature, there's not much meaning behind them.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can review the range of ways textile artists have been inspired by landscapes in art.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Greater contextual information on the artist's work can be found in the additional materials. You may wish to alter the imagery to better fit your project themes.

lessonKeywords.description: shapes, patterns, and structures found in the natural world (e.g. shells, plants, bones)
a lack of symmetry; when two sides of something are not identical but still balanced visually

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Artists use nature’s beauty and patterns to create textile works that reflect its structure and complexity.
Nature’s colours and patterns inspire textile designs that connect with viewers both visually and emotionally.
Natural forms in textiles can express emotion or memory, deepening the viewer's connection to the work.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: While some natural forms show symmetry, most have irregular, flowing shapes. Even symmetrical forms often have variations, this is part of what makes nature interesting to artists.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Natural forms are always perfectly symmetrical, like leaves or flowers.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can review the range of ways textile artists have been inspired by natural forms in art.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Artists explore the theme of inside and outside in different ways.
Artists use thresholds, barriers, and liminal spaces to express ideas.
Artists make choices about materials, techniques, and design elements to communicate meaning.
You can reflect on your own connections and ideas through textile art.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Inside and outside can also mean emotional states, identity, or private vs public. Artists use space, scale, and materials to explore physical and psychological boundaries.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Inside and outside just means indoors and outdoors.

lessonKeywords.description: A thing that can be seen or touched; often used in artwork to represent an idea, meaning, or story.
the arrangement of elements in an artwork
to show, mean, or represent something

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Textiles offer rich textures, colours and patterns that evoke touch and emotional engagement in artworks.
Fabric’s flexibility allows techniques like weaving, dyeing and quilting, inspiring creative reinterpretations.
Using traditional objects in textile art connects artists to heritage, preserving and celebrating cultural history.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Objects can be used in a range of ways in art. Objects can be used as a textile art material or as the subject of an artwork. Objects in art often contain symbolic meanings.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Objects in art are only depicted in realistic pictures.

lessonKeywords.description: the focus, topic or image of an artwork e.g. in a portrait the subject is the person who has been painted
the story or message that an artwork communicates about the subject
the use of objects, colours, or imagery to suggest deeper meanings

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Artists use textiles to celebrate diverse identities, culture, and history through fabric and technique.
By integrating textile methods, artists reimagine portraits, blending tradition with contemporary practice.
Artists use layering, stitching, and embellishing to add depth and narrative to portraits and figures.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: While capturing someone’s physical appearance can be part of a portrait, artists often go much deeper. Portraits can reveal who someone is, exploring culture, identity, relationships, life experiences and even social or political themes.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Portraits are just about what someone looks like and mainly focus on capturing a likeness.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can review the range of ways textile artists have been inspired by portraits and figures.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Plastic pollution is one of the biggest threats to the planet.
Artists transform waste into thought-provoking pieces that inspire sustainability.
The manipulation of waste materials can add meaning, deepening the thought provoking effect of the artwork.

lessons.unitTitle: The importance of nature in art

lessonKeywords.description: the visual appearance, structure or constitution of an object, referring to three dimensional objects
built elements such as buildings, streets, roads, parks, and bridges
the relative size or proportion of an object or artwork to its surroundings or itself

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: We can find amazing architectural structures in nature, such as the bees' nest and the snail shell.
Architects have used the structure of organic forms from nature in their building designs.
Drawing from natural forms can inspire architectural designs.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: We can all find new things that inspire us in the world around us.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: There are no new ways to be inspired by nature.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can design an architectural structure which takes inspiration from nature.

teacherTips.teacherTip: The Additional materials contains images to support drawings should you not have access to natural forms.  Recording the development process photographically for pupils' sketchbooks will enable opportunities for later reflection and evaluation.

lessons.unitTitle: The importance of nature in art

lessonKeywords.description: a connection between things that we make in our minds, like when you think of sunshine and holidays together
when an object, or image represents a bigger idea or feeling, it can help us understand deeper meanings in art
to decorate or add extra details to something to make it look nicer or more interesting
liquid clay used like glue to join two pieces of clay together

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Nature can represent themes such as growth, decay, rebirth, and spirituality.
Artists can focus on the moods and ideas that nature evokes, rather than just depicting a scene.
Artists can use natural materials like wood, stone, and clay to create their works.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Simple images or shapes can create associations to themes or ideas.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Only complex images or shapes can create associations.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can create a ceramic tile embelished with nature-inspired patterns and thematic designs.

lessonKeywords.description: looking, noticing and paying attention to something carefully
shapes that do not have straight lines and are found in nature
shapes that have uniform measurements and do not appear in nature
a way to document ideas, observations, and creative processes for future reference or reflection

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Throughout history artists often turn to nature as inspiration.
Artists draw to document ideas, observations, and processes. This can be experimental or from direct observation.
Artists explore nature through representation, as well as literally creating work with and in nature.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Artists can make art in and with nature as well as recording from nature.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Artists inspired by nature can only look carefully at natural forms and record them.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can create art that is inspired by nature using traditional materials and natural elements.

Hello, my name is Mrs. Carter, and I'm gonna be guiding you through our lesson today on art and environmental activism.
We're going to be thinking about how climate change affects the world and how artists work as activists to make change and to inspire others to make change.
You're going to need to do quite a bit of hard thinking and to really share your ideas and think deeply about the topic.
I'm sure we're going to have a fantastic lesson and you're gonna learn lots and lots.
Let's get started.
By the end of today's lesson, you're going to be able to say, "I can create art that inspires strong feelings about important issues." I wonder if you've already got strong feelings about issues to do with climate change and the environment.
We're going to need to use some keywords in today's lesson, and I want to make sure that you feel really comfortable with them.
So, we're going to go through them now.
Imagery.
A group of visual elements, like images to create a specific mood, evoke emotions, or convey deeper meanings.
Microplastics.

We're going to start looking at how we can use sketchbooks to record information.
We're then going to move on to creating a microplastic feast.
Let's get started using sketchbooks to record information.
Many artists create work about important issues going on in the world.
This can take many forms, including art activism.
What important issue do you think these works might be about? Jacob shared that he thinks this work is about climate change.
Laura adds, "Yes, they've used striking imagery." Artists use the power of imagery to communicate difficult realities about our planet.

True or false, artists use the power of imagery to communicate difficult realities about the planet.

Well done.
How did you get on? Great work if you said true.
Artists use the power of imagery to communicate difficult realities about the planet.

Environmental art raises awareness of the harm that we are causing to the planet and it calls us to action.
Selecting the most powerful imagery is an important element in this process.
How do you think artists decide what imagery to use? Sam is answering this question.
"Artists would have to research a lot about the important issue, so that they could select imagery that was powerful and relevant to the facts." Andeep adds, "Yes, and I bet they don't just use the first image they think of.
They must develop and refine their ideas." Where might artists record facts and refine ideas? Have you ever recorded facts and refined ideas in art? Where did you do it? Emma Blake Morsi created posters and billboards for the COP22 conference to raise awareness over safe water, making use of clouds as an impactful imagery.
Marcela Cantuaria created a work called "Abelhas," in 2016 to 2017, and it depicts environmental pollution caused by the textiles industry.
Interestingly, "Abelhas," actually translates to mean bees.
I wonder if you can think why she might have used that term.
Aida Muluneh worked with Wateraid in 2018 to create Water Life, a series of photographs to highlight water scarcity.

Some facts about them include 300 million tons of plastic waste are produced annually, 60% ending up in the environment.
Microplastics pollute the air, soil, and water.
Microplastics enter the food chain from marine wildlife all the way through to humans.
Recent studies have shown microplastics have been found in human blood and lungs.
Apples can have a microplastic content of 195,500 particles per gram.
Did any of those facts surprise you? I know that some of them were quite surprising to me.
This sketchbook page is recording that information in different ways.
We've got a clear title, written facts, and creative imagery.

The first part of this is to read the facts and discuss powerful imagery you could use.

Environmental art that raises awareness using shock tactics includes Chris Jordan's Medway series from 2013, which captures shocking photographs of animal carcasses inside of which plastic can be seen due to the animal's decay.
That work in particular makes you confront visually how plastic is inside of the creatures.
So, John Akomfrah's "Purple," from 2017 is an immersive video installation filmed across 10 countries, which highlights the shocking reality of climate change.
It also helps us to think about how climate change affects the world globally and also sometimes disproportionately.
Okay, another check for understanding, true or false.

In summary of our lesson, Art and environmental activism, we've learned that environmental art raises awareness of the harm we are causing to the planet and calls us to action.
The artists use the power of imagery to communicate difficult realities about the planet.
That many artists use sketchbooks in their practice to record facts, refine ideas, and select the most powerful imagery.
Artists can use either shock tactics or joyful encounters to raise awareness.
Well done for all of your work today.

I look forward to seeing you in our next lesson.

items that are not designed for the purpose of making art, but have been collected from more random sources

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Assemblage involves creating a composition by using found materials. It can be seen as a 3D collage.

lessons.lessonTitle: Planning and developing collage inspired by our hobbies and interests

lessonKeywords.description: in art refer to the factors that shape and inspire an artist's creative choices, style, and overall artistic voice
in art can be an opportunity for discovery and growth, often leading to unexpected and innovative results
the process of evaluating and learning from experiences to refine skills and creative direction

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Artists can find inspiration to develop a personal idea for a collage or assemblage from their interests
Identifying and planning the key aspects of a collage helps build confidence in the process
Selecting a range of materials means there can be playful experimentation before committing to a design

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Planning provides structure but doesn’t mean the design is fixed. Many artists start with an idea but adapt it through experimentation. A plan helps build confidence, but the best results often come from unexpected discoveries along the way.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Planning a collage or assemblage takes away creativity.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can develop a personal collage by planning key elements, experimenting with materials, and drawing inspiration from artists.

teacherTips.teacherTip: This lesson could be adapted to your students' context and local area.

lessons.lessonTitle: Creating and refining an abstract collage

lessonKeywords.description: artwork that does not depict a recognisable picture, place, person or object in the real world.
the area of an artwork that immediately captures your attention. It could be the brightest colour, the sharpest detail, or even the largest subject in the composition.
surrounding or highlighting part of an image to make it stand out, artists can use lines, shapes, colours, or even leave empty space around a subject to draw our attention.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: By refining our collage we can consolidate the idea or meaning
Small additions, like text or embellishments can add interesting details and focus attention
Trimming or creating a frame can pull an artwork together

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Abstract collages don’t need symmetry or recognisable images. The beauty of abstraction lies in experimenting to create something visually engaging which can express ideas or emotions and finding balance through the arrangement.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Abstract collages need to have perfect symmetry or recognisable shapes.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can make an abstract collage, using texture and pattern to compose and frame a strong focal point.

teacherTips.teacherTip: You might want to further develop prior work using photocopies or waste scrap papers in this lesson. This lessons could be personalised to your local area if there is an appropriate local artist you could reference.

lessons.lessonTitle: Exploring collage and composition through portraits

lessonKeywords.description: the use of different elements to create visual interest and complexity in a work, it can can also be created by contrasting elements such as light versus dark
how the visual weight of each element is distributed to make the composition feel stable
the arrangement of, imagery, shapes, colours, textures, marks and lines in an artwork

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: A collage combines varied materials like photos, paper and textures to build layers and create visual depth
Experimenting with composition by arranging and rearranging elements until the layout feels balanced
Collage can be used to explore portraiture which discuss social histories

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Collage is about careful selection, layering and composition to create meaning, tell stories, represent identity and explore social themes.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Collage is just about sticking random images together.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can create a collage portrait by selecting and collaging imagery to achieve a balanced composition.

teacherTips.teacherTip: You may want to have students select imagery in advance of the lesson or bring in photos of themseleves.

lessons.lessonTitle: Connecting and combining: trials and experiments with materials
lessons.unitTitle: First sustained project: working from a theme

lessonKeywords.description: to try out ideas, materials, or techniques
joining two or more different materials, techniques, or ideas
building up an artwork by adding one material or colour on top of another

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Artists often spend time experimenting with the physical properties of materials, such as texture and malleability.
Mixing different materials (e.g. paint and objects, or fabric with metal) allows artists to discover new visual effects.
Artists may develop techniques specific to the materials they are using, including pouring, dripping, or layering.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: In reality, while paint pouring involves chance, artists use technique, colour theory and control to create intentional and successful compositions. It’s both creative and technical.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: A common misconception about paint pouring is that it’s purely random and anyone can do it without skill.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can experiment with combining materials and making a paint pour.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Paint pouring is messy so it is advisable to have protective table coverings and aprons. Coconut hair serum is optional. One small squirt into the top of the prepared cups of layered paint will help to create many cells. Pupils may need to work collaboratively dependent on the space available.

I could mix cell clusters using paint mixed of glue

298
00:13:26.280 --> 00:13:28.530
and stick them down once the paint has dried.

299
00:13:28.530 --> 00:13:31.280
This would create tactile layers."

300
00:13:31.280 --> 00:13:32.587
And Andeep.

301
00:13:32.587 --> 00:13:34.860
"I could add threads to create map contour lines

302
00:13:34.860 --> 00:13:37.620
which I could develop as part of my landscape project.

303
00:13:37.620 --> 00:13:39.240
I could explore different color palettes

304
00:13:39.240 --> 00:13:42.180
and incorporate actual maps to create layers."

305
00:13:42.180 --> 00:13:43.683
Love all these ideas.

306
00:13:46.110 --> 00:13:48.240
Many artists use dripping and pouring techniques

307
00:13:48.240 --> 00:13:50.370
in their artwork, including:

308
00:13:50.370 --> 00:13:53.250
Fahd El Harti creates dripping portraits,

309
00:13:53.250 --> 00:13:56.220
applying paint directly by the brush without contact,

310
00:13:56.220 --> 00:13:59.190
relying on gravity and movement for effect.

311
00:13:59.190 --> 00:14:01.800
Monique Oliver whose work is poured directly from cups,

312
00:14:01.800 --> 00:14:03.000
bowls, or jugs,

313
00:14:03.000 --> 00:14:05.970
rarely using brushes and instead embracing spontaneity

314
00:14:05.970 --> 00:14:07.143
and paint behavior.

315
00:14:08.880 --> 00:14:11.400
For the next part of the lesson, you'll need:

316
00:14:11.400 --> 00:14:16.140
acrylic paint, PVA glue, multipurpose lubricant spray,

317
00:14:16.140 --> 00:14:19.050
heat gun, a surface to pour onto,

318
00:14:19.050 --> 00:14:22.230
a tray to catch the excess paint, stirrers,

319
00:14:22.230 --> 00:14:24.810
and large plastic cups which can be reused.

320
00:14:24.810 --> 00:14:27.000
So pause here while you gather all that you'll need

321
00:14:27.000 --> 00:14:28.600
for the next part of the lesson.

322
00:14:35.940 --> 00:14:37.770
That's great that you have everything you need.

323
00:14:37.770 --> 00:14:38.673
Let's continue.

324
00:14:40.230 --> 00:14:42.958
There are many ways of pouring paint, including:

325
00:14:42.958 --> 00:14:46.200
make the pouring medium using one third PVA,

326
00:14:46.200 --> 00:14:47.550
two thirds water.

327
00:14:47.550 --> 00:14:48.480
Mix thoroughly.

328
00:14:48.480 --> 00:14:49.780
This helps the paint flow.

329
00:14:50.970 --> 00:14:51.930
And then in each cup,

330
00:14:51.930 --> 00:14:53.400
add half a cup pouring medium

331
00:14:53.400 --> 00:14:55.170
with half a cup of paint color.

332
00:14:55.170 --> 00:14:56.043
Mix well.

333
00:14:57.630 --> 00:15:00.180
Once the cup is filled with paint and pouring medium,

334
00:15:00.180 --> 00:15:03.240
add one squirt of multipurpose lubricant spray,

335
00:15:03.240 --> 00:15:05.790
then stir once only.

336
00:15:05.790 --> 00:15:09.300
In each cup, pour layers of pouring medium/color mixtures

337
00:15:09.300 --> 00:15:11.493
on top of each other, starting with white.

338
00:15:12.480 --> 00:15:13.380
In the top of the cup,

339
00:15:13.380 --> 00:15:15.420
the paint will begin to react with the lubricant

340
00:15:15.420 --> 00:15:16.563
and create patterns.

341
00:15:17.970 --> 00:15:19.620
If many cells are wanted,

342
00:15:19.620 --> 00:15:21.690
add one squirt of coconut hair serum

343
00:15:21.690 --> 00:15:24.360
to the layers of paint, but do not stir.

344
00:15:24.360 --> 00:15:26.580
Stirring will cause the colors to merge too much

345
00:15:26.580 --> 00:15:27.453
at this stage.

346
00:15:28.890 --> 00:15:32.520
Position your surface such as a wooden board onto four cups

347
00:15:32.520 --> 00:15:35.163
or jars of equal height and stand in a tray.

348
00:15:37.445 --> 00:15:39.780
It is important that the jars/cups are level,

349
00:15:39.780 --> 00:15:41.430
otherwise the paint will run off one side

350
00:15:41.430 --> 00:15:42.513
after being poured.

351
00:15:44.190 --> 00:15:47.700
Place the board on top of the filled cup and flip over,

352
00:15:47.700 --> 00:15:50.073
keeping the cup securely in position.

353
00:15:52.165 --> 00:15:53.190
Lift the cup,

354
00:15:53.190 --> 00:15:54.630
allowing the paint to pour out

355
00:15:54.630 --> 00:15:56.643
and move around on the surface.

356
00:15:57.990 --> 00:16:00.450
Gently tilt the canvas so that the paint moves around

357
00:16:00.450 --> 00:16:01.503
on the surface.

358
00:16:03.630 --> 00:16:05.910
Allow the paint to drip off the edges of the canvas

359
00:16:05.910 --> 00:16:06.753
into the tray.

360
00:16:08.190 --> 00:16:10.290
The paint can be given a quick blast with a heat gun

361
00:16:10.290 --> 00:16:12.660
to encourage cells to appear in the paint.

362
00:16:12.660 --> 00:16:14.523
Alternatively, you can leave to dry.

363
00:16:16.320 --> 00:16:19.380
There are many ways to explore pouring techniques.

364
00:16:19.380 --> 00:16:21.990
Paint can also be poured quickly into a sink strainer

365
00:16:21.990 --> 00:16:23.283
in a clockwise motion.

366
00:16:24.990 --> 00:16:26.460
Once all the paint has been poured,

367
00:16:26.460 --> 00:16:28.810
the sink strainer can be lifted out of the way.

368
00:16:30.030 --> 00:16:34.470
This technique creates beautiful patterns, as we can see.

369
00:16:34.470 --> 00:16:37.650
The first color put into the pouring cup comes out last,

370
00:16:37.650 --> 00:16:39.550
ending up in the center of the design.

371
00:16:41.760 --> 00:16:43.800
Check for understanding, true or false?

372
00:16:43.800 --> 00:16:46.740
You must thin the paint before pouring to help it flow.

373
00:16:46.740 --> 00:16:48.633
Decide if this is true or false.

374
00:16:55.590 --> 00:16:57.510
Well done if you selected true.

375
00:16:57.510 --> 00:16:59.580
Now I'd like you to say a little more about your answer.

376
00:16:59.580 --> 00:17:01.083
Pause here while you do this.

377
00:17:09.000 --> 00:17:11.070
Perhaps you said something like this.

378
00:17:11.070 --> 00:17:12.930
Paint is usually mixed with a pouring medium

379
00:17:12.930 --> 00:17:15.513
as the paint would be too thick to move around.

380
00:17:17.730 --> 00:17:19.470
And now it's time for your next task.

381
00:17:19.470 --> 00:17:20.640
Create a paint pour.

382
00:17:20.640 --> 00:17:21.690
You should:

383
00:17:21.690 --> 00:17:24.810
choose a combination of colors that work well together.

384
00:17:24.810 --> 00:17:28.500
Choose a small canvas or small piece of board to pour onto.

385
00:17:28.500 --> 00:17:30.570
Have the water pots or plastic cups set up

386
00:17:30.570 --> 00:17:32.790
beforehand in the tray.

387
00:17:32.790 --> 00:17:35.130
Wear suitable gloves to protect your hands.

388
00:17:35.130 --> 00:17:37.710
So pause here while you have a go at this task.

389
00:17:37.710 --> 00:17:40.620
Enjoy, enjoy, enjoy creating a paint pour,

390
00:17:40.620 --> 00:17:42.053
I'll see you when you're finished.

391
00:17:48.570 --> 00:17:49.680
It's great to be back with you.

392
00:17:49.680 --> 00:17:52.170
How did you get on with creating a paint pour?

393
00:17:52.170 --> 00:17:53.883
There are many possible outcomes.

394
00:17:55.096 --> 00:17:57.690
And here we can see the paint was given a quick blast

395
00:17:57.690 --> 00:18:01.560
with the heat gun to encourage cells to appear in the paint.

396
00:18:01.560 --> 00:18:02.703
Really effective.

397
00:18:03.960 --> 00:18:04.793
Here's Jacob.

398
00:18:04.793 --> 00:18:06.840
"I chose to try the sink strainer method.

399
00:18:06.840 --> 00:18:09.300
I love how the color combination worked out.

400
00:18:09.300 --> 00:18:10.860
By adding glue to the cup first

401
00:18:10.860 --> 00:18:13.833
it meant that it came out last and ended up in the center.

402
00:18:14.940 --> 00:18:15.873
Just stunning.

403
00:18:17.460 --> 00:18:18.293
And Sophia.

404
00:18:18.293 --> 00:18:20.310
"I'm pleased with how my pour came out.

405
00:18:20.310 --> 00:18:22.140
I could experiment further with this technique

406
00:18:22.140 --> 00:18:25.020
using different color choices and different surfaces."

407
00:18:25.020 --> 00:18:25.983
You really could.

408
00:18:27.690 --> 00:18:29.520
In our lesson, connecting and combining:

409
00:18:29.520 --> 00:18:31.200
trials and experiments with materials

410
00:18:31.200 --> 00:18:32.790
we've covered the following.

411
00:18:32.790 --> 00:18:35.100
Many artists explore and experiment

412
00:18:35.100 --> 00:18:37.050
by combining a range of materials

413
00:18:37.050 --> 00:18:39.180
to see how they behave and interact.

414
00:18:39.180 --> 00:18:41.550
This hands-on exploration reflects how artists

415
00:18:41.550 --> 00:18:44.640
often develop ideas using mixed-media and layering

416
00:18:44.640 --> 00:18:47.163
rather than starting with a final outcome in mind.

417
00:18:48.930 --> 00:18:51.000
Artists pour paint to explore fluid movement,

418
00:18:51.000 --> 00:18:52.380
chance, and layering,

419
00:18:52.380 --> 00:18:53.970
allowing colors to blend naturally

420
00:18:53.970 --> 00:18:55.710
and create expressive effects

421
00:18:55.710 --> 00:18:57.783
that can't be achieved with a brush.

422
00:18:59.340 --> 00:19:01.410
Well done everyone for joining with this lesson.

423
00:19:01.410 --> 00:19:04.469
I loved exploring all the different ways we can connect

424
00:19:04.469 --> 00:19:06.810
and combine materials

425
00:19:06.810 --> 00:19:09.450
and all these different effects that we can create.

426
00:19:09.450 --> 00:19:12.060
I hope you enjoyed your paintful

427
00:19:12.060 --> 00:19:14.880
and these wonderful, wonderful creations

428
00:19:14.880 --> 00:19:16.380
that you've brought into being

429
00:19:16.380 --> 00:19:18.580
through these fantastic choices you've made.

430
00:19:19.470 --> 00:19:20.700
I've really enjoyed teaching you,

431
00:19:20.700 --> 00:19:23.250
and I hope you've enjoyed this lesson too.

432
00:19:23.250 --> 00:19:25.740
And I look forward to seeing you at another art lesson soon.

433
00:19:25.740 --> 00:19:27.423
Until then, stay creative.

lessons.lessonTitle: Presenting a portfolio: creating pages of documentation
lessons.unitTitle: First sustained project: working from a theme

lessonKeywords.description: a collection of your artwork, sketchbook work, experiments, and final pieces
the main idea, theme, or approach you choose to explore in depth
the big idea or subject that your artwork is based on
the story or journey shown through your artwork and sketchbook

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Decide on the theme or focus of your portfolio to highlight specific skills, projects, or a particular artistic style.
Select your most interesting work that aligns with your portfolio’s focus aiming for quality over quantity.
Showcase a range of styles, techniques, or themes to demonstrate your versatility and depth as an artist.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: It's much better to select work that clearly shows your ideas, development, artistic journey and skills.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: A common misconception about portfolios is that you need to include everything you've made.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can select a focus for my portfolio and create a narrative through the pieces chosen.

teacherTips.teacherTip: When selecting work for your portfolio, choose pieces that show your progress, creativity, and decision-making, not just the ones that look the most finished.

lessons.lessonTitle: Effective annotation: different ways to present ideas
lessons.unitTitle: First sustained project: working from a theme

lessonKeywords.description: a plan, idea or intention
adding notes, labels, or explanations to show your thinking, choices and ideas
electronic technology

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Quick sketches or diagrams can be used to illustrate concepts visually, making complex ideas more accessible.
Annotations can explain thoughts, processes, or decisions related to specific elements of a design.
Digital software tools can be used to annotate directly on images, documents, or presentations.
Videos, audio clips, or interactive slideshows help to engage the audience and present ideas dynamically.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Annotation can be short notes, labels, sketches, diagrams, or even audio recordings. It’s any way you add extra information to explain your ideas clearly.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Annotation has to be long, written paragraphs.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can present annotation effectively in a variety of ways.

teacherTips.teacherTip: It would be beneficial to have access to digital software for those students who prefer to annotate digitally

lessons.lessonTitle: Resourcing ideas through personal reflections, narratives and objects
lessons.unitTitle: First sustained project: working from a theme

lessonKeywords.description: think deeply about
the practice or art of telling stories
include or add something into another thing
where more than one medium or material has been used

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Reflect upon personal experiences, emotions and memories as sources of inspiration.
Draw from personal or fictional narratives to create a strong foundation for artwork.
Incorporate found objects to inspire and add layers of meaning to artwork.
Combine resources to create rich mixed media outcomes.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Many artists find that exploring difficult life experiences can lead to meaningful creative work.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Negative life experiences cannot be used as inspiration for creating artwork.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can reflect on personal experiences and narratives, incorporating these into my creative practice.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Support pupils to reflect upon their sources of inspiration.

lessons.unitTitle: First sustained project: working from a theme

lessonKeywords.description: your purpose or reason for making an artwork
how an artist reacts to a theme, idea, artist, or piece of work
the practical skills and methods you use to create your artwork

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Reflecting on whether the personal response effectively communicates the message or emotion intended.
Assessing whether the overall composition feels balanced and cohesive and that the elements work harmoniously together.
Evaluating and refining the technical aspects of a personal response.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Technical skill also includes mastery of materials, control of techniques and the ability to use those skills effectively in any style, whether abstract, expressive, or conceptual.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: A common misconception about technical aspects in art is that technical skill only means making artworks look realistic.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can make an artwork to communicate my intention and evaluate the technical aspects.

teacherTips.teacherTip: When discussing technical skill, remind students that it’s not just about neatness or realism, it's about how effectively they use materials and techniques to support their ideas. Encourage a wide range of technical strengths, from expressive mark-making to confident use of texture or layering

contentGuidance.contentGuidanceArea: Physical activity and equipment requiring safe use
contentGuidance.contentGuidanceLabel: Risk assessment required - equipment
contentGuidance.contentGuidanceDescription: Use of equipment that may require supervision for safety, e.g. scissors in KS1, needles, paint, knives, cooking.

lessons.lessonTitle: Evaluate the use of materials and techniques
lessons.unitTitle: First sustained project: working from a theme

lessonKeywords.description: the physical substances or tools an artist uses to create their work
the specific method or way an artist uses materials to create their work
to carefully judge or assess something by considering its strengths, weaknesses, and overall effectiveness
doing something with a clear goal, reason, or intention

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Reflecting on the impact of materials on artwork helps artists create informed creative decisions
Analysing the characteristics of materials encourages material choices to support conceptual or thematic communication
Evaluating and documenting the challenges encountered with materials leads to purposeful making

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: The quality of the outcome depends more on how materials are used, combined, and manipulated, rather than their cost or brand.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Expensive or professional materials automatically produce better artwork.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can evaluate the impact of different materials and reflect on their strengths and limitations.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Encourage pupils to test materials in small experiments before committing to them in a final outcome—this builds confidence, reduces waste, and often leads to unexpected creative discoveries.

I tried drawing with biro, which I felt I could control,

223
00:10:53.220 --> 00:10:55.617
then added areas of acrylic ink."

224
00:10:57.030 --> 00:10:58.503
Great choices, Alex.

225
00:10:59.700 --> 00:11:01.950
And now we're onto our next learning cycle,

226
00:11:01.950 --> 00:11:05.373
evaluating the success and challenges of materials.

227
00:11:06.600 --> 00:11:09.873
Many artists face challenges using materials and techniques.

228
00:11:10.740 --> 00:11:13.770
It's common for our materials to behave unpredictably,

229
00:11:13.770 --> 00:11:16.200
which can influence both the creative process

230
00:11:16.200 --> 00:11:17.613
and the final outcome.

231
00:11:18.960 --> 00:11:21.990
Struggling with materials or techniques isn't failure.

232
00:11:21.990 --> 00:11:24.810
It's how artists learn what works.

233
00:11:24.810 --> 00:11:27.063
Magical mistakes, I sometimes call them.

234
00:11:28.860 --> 00:11:31.590
Common challenges of art materials.

235
00:11:31.590 --> 00:11:33.000
Paper and card.

236
00:11:33.000 --> 00:11:35.940
It tears easily when wet or overworked.

237
00:11:35.940 --> 00:11:38.070
I wonder if you've had that experience.

238
00:11:38.070 --> 00:11:40.803
Warping and buckling when glue or paint is applied.

239
00:11:42.060 --> 00:11:43.320
Paint.

240
00:11:43.320 --> 00:11:46.290
The acrylic dries too fast to blend easily.

241
00:11:46.290 --> 00:11:49.263
Streaking or brush marks can appear unintentionally.

242
00:11:50.370 --> 00:11:52.143
Coverage can be unpredictable.

243
00:11:53.730 --> 00:11:55.650
Textiles and stitching.

244
00:11:55.650 --> 00:11:58.920
Fraying edges, especially with loose weaves.

245
00:11:58.920 --> 00:12:00.993
Needles or threads can tear paper.

246
00:12:02.490 --> 00:12:04.230
Inks and pens.

247
00:12:04.230 --> 00:12:06.210
Bleeding through paper,

248
00:12:06.210 --> 00:12:07.713
smudging before drying,

249
00:12:08.730 --> 00:12:10.893
permanent marks which cannot be undone.

250
00:12:12.720 --> 00:12:14.040
Clay.

251
00:12:14.040 --> 00:12:16.320
Cracking as it dries,

252
00:12:16.320 --> 00:12:18.693
heavy and fragile once fired or set,

253
00:12:19.680 --> 00:12:23.253
takes time to dry/fire before being able to paint or glaze.

254
00:12:24.690 --> 00:12:26.820
Mixed-media combinations.

255
00:12:26.820 --> 00:12:28.623
Some materials don't adhere well.

256
00:12:29.460 --> 00:12:33.150
Differences in flexibility or absorbency can cause warping,

257
00:12:33.150 --> 00:12:34.713
cracking, or separation.

258
00:12:35.760 --> 00:12:39.153
Hard to predict how different materials will react or age.

259
00:12:40.800 --> 00:12:42.630
Let's have a check for understanding.

260
00:12:42.630 --> 00:12:44.910
Why is it important to test materials

261
00:12:44.910 --> 00:12:47.490
before using them in final work?

262
00:12:47.490 --> 00:12:50.163
Is it A, to use up old supplies,

263
00:12:51.060 --> 00:12:53.373
B, to see how they behave,

264
00:12:54.450 --> 00:12:57.540
or C, to copy someone else's idea?

265
00:12:57.540 --> 00:12:59.640
Pause here while you decide why it's important

266
00:12:59.640 --> 00:13:02.913
to test materials before using them in final work.

267
00:13:11.490 --> 00:13:13.260
Well done if you selected answer B.

268
00:13:13.260 --> 00:13:16.170
Indeed, it's important to test materials before using them

269
00:13:16.170 --> 00:13:18.633
in final work to see how they behave.

270
00:13:21.150 --> 00:13:23.940
Some artists are well known for experimenting with materials

271
00:13:23.940 --> 00:13:25.950
as part of their creative process,

272
00:13:25.950 --> 00:13:28.500
including Jessica Stockholder,

273
00:13:28.500 --> 00:13:30.750
who combines blending painting, sculpture,

274
00:13:30.750 --> 00:13:33.990
and everyday objects in vivid installations.

275
00:13:33.990 --> 00:13:35.640
She sources extension cords,

276
00:13:35.640 --> 00:13:38.250
buckets, carpet, stools, and plastic containers

277
00:13:38.250 --> 00:13:41.703
and assembles them into large-scale installations.

278
00:13:42.690 --> 00:13:45.360
Veronica Ryan, who uses natural materials,

279
00:13:45.360 --> 00:13:49.200
seeds, fruit shapes, thread, plaster to explore memory,

280
00:13:49.200 --> 00:13:50.703
migration, and healing.

281
00:13:51.750 --> 00:13:54.870
And Jeff Koons, known for using industrial processes

282
00:13:54.870 --> 00:13:58.680
and materials like stainless steel with mirror finishes,

283
00:13:58.680 --> 00:14:02.193
which blurs lines between craft, design, and fine art.

284
00:14:03.060 --> 00:14:05.850
So these are just some artists who are well known

285
00:14:05.850 --> 00:14:07.260
for experimenting with materials

286
00:14:07.260 --> 00:14:09.333
as part of their creative process.

287
00:14:10.890 --> 00:14:14.340
What does it mean to evaluate the materials used in artwork?

288
00:14:14.340 --> 00:14:15.600
Pause here and share with someone.

289
00:14:15.600 --> 00:14:16.500
What do you think?

290
00:14:24.570 --> 00:14:26.220
Thanks for sharing.

291
00:14:26.220 --> 00:14:28.020
To evaluate the materials used means

292
00:14:28.020 --> 00:14:30.300
to carefully assess how they behaved

293
00:14:30.300 --> 00:14:33.000
and responded during the creative process.

294
00:14:33.000 --> 00:14:34.770
How they contributed to the success

295
00:14:34.770 --> 00:14:36.720
of the final outcome matters.

296
00:14:36.720 --> 00:14:38.670
It really does.

297
00:14:38.670 --> 00:14:40.950
Why does evaluating materials matter?

298
00:14:40.950 --> 00:14:42.270
Pause here and share with someone.

299
00:14:42.270 --> 00:14:43.203
What do you think?

300
00:14:48.660 --> 00:14:50.160
Thanks for sharing.

301
00:14:50.160 --> 00:14:53.010
Evaluating materials improves future work.

302
00:14:53.010 --> 00:14:54.930
Understanding how materials behave

303
00:14:54.930 --> 00:14:57.030
helps you make better choices next time,

304
00:14:57.030 --> 00:14:58.443
improving your results.

305
00:14:59.850 --> 00:15:02.670
Evaluating materials supports problem solving.

306
00:15:02.670 --> 00:15:05.580
Evaluating reveals what worked well and what didn't,

307
00:15:05.580 --> 00:15:08.763
guiding you to adjust techniques or try alternatives.

308
00:15:10.470 --> 00:15:13.710
Evaluating materials deepens artistic intent.

309
00:15:13.710 --> 00:15:16.620
Reflecting on materials connects technical decisions

310
00:15:16.620 --> 00:15:18.993
to the meaning or feeling you want to convey.

311
00:15:21.390 --> 00:15:23.700
Evaluating materials builds confidence.

312
00:15:23.700 --> 00:15:26.310
Knowing how materials respond boosts your confidence

313
00:15:26.310 --> 00:15:28.770
to experiment and take creative risks.

314
00:15:28.770 --> 00:15:30.213
It's what art is all about.

315
00:15:32.010 --> 00:15:34.410
Evaluating materials documents your process.

316
00:15:34.410 --> 00:15:35.730
Keeping track of successes

317
00:15:35.730 --> 00:15:37.650
and challenges creates a record

318
00:15:37.650 --> 00:15:40.230
that supports your growth and learning journey.

319
00:15:40.230 --> 00:15:42.230
Perhaps you had some answers like these.

320
00:15:44.370 --> 00:15:45.780
Let's have a check for understanding.

321
00:15:45.780 --> 00:15:47.100
True or false,

322
00:15:47.100 --> 00:15:50.190
evaluating materials can help you solve problems you had

323
00:15:50.190 --> 00:15:51.870
during your process.

324
00:15:51.870 --> 00:15:52.950
Pause here and decide.

325
00:15:52.950 --> 00:15:54.693
Is this true or false?

326
00:16:02.670 --> 00:16:04.710
Well done if you selected true.

327
00:16:04.710 --> 00:16:07.470
And now I'd like you to say a little more about your answer.

328
00:16:07.470 --> 00:16:09.033
Pause here while you do this.

329
00:16:16.470 --> 00:16:18.510
Perhaps you said something like this.

330
00:16:18.510 --> 00:16:20.850
It helps you solve problems during your process

331
00:16:20.850 --> 00:16:23.160
because it lets you understand what caused issues

332
00:16:23.160 --> 00:16:24.960
so you can adjust your techniques

333
00:16:24.960 --> 00:16:27.123
or choose different materials next time.

334
00:16:28.740 --> 00:16:30.900
And now we're onto our next task.

335
00:16:30.900 --> 00:16:32.780
Evaluate the success and challenges

336
00:16:32.780 --> 00:16:35.850
of materials used in your artwork.

337
00:16:35.850 --> 00:16:38.430
The evaluation could be made digitally, written,

338
00:16:38.430 --> 00:16:40.083
or recorded as voice notes.

339
00:16:41.160 --> 00:16:42.540
Observe carefully.

340
00:16:42.540 --> 00:16:45.180
Pay attention to how each material behaves,

341
00:16:45.180 --> 00:16:48.210
its texture, drying time, flexibility,

342
00:16:48.210 --> 00:16:50.433
and how it interacts with other materials.

343
00:16:51.360 --> 00:16:52.860
Evaluate honestly.

344
00:16:52.860 --> 00:16:55.170
Think about what worked well and what didn't.

345
00:16:55.170 --> 00:16:56.580
Challenges are part of learning,

346
00:16:56.580 --> 00:17:00.063
so don't be afraid to note mistakes or unexpected results.

347
00:17:01.140 --> 00:17:02.700
And connect to your outcome.

348
00:17:02.700 --> 00:17:05.730
Evaluate how the materials affected the look, feel,

349
00:17:05.730 --> 00:17:07.440
and meaning of your artwork

350
00:17:07.440 --> 00:17:10.893
and how this influences your choices in future projects.

351
00:17:12.030 --> 00:17:15.270
So pause here while you have a go at evaluating the success

352
00:17:15.270 --> 00:17:17.943
and challenges of materials used in your artwork.

353
00:17:19.320 --> 00:17:20.993
I'll see you when you're finished.

354
00:17:28.410 --> 00:17:29.670
It's good to be back with you.

355
00:17:29.670 --> 00:17:33.270
How did you get on with that task of evaluating the success

356
00:17:33.270 --> 00:17:36.450
and challenges and materials used in your artwork?

357
00:17:36.450 --> 00:17:38.197
Let's hear from Jun.

358
00:17:38.197 --> 00:17:39.870
"With my mixed media cells,

359
00:17:39.870 --> 00:17:43.710
I experimented with acrylic paint, PVA, and hot glue.

360
00:17:43.710 --> 00:17:45.900
I found the hot glue quite hard to control,

361
00:17:45.900 --> 00:17:47.550
but it did stick well.

362
00:17:47.550 --> 00:17:49.470
I tried adding color to the hot glue,

363
00:17:49.470 --> 00:17:52.017
which took many attempts using different paints."

364
00:17:53.490 --> 00:17:54.877
And let's hear from Izzy.

365
00:17:54.877 --> 00:17:57.180
"I chose to make a mixed media tree

366
00:17:57.180 --> 00:17:59.310
stitched onto layered paper.

367
00:17:59.310 --> 00:18:01.080
It was a challenge not to tear the paper,

368
00:18:01.080 --> 00:18:04.050
which I resolved once I got the tension right.

369
00:18:04.050 --> 00:18:06.930
I learnt that it was better to stitch into thicker layers.

370
00:18:06.930 --> 00:18:08.640
I'm pleased with the effect as it has a lot

371
00:18:08.640 --> 00:18:10.407
of texture and interest."

372
00:18:13.530 --> 00:18:15.240
Pause here and share with someone your impressions

373
00:18:15.240 --> 00:18:17.553
of Izzy's finished artwork.

374
00:18:25.410 --> 00:18:27.480
Thanks for sharing your impressions.

375
00:18:27.480 --> 00:18:28.950
And finally, I'd like you to share

376
00:18:28.950 --> 00:18:30.090
with each other your artwork,

377
00:18:30.090 --> 00:18:32.100
but not to share what were your successes

378
00:18:32.100 --> 00:18:35.280
and challenges of the materials you used,

379
00:18:35.280 --> 00:18:38.880
but see if the other person can have a go at working out

380
00:18:38.880 --> 00:18:40.500
what perhaps some of those successes

381
00:18:40.500 --> 00:18:41.820
or challenges might have been

382
00:18:41.820 --> 00:18:43.830
just by looking at your artwork.

383
00:18:43.830 --> 00:18:45.280
Pause here while you do this.

384
00:18:54.900 --> 00:18:56.450
Thanks for having a go at that.

385
00:18:57.600 --> 00:19:00.150
I wonder if you were able to accurately work out

386
00:19:00.150 --> 00:19:01.710
the successes and challenges

387
00:19:01.710 --> 00:19:04.413
of the materials used in each other's artworks.

388
00:19:06.090 --> 00:19:09.480
In our lesson Evaluate the Use of Materials and Techniques,

389
00:19:09.480 --> 00:19:11.640
we've covered the following.

390
00:19:11.640 --> 00:19:13.140
Many artists explore

391
00:19:13.140 --> 00:19:15.330
and experiment with different techniques

392
00:19:15.330 --> 00:19:17.070
and materials purposefully

393
00:19:17.070 --> 00:19:20.130
to understand how they behave and interact.

394
00:19:20.130 --> 00:19:23.430
This practical hands-on approach reflects the way artists

395
00:19:23.430 --> 00:19:25.860
often often develop ideas through testing, combining,

396
00:19:25.860 --> 00:19:27.690
and layering rather than beginning

397
00:19:27.690 --> 00:19:29.373
with a fixed final outcome.

398
00:19:31.440 --> 00:19:33.450
Evaluation is important in analyzing

399
00:19:33.450 --> 00:19:35.160
how effectively chosen materials

400
00:19:35.160 --> 00:19:38.220
and techniques contributed to the intended concept

401
00:19:38.220 --> 00:19:39.453
or visual outcome.

402
00:19:40.680 --> 00:19:42.900
Well done everyone for joining in with this lesson.

403
00:19:42.900 --> 00:19:46.920
It was great to explore materials, how they react,

404
00:19:46.920 --> 00:19:51.540
what they get up to when combined, when layered, and so on.

405
00:19:51.540 --> 00:19:53.400
And great to get into that analysis

406
00:19:53.400 --> 00:19:57.060
and really looking at how your materials have played

407
00:19:57.060 --> 00:20:00.660
a part in creating your final outcome.

408
00:20:00.660 --> 00:20:02.160
I hope you've enjoyed this lesson,

409
00:20:02.160 --> 00:20:03.810
I've really enjoyed teaching you,

410
00:20:03.810 --> 00:20:05.100
and I'm looking forward to seeing you

411
00:20:05.100 --> 00:20:06.930
at another art lesson soon.

412
00:20:06.930 --> 00:20:08.733
Until then, stay creative.

lessons.transcript_sentences:
Hello everyone.
How are you today? I hope you're feeling really, really good.
My name is Ms. Sassal, and I'll be your art teacher for this lesson, which I am very pleased about because today we're looking at artists and designers who're such inspiring people.
Our lesson is called "The Work of Artists and Designers.
The Elements of Art." and our lesson comes from the unit of work.
"First Sustained Project Working From a Theme." So if you are ready to get into this topic and have some energy, focus and enthusiasm, we'll begin.
The outcome for today's lesson is I can analyze how artists use materials to communicate a theme and experiment with materials to express my own theme.
There are some keywords in our lesson.
They are element, analyze, and theme.
Let's find out what these words mean.
Element, the elements of art are the basic parts used to make artwork.
Analyze, to look closely at the different parts of an artwork.
And theme, the main idea or message that an artwork communicates.
These are our keywords, let's look out and listen out for them.
They'll be coming up in our lesson today.
Our lesson is called The Work of Artists and Designers, Elements of Art, and it has two learning cycles, analyzing the impact of the elements in artwork.
And examining how material choices can serve a theme.
Let's begin by analyzing the impact of the elements in artwork.
So let's begin with this question.
How do artists create mood and meaning in their work? Pause here and share with someone.
What do you think? Thanks for sharing your ideas.
And now let's take a look at this artwork.
What mood does this image evoke? Does the subject matter affect your decision? And do the colors influence the impact? Pause here while you answer these questions.
Thanks for sharing.
Artists create mood and meaning in their work through a combination of elements, materials, and techniques.
Can you remember what some of the elements of art are? Pause here and share with someone.
Thanks for sharing.
Let's have a look at them.
We've got color, form, line, pattern, shape, texture, and tone.
I wonder if you came up with some of these.
Artists sometimes use limited palettes to influence how a viewer feels.
How have the colored elements influence the mood of this portrait? Pause here and share with someone.
Thanks for sharing.
June and Izzy are analyzing the portrait of the blue lady.
I think the lady looks sad in a portrait, but I think that's because of her expression as her mouth has turned down.
And Izzy, as people age, their mouth might turn down naturally, and that doesn't necessarily mean they're sad, but I think the color blue gives this portrait a low mood.
Wonder if you had similar thoughts.
Through careful choices and combination of elements like color, artists shape how we experience their work emotionally.
Warm colors, reds, oranges, yellows can create feelings of warmth, energy, or urgency.

00:11:39.090 --> 00:11:41.610
